#2801. Dolphins news: Reactions to Miami’s Week 10 loss to the Colts

The Miami Dolphins lost to the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday, falling 24-22 and dropping to 1-8 in 2026. The game featured Miami starting a quarterback in his NFL debut, a shuffle among the defensive tackles due to injuries, an All-Pro center dealing with a conucssion, and a starting wide receiver missing the game due to injury. Yet, none of those were the reason behind Miami's two-point loss.

Football is a team sport, and there are always moments on offense and defense that could have been executed better. The Dolphins' offense gave up a defensive touchdown on a sack fumble – not ideal. The defense could have been tougher against the run, stopping Jonathan Taylor and Seth McGowan from leading the team to over 170 yards on the ground. But, even with those issues, Miami was within two points of pulling off the upset win.

Miami did enough to win on offense and defense. They fell apart on special teams, specifically with placekicking. Kicker Zane Gonzalez missed a 47-yard field goal in the first quarter. After connecting on a 53-yard kick, he missed an extra point in the third quarter. He also missed a 51-yard field goal in the fourth quarter. Miami lost seven points on three kicks from Gonzalez. Even the extra point would have changed things; a converted extra point in the third quarter could have let Miami kick a tying extra point in the fourth quarter instead of attempting a failed two-point conversion.

Maybe it is too harsh to blame the loss on a single player, but Gonzalez missed kicks Miami had to have, and this is not the first misses he has had recently. Gonzalez has struggled since joining the Dolphins, first on the practice squad, then being promoted to the active roster for Sunday. In four games, he is 6-for-10 on field goal attempts and 6-for-7 on extra points. Gonzalez has also struggled on kickoffs, leading Miami to move to punter Bradley Pinion to handle those responsibilities.

Miami should have come out of Indianapolis with a win. It was there for the taking. They just could not connect on the kicks that would have changed the result. The kicking woes were among the top talking points around the web following the game.

#2800. Not a cold streak; the Utah Jazz are historically bad

When the buzzer sounded on San Antonio's 110-102 win in Salt Lake City, the reigning Western Conference champions tallied their 12th consecutive win, pushing their record to an NBA-leading 12-2. The Utah Jazz, losers of Sunday's Delta Center duel, likewise extended an active streak of 12 games. 12 losses in a row.

12 straight losses are tied for the second-longest losing streak in franchise history, but that's not even the worst part of this all.

This is only the second time the Jazz have started a season 1-13. The first time? The Jazz played their home games in New Orleans, Louisiana, and were playing their very first season as an NBA franchise. That 1974-75 team opened the season with a 1-16 record and fired head coach Scotty Robertson following their 14th loss.

This Utah Jazz team isn't just bad — they're historically bad.

Yes, this year's team has been playing at a deficit when it comes to injuries. They would have likely picked up a few more wins to this point were Jaren Jackson Jr., Jusuf Nurkic, and Lauri Markkanen not seated courtside, modeling the Polo Fall 2026 line at the end of the bench. Even so, Utah's foundation is riddled with cracks and is nowhere near the level of a playoff participant.

Undersized at the wing, Utah is consistently out-physicaled and outdone athletically against every team they've faced.

It's not all bad news, though. The Jazz's stars and veterans are all expected to return in a month or so, and they have already faced each of the Western Conference's top-six teams. After facing this slate in the early season, Utah's schedule will only get easier:

Even at full strength, Utah couldn't have reasonably expected to escape that gauntlet with a winning record.

The biggest issue facing the Jazz right now isn't injuries. It isn't inexperience. It isn't even personnel. The Jazz simply don't know how to win — they've never tried before.

It's a team that has grown accustomed to losing for the last four years, and those habits have reappeared night after night.

They took San Antonio and New Orleans into overtime, only to concede a 12-0 run in each of those additional five-minute periods. They fumbled away a 10-point third-quarter lead against Houston but clawed back to within one point at the 2:46 mark, only to relinquish a 2-8 run in crunch time. Down just one point against Memphis with one minute remaining, Utah failed to score again. Behind LA by one point with three minutes to go, the Jazz still couldn't seal the deal with JJJ and Markkanen active.

They've put themself in a position to win several times, but only once did they hold on to win.

How's this for glass-half-empty: Utah is one Dejounte Murray jumper away from being 0-14.

The Jazz front office continues to back Will Hardy as head coach, determined to support the man who patiently endured four years of non-competitive basketball to lead Utah back into the playoffs when the time is right. Just as Utah's roster is learning how to win in a competitive NBA, Hardy's baptism by fire has likewise left him a bit seared.

Now is not the time to take drastic measures — still 68 games to go in the season — but Utah's issues are buried much deeper than a string of bad luck.

Calvin Barrett is the Associate Editor for SLC Dunk and a Utah Jazz columnist for the Standard-Examiner. Originally from Springville, Utah, he currently writes from his desk in Japan.

#2796. 49ers stun Cowboys, Chiefs and Bengals impress - NFL week 10

The NFL's brightest stars lit up week 10 of the 2026 season with some astonishing plays on Sunday.

The likes of Brock Purdy, Christian McCaffrey, Patrick Mahomes, Jahmyr Gibbs and Ja'Marr Chase showcased their skills with some explosive action to help their teams to victory.

The San Francisco 49ers produced a historic display in Dallas while there were also big wins for the Kansas City Chiefs, Detroit Lions and Cincinnati Bengals.

It means the 49ers and Buffalo Bills continue to share the league's best record (8-1), while five teams moved to 7-2, including the in-form Jacksonville Jaguars.

Christian McCaffrey scored his final touchdown just as the San Francisco 49ers' general manager John Lynch made his way to the sideline in the fourth quarter [Getty Images]

The San Francisco 49ers and Dallas Cowboys have a fierce rivalry stretching back to the 1990s and they delivered another classic with a shootout in Texas.

Brock Purdy showed why he is among the leading contenders for the Most Valuable Player award as the 49ers won 46-40, racking up 584 yards of offence - the most Dallas have ever allowed at home.

San Francisco had three touchdowns of more than 65 yards, while Purdy threw for a career-high 389 yards and three touchdowns. The quarterback even blocked for one of the 49ers' other three scores, a 70-yard run by Deebo Samuel on a reverse trick play.

The highlights were two Purdy passes to Christian McCaffrey. The first saw Purdy show remarkable poise as he scrambled out of the pocket before finding McCaffrey for a 74-yard score, while the second was a perfectly-executed play over the middle that saw McCaffrey sprint in untouched from 66 yards.

Dual-threat running back McCaffrey finished with three scores and 223 total yards, including a career-high 161 receiving yards.

Purdy's MVP rival Josh Allen had a relatively quiet game as the Buffalo Bills won 31-12 at the New York Jets, while the Jacksonville Jaguars won 40-23 at the Tennessee Titans.

Including the end of last season, the Jaguars have won 15 of their past 17 regular-season games and must be considered Super Bowl contenders, especially after bringing in three key defensive players before the trade deadline on Tuesday.

Joe Burrow became the new MVP favourite last week and continued his superb form as the Cincinnati Bengals romped to a 38-18 win in their divisional match-up against the Pittsburgh Steelers.

New Manchester United boss Mauricio Pochettino was among the crowd as Burrow was involved in four touchdowns for the fifth straight game, tying an NFL record.

The Bengals quarterback had 300 passing yards before half-time and finished with 409. Most of them were to Ja'Marr Chase, who claimed 231 yards from just 11 catches for the 7-2 Bengals.

Their divisional rivals, the Cleveland Browns, pulled off another comeback as they recovered from 17-0 down to beat the Houston Texans 27-24.

The Browns have won their opening four home games for the first time since 1963 and are now 6-4.

Quarterback Deshaun Watson led the Browns to a game-winning drive in the fourth quarter of all six of those wins and he said this one was "definitely special" as it came against his former team.

Amon-Ra St Brown met Bayern Munich forward Jamal Musiala at the Allianz Arena and waved the German flag before and after Sunday's game [Getty Images]

Munich staged the penultimate international game of the season and just playing in Germany was a "dream come true" for the Detroit Lions' wide receiver Amon-Ra St Brown.

The 27-year-old's mother is German, and he and his two brothers speak the language fluently and have been regular visitors to their mother's homeland.

St Brown, who arrived wearing lederhosen and waved the German flag as he ran on to the field, scored two touchdowns as the Lions charged to a 35-10 win over the New England Patriots.

Yet St Brown was outshone by team-mate Jahmyr Gibbs, who had 99 receiving yards, 153 rushing yards and two touchdowns, taking him to 62 overall - a new NFL record in a player's first four seasons.

The Patriots lost Drake Maye to an ankle injury when he was sacked on the game's opening drive by Aidan Hutchinson, who injured his knee as he celebrated, and the Lions fear it is a significant injury.

Detroit, the Minnesota Vikings and Chicago Bears are now all 7-2 in the ultra-competitive NFC North, with the Vikings bouncing back after suffering back-to-back defeats.

Kirk Cousins returned to Minnesota before the trade deadline on Tuesday and the veteran quarterback led them to a 30-10 win at their other divisional rival, the 6-4 Green Bay Packers, with their defence claiming eight sacks - the most in a single game this season.

The Las Vegas Raiders allowed Cousins to rejoin Minnesota as they felt Fernando Mendoza, this year's first overall draft pick, was ready to become their starting quarterback.

Mendoza's first start came against the Seattle Seahawks, the Super Bowl champions, and he managed to run in a 10-yard touchdown on the Raiders' opening drive.

But the Raiders' offence then struggled and Mendoza was sacked six times as the Seahawks won 21-13.

"It's good to get punched in the face because now it's a great opportunity to grow and learn," said Mendoza.

Seattle quarterback Drew Lock made two big touchdown passes on the run, one to Cooper Kupp and the other a 71-yard score by Jaxon Smith-Njigba.

How mum's struggle inspired Mendoza's rise to top NFL draft pick

The Kansas City Chiefs' run game has caught the eye so far this season, in particular new signing Kenneth Walker, but he was out injured on Sunday as Patrick Mahomes reminded everyone he has one of the best arms in the business.

For the first time since 2022, the three-time Super Bowl winner threw for five touchdowns, plus 348 yards, as Kansas City won 35-13 at the Atlanta Falcons.

Running back Emmett Johnson stepped up in the absence of Walker to claim 101 rushing yards, 70 receiving yards and two touchdowns.

Mahomes made explosive plays to Cyrus Allen and Andrew Armstrong for their first NFL scores, while fellow wide receiver Josh Downs scored on his debut after the Chiefs traded for him on deadline day.

That took Mahomes to 332 career touchdown passes, including the play-offs, putting the 31-year-old top of the all-time list for the most in a player's first 10 seasons.

The Chiefs are 7-2 and will need their receiving corps to ease the burden on Walker during a tough five-game stretch after next week.

#2793. Stats Rundown: 3 numbers to know from the Mavericks’ 131-94 loss at the Boston Celtics

The Dallas Mavericks lost in embarrassing fashion, 131-94 to the Boston Celtics Sunday night in Boston. This is the Mavericks third loss in a row to drop the team back to .500 at 7-7, with all three losses being fairly dispiriting.

It started awful and never got better, with the Mavericks trailing by a double-take-inducing 33 points at the end of the first quarter. The Mavericks had zero gumption or energy to start the game, after losing a game Saturday night to a Cleveland team with zero of their starters active.

Zaccharie Risacher led the Mavericks with 18 points. Jayson Tatum led Boston and all scorers with 32, as the Celtics shot over 50 percent from the field and over 40 percent from three.

It's early, but the Mavericks have reached their first crisis point of the season — if they want to be the surprise playoff team people thought after the team started 7-4, the turnaround has to happen quickly.

The Mavericks didn't shoot the ball poorly, considering their personnel, but even with 14 made threes, the Celtics still made nine more three pointers. It was a gap too wide to overcome.

Boston is a machine, and the Mavericks couldn't keep up. Dallas' defense features a lot of forwards and bigs, but the footspeed and defensive talent on the perimeter waxes and wanes — Dallas can recover with splashy defensive plays and deflections, but the team is prone to blow-bys since the Mavericks don't have much point-of-attack defense. The Celtics got the Mavericks into rotation early and Dallas never recovered.

After a meteroic start to the season, Flagg is officially in a slump. He was 5-of-15 against the Celtics, including 2-of-6 from three. Flagg has been under 40 percent from the field in four of the eight games he's played in November, and been under 45 percent in six of the eight. He's now shooting just 42 percent in November, and 26 percent from three.

Dallas' lineup did him no favors tonight, as Dusty May rolled out the Jason Kidd/Nico Harrison special from a year ago, with Flagg running point next to four non-shooting threats in PJ Washington, Caleb Martin, Naji Marshall, and Daniel Gafford. Washington and Martin have solid percentages this season, but they don't warp the defense with their spacing, especially without a lead guard to disrupt the defense. Flagg was seeing two, three, and even four bodies in front of him inside the three point line on just about every drive.

This is a problem for the Mavericks. Flagg is obviously a special talent, but the apex version of him is usually unlocked when next to a competent lead guard that can get downhill. We saw this last season and we've seen it again this season, as Dallas has played very well with Kyrie Irving and Flagg on the floor together. This is no knock on Flagg, but playing him without a credible guard talent next to him is like trying to win a game with one arm tied behind your back.

Unfortunately Dallas hasn't prioritized a lead guard in the last two offseasons. Dallas used the ninth overall pick in this summer's draft for Morez Johnson Jr., another big and then brought in another big in Santi Aldama via trade. Dallas' only guard moves were a smaller move for end-of-the-bench prospect Marcus Sasser, who's shown flashes, and using a late first-rounder for Sergio de Larrea, who is currently injured. Walter Clayton Jr. joined the team a week before the season started on a two-way contract and was almost immediately the team's backup point guard. The Dallas guard rotation is bleak, and especially so when guys like de Larrea and Max Christie are injured.

Bottom line: the Mavericks have to prioritize the guard position over the course of the next 18 months, whether that's at the upcoming trade deadline, next summer's draft, or the ensuing offseason. It's going to hold this whole thing back until it's resolved.

It says a lot about how bad Dallas is as a defensive rebounding team when the Celtics can get 18 offensive boards on a night where they were shooting the leather off the ball. There weren't a lot of misses for the Celtics to go get, and yet they still found themselves with a sizable offensive rebounding advantage (18-11).

Dallas cannot be this big of a team and still fail to rebound the ball consistently. It's just an untenable combination. If the Mavericks want to be a big, lengthy, athletic team, then they have to play like it. It does the team no good to be this big as a roster and this bad at rebounding. The trickle down effects are apparent. Nothing else to say, except the Mavericks just have to be better.

#2789. Why Lakers must figure out how to support Luka Doncic late in games

Luka Dončić continues to dominate as a scorer this season, but the Los Angeles Lakers will have to find a way to support their star player.

Lakers coach JJ Redick referred to Dončić as one of the league's best scorers before a game against the Phoenix Suns on Sunday, a sentiment shared by Giannis Antetokounmpo of the Miami Heat earlier this month.

Dončić nearly produced a double-double with 43 points on 13-of-28 shooting and nine assists for Los Angeles in the 131-123 road victory, living up to his coach's remarks.

Despite having one of the best records in the league (12-2), the third-year coach had other remarks and expectations for his team; he used the recent three-day break to share a 21-page analytics presentation with his players to serve as an internal audit on both offense and defense.

"A lot of good things and a lot of things to clean up," Lakers forward Ziaire Williams told reporters on Nov. 13. "Being first in the (Western Conference), with the stuff that they showed us, you would think we were almost last."

It is the Lakers' eighth straight win, with the last four coming on the road, but one of those aspects of the game that needs to be cleaned up is apparent.

Dončić and Austin Reaves, who was out Sunday due to injury, have proven they can win games together and can also take on a role as the high-scoring threat with the other out of the lineup.

Beyond the two stars, there's some inconsistency with the team's depth to help complement that scoring and allow its superstars an opportunity to rest.

Dončić ushered the Lakers to a quick start once again this season, scoring eight of the team's first 10 unanswered points. He finished the first quarter with 20 of the team's 33 points in the first quarter.

"We're working too hard and we're playing too hard to build these leads," Redick said during the postgame press conference on Sunday. "It's a disservice to each other to take your foot off the gas."

Los Angeles has held the lead in 76.8% of the game time this season, which is the best in the NBA, according to the Lakers. The team also has displayed its offensive dominance during its recent four-game stretch, having led for 92% of the game time.

The Lakers went wire-to-wire on Sunday, leading by as many as 31 points during the game, but allowed the Suns to battle back into the game with 43 points in the final frame.

"I wasn't planning to play in the fourth quarter," Dončić told reporters after the game. "We got to get better at that. I know we won eight in a row, but we got to get better at that.

"Once we get up, we got to stay there. We got to work on that."

Dončić gave credit to the Suns, who played aggressively while Los Angeles started the fourth quarter "a little bit sloppy."

Redick has stated multiple times this week that the Lakers' desire is to work toward being a top 10 defense in the NBA. The Lakers rank near the middle of the pack in terms of defensive rating, allowing close to 114 points per game.

After the game, Redick recalled a moment that could be featured in his next audit for the defense.

"We did a lot of good things through three quarters," Redick explained on Sunday. "... In the fourth, when (the Suns) are walking it up and we don't even talk and get matched up.

"They hit wide-open 3s and get going. You just can't allow that. You have to play for 48 minutes. We are going to need our defense to win us games."

The Lakers will have another chance to work toward Redick's defensive expectations against the Charlotte Hornets on Tuesday, Nov. 17 at 11 p.m. ET (8 p.m. PT).

#2788. Was that a fair penalty called on CB Kamari Lassiter? Texans HC DeMeco Ryans weighs in

It was worth asking Houston Texans head coach and defensive play-caller DeMeco Ryans about the phantom penalty called on third-year cornerback Kamari Lassiter after Sunday afternoon's 27-24 loss to the Cleveland Browns.

Lassiter, who has a season to forget after a career-best year last fall, was once again flagged late in the fourth quarter for an unnecessary roughness penalty with about 1:18 left after trying to break up a contested ball to Tylan Wallace on the Browns' final drive.

The hit not only took away a third-and-long at the Browns' 50, but also added 15 yards and set up Cleveland's offense at the 30. Two plays later, Cleveland would secure the win behind a 5-yard touchdown run from Quinshon Judkins.

So, what did Ryans, who has been in the middle of plays such as those, think of the penalty?

"I saw Kamari going up for the football," Ryans said postgame. "Nothing was intentional there by Kamari. He's going up for the football. I'll have to look at it and see how that is a penalty on him."

Lassiter told reporters who made the trip that he didn't know what else to do in that situation, especially given that other defenders haven't been flagged for that in the past. As a defender, the primary goal is to take away the ball. Lassiter did exactly that one he saw Wallace try to complete the catch.

"The ball's in the air, I'm trying to go get the ball," Lassiter told reporters. "And if he's touching the ball, I'm trying to violently get the ball out of his hands."

Instead, that penalty played a critical role in the Browns' victory. Sitting at 3-6, it would take the run of a lifetime for the Texans to make it back into postseason conversation.

For the first time since his arrival, Ryans might be hitting the offseason earlier than expected. And while that one play may have been a ticky tacky call that leans in favor of only one referee, penalties once again have hurt Houston's chances of righting the ship before the holidays.

"When you have 13 penalties, especially there late in the game - we need to move the football, and we get penalties on special teams, penalties offensively, penalties on defense," Ryans said. "All three phases had critical penalties that hurt us."

The Texans return home on a short week to welcom in the Indianapolis Colts for Week 11 on Thursday Night Football.

#2787. 10 things we learned from Patriots vs. Lions

For a second week in a row, the New England Patriots got blown out by an NFC North team on Sunday. Once again, they looked listless and disengaged for the majority of the game.

Let's get into our lessons learned from the Patriots' 35-10 loss to the Detroit Lions in Germany.

The Patriots haven't had many playmakers on offense this year, but Drake Maye has still put together a (mostly) solid year. Without him, however, it looks like one of the worst offenses in football.

Sunday's game was concrete proof of that. Tommy DeVito couldn't get the ball to open receivers, separation was on and off, and they couldn't run the ball. If Maye misses time after the bye, and it's looking increasingly likely that that is going to be the case, it's going to be tough to watch.

Speaking of Tommy DeVito, after Drake Maye went out with an injury, the Patriots were forced to turn to him. The media likes DeVito and the Patriots clearly like him too, since they gave him a contract extension this offseason. Unfortunately, he just isn't that good of a quarterback.

On Sunday, he missed open receivers left and right and on more than one occasion threw guys directly into contact. I understand that he's the backup inserted on short notice, and that the Patriots aren't asking him to be a great player because they really don't want him playing at all, but it would be nice if he was at least able to competently run the offense. Against Detroit, he wasn't.

A.J. Brown's inability to do anything positive this year has been almost laughable. He got hurt in the first game, missed a good chunk of time on injured reserve, came back, was a non-factor, and then got hurt again. He returned on Sunday, was unable to get open and had a drop as well. He finally made a nice catch-and-run to move the stick on a third down, and then promptly went to the locker room with a hamstring injury.

It's been a rough year for Brown, and the Patriots front office: they effectively bid against themselves to trade for him and still gave up a first-round pick in 2028 to do so. Unless he somehow manages a complete 180, the trade is going to go down as a massive failure, and potentially hamstring the Patriots for years to come.

Their defense was the reason the Patriots made the Super Bowl last year, and the hope was that it would take another step forward in 2026. Unfortunately, that has not happen and the unit has instead taken a step back.

It did register a couple of turnovers on Sunday, but the unit was unable to stop its opponent more or less all day long. They came out without any fire, missed tackles all over field, and put the Patriots in a hole right away.

We all were impressed with the job that Zak Kuhr had done last year, but the league has seemed to figure him out, and whatever he's doing isn't working. Yes, they have dealt with some injuries, but, for the most part, the defense has been fairly healthy. They have been out-coached, out-played, and, to be frank, it oftentimes looks like the other team simply wants it more than they do.

With this defense, the Patriots aren't going anywhere, especially if Drake Maye ends up missing time.

Christian Gonzalez is one of the best corners in the NFL, and surely one of the best players on the Patriots. The last two weeks, however, saw him have back-to-back rough games for the first time in his career.

On the game's first third down against the Lions, his struggles continued, when Amon-Ra St. Brown caught a pass in the flat, shook Gonzalez into oblivion, and then took the ball 56 yards for a touchdown. It was a bad start for Gonzalez, who later also fell victim to a pick play on another St. Brown score.

it wasn't all bad, however. He also registered an interception on a play where he ran the route for St. Brown and undercut him for the pick. It was a play that showed the player he has been, and will try to be again.

While we are on the topic of interceptions, the Patriots have finally won the turnover battle for the first time this season. They picked off Jared Goff twice, and only turned it over once.

In a game where they got embarrassed again, and with everything looking absolutely terrible in New England now, I'll take any positive notes I can get. Now, if they only were able to go a game without turning the ball over…

The NFL is filled with players who are really fast, really strong, and really elusive. None of those players, however, measure up to Gibbs. His ability to stop and start is ridiculous, and his speed is nothing short of blazing.

He leads the NFL in touches, and there is no sign of him slowing down. People had thought that TreVeyon Henderson would be the Patriots' version of Gibbs, but there is no one in this league like him, and, just like most teams that have played the Lions this year, New England had no chance of stopping him on Sunday.

In fact, he ended up out-gaining them by himself: Gibbs had 153 rushing yards and 99 receiving yards for a total of 252 yards. The Patriots offense finished the day with a grand total of 151.

The Patriots activated Gilliam off of injured reserve before the game, and they were hoping he would be a factor in the running game and on special teams. Instead, the Patriots couldn't run the ball to save their lives, Gilliam twice ran into his return man when he was trying to block, and he also committed two penalties on special teams.

Personally, I didn't love activating him off the IR, and, for Sunday at least, the Patriots didn't get any better with him on the field. With Drake Maye set to miss time, however, they might have to start relying on him and the running game.

Mike Vrabel did a fantastic job last year, there is no denying it. The culture he was trying to build was obvious, and the result was a mentally and physically tough team that reveled in the opportunity to go on the road and prove itself.

This year, however, the team has been a disaster. There have definitely been a lot of injuries, but the mental toughness has almost completely disappeared. The amount of pre-snap penalties is alarming, and the unforced errors in judgement and physical play have been bad. To go along with that, the way that he and some of the players have been speaking to the media is confusing as well.

If you're going to be a culture guy, then the culture has to matter, and it doesn't look good right now. I'm not saying that they should fire Vrabel or anything, but it bears watching. If the team doesn't start playing better, and they don't fix the fundamentals (turnovers, penalties, tackling), then there might be a reason to move on sooner rather than later.

Obviously, not every team is going to be great every year, but he has hand-picked a lot of these guys for the culture here because he coached them before. If this team has any sort of culture issue, it's squarely on Vrabel's shoulders.

(I also think that it's notable that they seemingly rushed A.J. Brown back twice instead of giving him a long rest, and he's been hurt both times. Maybe that's the medical staff, but it's ultimately the coaching staff who makes the decision to play the guys, even if they are physically cleared.)

Perhaps no team in the NFL has needed a bye week as much as the Patriots do. They played two bad games in a row, have a ton of injuries, including at quarterback, and desperately need to get their minds right and get healthy. The Patriots are going to have to come up with something significantly better than what they've brought lately, because they are getting crushed and look like a team on the verge of giving up.

A reset over the bye seems necessary, and might help them get back to a spot where they look like a competent and competitive football team.

#2785. Dylan Harper plays the hero as Spurs beat Jazz, extend win streak to 12

It was an ugly one and too close for comfort, but the Spurs got their 12th win in a row in their visit to Salt Lake City. Despite not playing particularly well, San Antonio escaped with a 110-102 victory to hand the Jazz their 12th straight loss, in large part thanks to Dylan Harper fourth-quarter heroics.

All the ingredients required for a strange game that could get more complicated than expected for the Spurs were there. It was a Sunday matinee; De'Aaron Fox was out; the Jazz had already played the Silver and Black twice in the young season; it was a one-game road trip at altitude. Yet it was hard to imagine just how weird things would be, especially in the first half. Mo Bamba turning into Stephen Curry was hard to predict, and so was Jordan McLaughlin being the first guy to reach double digits for the visitors. San Antonio's defense being lethargic early was no surprise but the way Utah was making them pay by hitting jumpers was. On the other end, meanwhile, Fox was missed in the halfcourt, so transition offense had to pick up the slack. It wasn't the most well-played bout of the season, but it was entertaining and close, as the score was tied after one.

The Spurs have been relying on their talent to overwhelm opponents even when the execution and occasionally the energy have been far from ideal, and to some degree, they achieved that against the Jazz in the first half. This time, however, getting a superstar performance from Wembanyama and a couple of other contributors to step up simply wasn't enough to create a lead, like it has in past games. Utah was confident after the strong start and didn't let a few missed jumpers discourage them. Defensively, they had no answers for The Alien, who had his three-point shot going, but were happy to sit back and watch others fall into bad habits and take the bait of driving or shooting when the other option would have been preferable. It was clear that San Antonio was going to have to take the win, because the Jazz were not going to give it away without a fight.

During two different stretches of the third, it seemed like the Spurs were finally going to impose their will. A strong start allowed them to carve a double-digit lead, but errant shooting and lackadaisical defense followed, and the home team quickly caught up. Then when the bench checked in, they managed to put together a rare run for a group that has struggled often, putting the Silver and Black up nine after an alley-oop dunk from the oft-maligned Luke Kornet. Alas, Utah once again rallied after a timeout, shooting their way back while San Antonio's jumpers refused to fall. Holding serve while the second unit was in would have normally been enough if the starters had come in rested to close the frame strong, but it just didn't happen. The game was tied going into a final period, and it didn't feel impossible to see two streaks being snapped on a shocker of an ending.

Fortunately, an overall strange game finished with the most logical result. The Jazz, who have struggled with maintaining leads, especially at the end of games, looked like the young, shorthanded team that they are in the clutch. Keldon Johnson, last year's Sixth Man of the Year, was the sparkplug San Antonio needed all game long, but elevated his impact with some crucial plays late. And Dylan Harper, who showed in the playoffs that he's not scared of the big moments, took over as the first option that Wembanyama couldn't be because of how much attention Utah was paying to his every move on offense. The young guard dropped 18 of his career-high 31 in the final period to keep the Spurs close enough to take advantage of the mistakes the home team would make down the stretch. It wasn't the prettiest of wins, but it was enough to keep the streak going.

What makes Dylan Harper such a scary young player is that a lot of what he does at this point in his career, on both ends, seems mostly done on instinct and sheer talent. He's a smart, polished player in some ways, but in others, he just… does things that happen to get good results more often than not. For most of the game he wasn't particularly efficient and at times forced things, but when the team actually needed someone to take over, that same hyper-aggressiveness and confidence that sometimes leads to poor decisions was the reason why he was ready to explode offensively. Harper is already a fantastic player who will only get better as a decision-maker, which should terrify every other team in the league.

While Harper's heroics will rightfully get most of the attention, Wembanyama's first half was also needed for the Spurs to escape with a win. Moreover, the Jazz' devoting so much attention to him on dives to the basket opened things up for others, including Harper on his consecutive fourth-quarter threes. The big guy did his job.

The third spot on the podium belongs to Keldon Johnson. In a game in which Devin Vassell and Julian Champagnie combined for 10 points on 17 shots and Harrison Barnes and Carter Bryant didn't move the needle off the bench, San Antonio needed someone who wasn't a guard or a center to step up. Johnson's made contributions in different areas, as accurately reflected by his stat line. A great mix of aggressiveness on offense and energy plays for a veteran who continues to reinvent himself.

The Spurs missed Fox, which isn't surprising, since he's their best half-court orchestrator, but Stephon Castle slotted in nicely in his old role as primary playmaker and had 20 points and nine assists. Jordan McLaughlin was decent off the bench as well, hitting some shots in the first half. Against better opponents, Fox's absence could be a bigger problem, but San Antonio survived without him.

The Spurs will kick off a three-game homestand by taking on one of the best teams in the East. It should be a good test for a San Antonio team that has not faced a lot of good opponents lately.

#2782. 5 things we learned from the Chiefs feasting on Dirty Bird

For most of the first half, it looked like the Kansas City Chiefs were the better team, even if the offense on the field didn't reflect that. Then, just before halftime, the Chiefs trotted Harrison Butker out to attempt a field goal — and he made it!

Harrison Butker actually made a field goal.

An Atlanta Falcons player jumped offside.

The extra five yards gave the Chiefs a first down. The very next play, quarterback Patrick Mahomes threw a dime to his brand-new target, Josh Downs, who brought in the pass for a touchdown.

Here are five things we learned from the Chiefs' 35-13 victory over the Falcons.

I say this a little tongue-in-cheek. We've known this team was better than their 2025 iteration pretty much from the jump. But it's like they say, you are only as good as your record. And up until now, the Chiefs had not surpassed their disappointing 6-11 record from a year ago.

With this week's drubbing of the hapless Falcons, the Chiefs have amassed their seventh win of the season, ensuring that no matter what happens the rest of the way out, they've locked up a better record than last year.

Now, the only question that remains is: how much better are they?

A lot has been said about the decline in the Chiefs' air yards per attempt in recent years, including their modest 4.15 air yards per attempt over the last four games heading into Atlanta.

Over the years, we've heard every speculated reason for why the Chiefs couldn't seem to find success throwing the deep ball.

Some said it was because we traded away Tyreek Hill.

Some said it was because Mahomes had lost his ability to throw the ball 20+ yards accurately.

Some blamed it on coaching and playcalling.

Some said it was a deficit of talent at the receiving position.

Some said teams adapted to take away the deep ball.

Most said it was a combination of all four — but we now have definitive empirical evidence that rules Mahomes out of the equation. On Sunday, Mahomes completed six out of seven passes downfield.

Mahomes never lost the ability to throw the ball deep — he just needed the pieces to fall back into place for it to make sense to air it out.

We knew the Chiefs needed help at wide receiver.

We knew that the Chiefs had their eyes set on trading for wide receiver Josh Downs from the Indianapolis Colts.

And when they pulled off the trade just before the deadline, we all crossed our fingers and prayed he was the missing piece to this passing attack. And while the jury is still out on whether the issues around this passing attack are fully solved, I think it's fair to say Downs looks like everything we were hoping for.

Sure, it's a small sample size, and he's not a superstar.

But he's a good route runner, with great hands, and a smart head on his shoulders.

Something the Chiefs have been missing at wide receiver for the last couple of seasons.

The only question now is, just how good is Josh Downs?

It's hard to say, especially when he's had the likes of Anthony Richardson, Gardner Minshew, and Daniel Jones throwing him the football over the last four seasons.

Another thing that the jury is still out on is how much better this team is with Downs on it?

Maybe we already knew this one before this game.

But there is a difference between being the change-of-pace back and being the workhorse expected to put the offense on your shoulders and carry it downfield to the promised land.

With starting running back Kenneth Walker sidelined with injury, the Chiefs rookie running back got his first chance to be the first man up in the backfield, and boy howdy, he did not disappoint.

This Twitter post sells Johnson short. According to ESPN, Johnson finished the game with 101 rushing yards, 70 receiving yards, and two touchdowns.

I don't think there is any question that Johnson has been the best rookie running back in the NFL this season. It's not surprising, considering he was fourth in the nation in rushing last season while playing at Nebraska.

A lot will be made this week about the Chiefs rediscovering their deep ball.

But none of the above happens without Johnson keeping the defense honest.

We obviously want Kenneth Walker III back as soon as possible, but until then, we've got E-Money.

With the turmoil at the Chiefs' offensive tackle position this season, Kansas City has at least been able to rest on the fact that when left guard Kingsley Suamataia is not in head coach Andy Reid's doghouse, the Chiefs have one of the better interior offensive lines in the NFL.

So when right guard Trey Smith left the game with a concussion, the Chiefs had no choice but to put Mike Caliendo back in.

#2779. Syracuse’s Kiyan Anthony Proves Haters Wrong

NEW YORK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 15: Kiyan Anthony #7 of the Syracuse Orange reacts during the first half against the St. John's Red Storm at Madison Square Garden on November 15, 2026 in New York City. (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images)

NEW YORK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 15: Kiyan Anthony #7 of the Syracuse Orange shoots a jump shot against Ian Jackson #11 of the St. John's Red Storm during the second half at Madison Square Garden on November 15, 2026 in New York City. (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images)

The verdict is still very much out on whether the Syracuse Orange men's basketball team is any good.

But even though SU was run away from in the second half on Sunday night by St. John's at Madison Square Garden, something important happened: Kiyan Anthony continued to look like a rising star.

Kiyan led Syracuse in scoring for the night, but it was the way he did it that was as impressive as anything.

This was a stage his father, Carmelo, knew quite well — as a Knicks star, many of 'Melo's best nights came at MSG.

And on this night, 'Melo was there. So too were Russell Wilson and his wife Ciara, friends of the family.

It's Madison Square Garden. Big names show up. Some showed up specifically to watch Kiyan, others just to take in the game, but they all saw Kiyan show out.

After a freshman season filled with inefficiency and question marks, Kiyan wasn't certain to develop into a quality high-major player.

Right now, he's getting buckets like you'd hope for from a dude with his lineage.

GettyNEW YORK, NEW YORK – NOVEMBER 15: Kiyan Anthony #7 of the Syracuse Orange reacts during the first half against the St. John's Red Storm at Madison Square Garden on November 15, 2026 in New York City. (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images)

Kiyan led the Orange in scoring on Sunday night with his 17 points.

He shot 7-for-12 from the floor, including 1-for-4 from 3-point range, and he was 2-for-3 from the foul line.

Kiyan added four assists, two rebounds and no turnovers.

The passing is a pleasant surprise, as well — it's another area he didn't seem particularly adept in as a freshman.

GettyNEW YORK, NEW YORK – NOVEMBER 15: Kiyan Anthony #7 of the Syracuse Orange shoots a jump shot against Ian Jackson #11 of the St. John's Red Storm during the second half at Madison Square Garden on November 15, 2026 in New York City. (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images)

For Kiyan's doubters, it'd be easy to write off one or two decent games as a fluke.

Right now, though, Kiyan is looking like a dynamic scorer. Particularly when he gets himself going downhill toward the hoop, he's finding a variety of ways to score with touch and skill.

And one way to recognize just how good he was Sunday night — Kiyan had three and-ones, three players on which he was fouled while shooting and still made his shot. That's just an indicator of his strength, tenacity and ability.

Kiyan always was going to have the bar set quite high from the very beginning, and it's highly unlikely that he'll ever be as good as his dad — who is one of the best hoopers ever

But can Kiyan be a useful player for Syracuse? It's clear that he already is. The Orange offense is more dangerous with Kiyan on the floor, a major development relative to his freshman season.

#2778. The Good, Bad & Ugly from the Miami Dolphins Week 10 loss to the Indianapolis Colts

The Miami Dolphins were extremely shorthanded heading into their Week 10 road-trip against the Indianapolis Colts. Starting quarterback Malik Willis was placed on injured reserve earlier in the week with a lingering groin issue. Stud center Aaron Brewer missed Sunday's tilt due a concussion he suffered in last week's loss to the Detroit Lions. Defensive leader Zach Sieler tore his biceps in that same loss — forcing him to not only miss Miami's game against Indianapolis, but the rest of the 2026 season as well.

Well, as we all know, adversity is opportunity.

The Dolphins — while starting rookie quarterback Kyle McCord — nearly overcame all of that adversity to upset their foes on Sunday. Instead, despite a spirited effort from Jeff Hafley's squad, Miami lost by two-points against Indianapolis, dropping their record to 1-8 on the year after falling by a score of 24-22.

In a season where finding bright spots has sometimes felt like searching for a needle in a haystack, seeing two young players make game-changing defensive plays for Miami on Sunday was encouraging.

Rookie safety Michael Taaffe and rookie cornerback Chris Johnson each came away with an interception of Colts' quarterback Daniel Jones.

Taaffe got things started with an interception with 10:30 left in the second quarter — giving Miami's defense a much-needed takeaway while the Colts were driving for points. It was Taaffe's third interception on the season. Not bad for a 5th round pick!

But it was Johnson who provided the highlight of the afternoon.

Miami's 1st round rookie cornerback intercepted Jones with 8:52 left in the 3rd-quarter and returned the ball 59 yards for a dazzling touchdown — giving Miami a big lift and injecting some life into a game that was quickly getting away from the South Florida squad.

Obviously, one game doesn't make a career, but Taaffe and Johnson have been playing solid football for the Dolphins all season long. There hasn't been a whole lot to celebrate in Miami this year, but seeing two rookies stepping up when their team needs them is part of the fuel that keeps the fires of hope burning as Dolphins fans look towards a brighter future.

Now, if only the rest of the defense could figure out how to stop somebody…

On Sunday, Indianapolis ran the football 34 times for 172 yards, averaging a whopping 5.1 yards per carry.

The Colts didn't need to get particularly creative. They didn't need to rely on some elaborate offensive scheme or trick plays. They lined up, handed the football to their running backs Jonathan Taylor and Seth McGowan, and repeatedly found themselves moving the chains.

The Indianapolis rushing attack consistently found room to operate, putting Miami's defense on their heels and making life difficult for the Dolphins throughout the afternoon, despite the fact that Miami's defense only gave up 104 yards passing.

When an opposing offense can consistently pick up five yards every time it hands the ball off, you're eventually going to run out of opportunities to get off the field.

The Dolphins have plenty of things to figure out defensively, but stopping the run needs to be near the top of that list — especially when a date with Josh Allen, James Cook and the Buffalo Bills is circled on the calendar for next Sunday.

Zane Gonzalez misses two field goals and an extra-point try in a two-point loss

When the Dolphins gave kicker Riley Patterson his walking papers on October 20th so they could sign Zane Gonzalez to take over kicking duties for the team, fans were encouraged by the move.

Fast forward four games and that warm and fuzzy feeling has vanished in a hurry.

On Sunday, Gonzalez missed two field goals and an extra point try. That's 7 points Gonzalez was unable to put on the board for a Dolphins team desperate for them.

Reminder: Miami lost Sunday's game by two points.

Gonzalez's first missed opportunity came on a 47-yard attempt in the first quarter. Later, after Miami had clawed their way back into the game, he missed the extra point try following Chris Johnson's spectacular interception return for a touchdown.

However, Miami's kicker saved his most heart-breaking moment for the fourth quarter when he missed a long try that would have given the Dolphins the lead in a tight, back-and-forth contest.

As I gaze into my crystal ball, I predict the Dolphins to look elsewhere for a place kicker in very short order.

The Dolphins, with their backs against the wall, played a close game against the Colts on Sunday. Alas, they fell short — dropping the team's record to 1-8 on the year. Were you impressed with quarterback Kyle McCord's first start? Let me know in the comments below or on Twitter at @MBrave13. Fins up.

#2777. Recap: Rockets rout Wizards, 147-119

The Washington Wizards fell to the Houston Rockets, 147-119, on Sunday night at Capital One Arena, extending their losing streak to seven games. The Wizards trailed by as many as 37 points and were it-rebounded by 19.

Coming off a 30-point performance against the Detroit Pistons on Thursday, Alex Sarr scored eight quick points on 3-of-3 shooting, including a three-pointer, to give Washington an early 13-12 lead.

The Wizards closed the first quarter trailing 36-31, with Sarr leading the way with 10 points. Anthony Davis, who also scored 30 against Detroit on Thursday, had a much quieter start, missing all three of his field-goal attempts, including several looks around the rim.

Houston opened the second quarter with a 7-0 run and eventually stretched its lead to 12. Sarr briefly halted the momentum with another three-pointer, but the Rockets continued to pull away. Houston's lead reached 17 with 6:29 remaining in the half, as Amen Thompson and Kevin Durant helped fuel the offensive surge. Thompson started 3-for-3 from beyond the arc, while Houston shot 56% from three-point range in the first half.

Washington went into the break trailing 73-54 despite Sarr's 15 points, four rebounds and two assists. The rest of the Wizards' starting lineup — Trae Young, AJ Dybantsa, Kyshawn George and Davis — combined for just 18 points.

Houston picked up right where it left off to start the third quarter, opening the period with a 12-4 run, and the game wasn't competitive from that point forward.

Thompson (26 points), Durant (25), Tari Eason (25) and Alperen Sengun (21) all scored 20+, while Sarr (25) was the only Wizard to finish with more than 20 points. Dybantsa scored 16 and grabbed seven boards, Davis finished with 14 points and eight rebounds, and George tacked on 11 points and four assists. Will Riley knocked down two three pointers and scored 14 points off the bench.

The Wizards will turn around to host the Memphis Grizzlies on Monday night at 7:00 p.m. ET at Capital One Arena.

#2776. Christian McCaffrey on career-high receiving yards: You just catch it and run as fast as you can

The 49ers running back had never had more than 121 receiving yards in a single game. He had 161 receiving yards on four catches Sunday against the Cowboys, scoring on catch-and-runs of 74 and 66 in the 49ers’ 46-40 win.

“You never know,” McCaffrey said. “You go into each game. You don’t really predict anything. Again, you just have to have the right mindset on a play that’s going to break. You trust your instincts and play fast.”

His first receiving touchdown came when Brock Purdy rolled to his right to buy time and found McCaffrey running free on the scramble drill.

“It really is backyard football at that point,” McCaffrey said. “We all played it as kids at recess, and you draw up plays on your hand, and it never happens. You ever tell a 5-year-old to run a post route, and he just runs a corner and something else, but he’s open? That’s kind of what that was. Again, I think those little decisions that you make in games, from Brock to scramble, not to just surrender the play but to keep it alive. That’s a big deal. There’s no planning that goes into that. It’s just him doing a great job playing ball.”

What turned out to be the game-winning touchdown came with 3:23 remaining when Purdy found McCaffrey, who was matched up against Von Miller, over the middle.

“They brought pressure,” McCaffrey said. “They dropped a D-end on me, so that’s a perfect look for that play. Again, it was a great job by Brock getting the ball where it needed to be. It made it easy for me.

“You just catch it and run as fast as you can to try to score. Don’t overthink it. You hope that nobody catches you, and you hope that you’re really fast so your teammates don’t catch up to you to celebrate, because it makes you look slow. We’ll have to check the tape.”

McCaffrey had a 16-yard touchdown run and 62 yards rushing. He is the first player in the Super Bowl era with at least 150 receiving yards, two receiving touchdowns, 50-plus rushing yards and at least one rushing touchdown.

#2775. Lazio, Gattuso chiede di più per lo staff. Frattesi: «mi ha salvato la vita»

Dopo il gol in Italia-Francia, il centrocampista racconta quanto siano stati importanti giocare e sentire fiducia.

La Lazio vuole prolungare il contratto di Gennaro Gattuso fino al 2029, ma il tecnico prende tempo e pone una richiesta nella trattativa: un aumento per il suo staff di nove persone. Prima di decidere, vuole anche capire che cosa accadrà nel mercato di gennaio.

CLICCA QUI E SEGUI LAZIOPRESS.IT ANCHE SU INSTAGRAM

Alla pausa per le nazionali di novembre, i biancocelesti sono primi da soli in Serie A con 29 punti. Hanno la miglior difesa e il terzo miglior attacco del campionato. La squadra gioca con forza e aggressività, coinvolgendo tutti gli undici uomini sia nella fase difensiva sia in quella offensiva.

Gattuso ha dato alla formazione un’identità riconoscibile. che riprende quanto riportato dal Messaggero, la dirigenza si è già messa al lavoro per trovare un accordo con l’allenatore. Il suo rendimento sta attirando anche l’interesse di diverse squadre europee.

Il contratto attuale lega Gattuso alla Lazio fino al 2027 per 1,2 milioni di euro. È prevista un’opzione di rinnovo fino al 2028 collegata al dodicesimo posto, ma il club sta trattando una scadenza più lontana. Il percorso della squadra arriva nonostante le difficoltà economiche della società e le contestazioni dei tifosi nei confronti del presidente Claudio Lotito.

Gattuso, per ora, non ha dato una risposta. Vuole vedere se a gennaio resteranno le limitazioni che in estate hanno condizionato gli acquisti della Lazio e se la società dovrà effettuare cessioni. Lotito gli ha promesso che nella sessione invernale non ci saranno partenze, ma l’allenatore attende gli sviluppi del mercato.

Nella trattativa c’è poi la questione dello staff. I nove collaboratori guadagnano attualmente circa 700mila euro complessivi, poco più di 77mila euro a testa in media. Per Gattuso la cifra non riconosce adeguatamente il lavoro svolto negli allenamenti e i risultati ottenuti in campo.

#2773. Falcons – Chiefs recap: Wilting away in Mercedes-Benz Stadium

If you were daydreaming about an improbable run, simply hoping for a miracle, or just looking for something enjoyable as the season very slowly winds down, the Falcons were determined to ensure your Sunday left you bereft. The quality of the opponent aside—the Chiefs are very good, obviously—this was the bottom for the Falcons, and the point at which team and fanbase alike need to fully accept certain hard truths about the Atlanta Falcons of 2026.

Those truths? The first and most obvious one is that this is a bad football team at the moment. Despite some promising signings and trades, the talent level is not good enough across the board to make them a playoff-caliber team even in a weak NFC South, something the Falcons appeared to accept when they traded away Jessie Bates and Ryan Neuzil. Also, while this team has more resources than just any other team in the NFL, they are going to need every dollar and draft pick just to overhaul what they have in a way that brings their talent level up to where it needs to be and exorcises all the weird ghosts that have been awkwardly floating around this team for most of the last decade. And finally, there are very few positions on this roster that are actually settled with 2027 looming, meaning this team could look very, very different than it does now by May of next year.

There is a Sunday every year in this miserable stretch of losing seasons where the terrible weight of losing lands especially heavy on my shoulders, and this is the one for 2026. More than likely, I'll come out of the bye ready to joke about the Falcons reeling off some unlikely wins and finishing this year with a losing record for the ninth straight season, and we'll all lock arms and head into a pivotal offseason daring to dream of something better. But I'll tell you with naked honesty that this Sunday got to me in a way the previous nine games did not, as I saw the this team continue a frankly brutal three game slide and make it fully clear just how limited their ceiling for this season really is. At 3-7 and driving that stake into this team's hopes with relish, the Falcons ensured I can fully give up on 2026 and just try to find the bright spots in what's to come, and I do intend to take full advantage. I hope you will, as will.

For now, though, we'll be digesting a game where Patrick Mahomes threw for five touchdowns and the Chiefs ran all over Atlanta despite not having Kenneth Walker, and the defense was still the more impressive unit. Atlanta's offense has now scored 17 or fewer points in three straight games, which begs the question of whether Tommy Rees is the right coordinator, Penix is the right quarterback, and almost every player on that side of the ball is going to be part of the next great Falcons offense outside of Bijan Robinson, Chris Lindstrom, and Drake London. That seems like an overreaction to one game—and perhaps even three games—but this is an evaluation year for a regime with the resources to make substantial changes in 2027, and an offense studded with talented players looking this crummy will give them genuine pause. The Chiefs are a good, well-coached team, but the gulf between them and a frankly hapless Falcons team should give them further pause.

The bye week will give these Falcons a chance to reset and try to make something of the rest of this year, but the fate of this team seems beyond obvious at this point. As we have so many times over the past decade, we Falcons fans are left to look ahead to better days after the last bloom has fallen off the rose. May this coming offseason finally bring those long-elusive days to us, so that we may put games like in the past where they belong.

He hasn't looked superhuman very often lately, but Bijan Robinson remains a player defenses fear and a back capable of breaking some jaw-dropping runs. His best carries in this game were like that, where through sheer will, balance, and power he managed to reel off 10-plus yards despite the at-times nonexistent threat of the Falcons passing game working against him. Someday the offense will sputter to life again and he'll look like the Bijan of old.

Jahan Dotson would ideally be your third receiver, but even with his ups and downs he's been a very credible receiving threat for this team, and has had some really good weeks. He was a better pass away from a touchdown today and finished second on the team with three receptions for 63 yards, and is on his way to a career year in an offense that can and wants to get him the ball.

Drake London deserves a medal of some kind. His career has been defined by a revolving door of play callers, quarterbacks, and surrounding personnel, and yet he continually blocks his ass off and shows out as the team's best receiver. He somehow had over 100 yards in this one despite the passing game being dormant much of the day, and London deserves better than the results this team sees in the win and loss columns weekly.

Harold Perkins had a couple of ugly reps on the first defensive drive, and that must have galvanized him because he was a man possessed after that point. Perkins was fantastic against the run, a demon as a pass rusher, and more stingy in coverage after that point, standing out over and over again no matter what he was asked to do. There's little question Perkins is a player the Falcons plan to count on in 2027 and beyond, and he showed why on Sunday.

Brandon Dorlus and Gervon Dexter remain one of the best duos on the interior in the NFL, and Dexter in particular was a man possessed with five pressures, three run stops, and multiple plays where he rampaged through the overmatched Chiefs offensive line like Godzilla through the financial district. If the Falcons can bring more consistent pressure off the edge to help out D&D, quarterbacks will be miserable.

The defense did the heavy lifting on Sunday against a good Chiefs team minus key pieces, and reminded us they're the unit that is much closer to being a finished product, even if the overall results were still rough. It's not that difficult to talk yourself into Billy Bowman Jr., Xavier Watts, Kendal Daniels, Perkins, Dorlus, Dexter, and company just getting better a year from now with better complementary pieces around them.

Jake Moody came uncomfortably close to missing an extra point, but otherwise he was excellent. Moody hit both short field goal tries and had the NFL's first successful onside kick attempt, with a major assist from Chris Blair, in his Falcons debut. Hopefully he can prove to be the team's long-term solution at kicker, and the early returns were promising, even if the kicks weren't particularly challenging.

Blair, as mentioned above, had a phenomenal play. He wasn't quite there on a potential touchdown pass from Penix, but the onsides kick recovery was flawless, as Blair very confidently grabbed it away from a sleepwalking Xavier Worthy and kept his feet inbounds to give Atlanta a last gasp chance they couldn't take full advantage of.

Yes, the offense has holes and weaknesses that need to be addressed in the offseason, but it's not so bereft of talent that it should look like it did on the first four drives. The Falcons started this game with one productive Bijan Robinson carry, one eight yard catch for Kyle Pitts, and a whole lot of incompletions, penalties, and ineptitude that led to four straight three-and-outs. That represented all four drives in the first quarter, and was evidence enough that this team selling at the deadline was an accurate read of their potential. It was, as the broadcast noted, the first time since 2000 that the Falcons started the game with four straight three-and-outs.

Michael Penix Jr. simply can't miss this consistently if this offense is going to be anything of note. On the first pass of the game he had an open Drake London and missed him, and his misfires piled up throughout the first half as Atlanta continually frittered away their drives. Matt Ryan praised Penix before the game but made it clear the Falcons were looking for more consistency from him, and consistency continues to elude the third-year quarterback, given that this was another forgettable day from a player who continues to look like he needs ideal situations to thrive. If that continues, it's unlikely he'll be the starter in September 2027.

Kyle Pitts has become something of an avatar for this offense. Both are highly regarded for their potential, capable of absolutely eye-popping weeks, and yet prone to inconsistency and dreary performances. Pitts had a solid four catches for 50 yards, but that's not outstanding production, he wasn't a huge factor after the catch, and he had one catch stripped for a Chiefs turnover. A player who seemed destined to thrive in Kevin Stefanski and Tommy Rees' offense just hasn't.

Jawaan Taylor was called out during the broadcast for giving away the play call with his stance and then had multiple false start calls. The Falcons will be in the market for a new right tackle in 2027.

Jake Matthews was hit with three separate penalties, and the legendary left tackle appears to be closing in on the end of the line. Did the Falcons want to have to replace both tackles in 2027? They'll chalk this up as an off day for Matthews, who was pretty solid outside of those penalties, but Father Time is tapping his foot and Bill Callahan seems likely to put his stamp on more than just the center position.

The Falcons defense was by far the better unit through the first half, but they still had brutal lapses that gave the Chiefs a 14-3 lead. The worst single play was on Emmett Johnson's touchdown grab in the first quarter, which saw two Falcons get a shot at bringing Johnson down and utterly failing to do so, as missed tackles and bad angles led to both Kansas City scores. It's hard to hold it against them too much given that they were on the field nearly constantly, but miscues are miscues, and Atlanta had tons of them.

The run defense is a five alarm fire at this point. Johnson is a promising backup for Kansas City, but he is no Walker, yet his production suggested he was possessed by the veteran back's spirit. Since dominating some lousy ground games early on in the year, the Falcons have been among the least inspiring defenses in football and are both struggling to get into position and struggling to tackle opposing backs for going on six weeks now.

This was a very, very tough game for Atlanta's secondary, which Mahomes picked apart with his usual precision. A.J. Terrell allowed three receptions for 86 yards and two touchdowns, C.J. Henderson gave up three more for 97 yards and a score, and Billy Bowman Jr.'s mostly strong day was undone by three grabs for 41 yards and another score. Terrell in particular has been brutal the past two weeks, and the Falcons have to figure something out in the back end before Kirk Cousins tries out his spin on a revenge tour in two weeks.

The Falcons had Tommy Rees down on the sidelines, which is usually a sign that the offense is struggling (it is) and the team is taking a hard look at their coordinator's fortunes (to be determined), and the offense put up another dud of a performance. Cooper Rush being the quarterback badly hurt the Falcons the first two weeks, but they've already turned the ball over on offense more than they did in 2025 and now have scored 17 or fewer points in five of their ten games and three straight weeks. There are so many execution errors and penalty issues that you can't lay this all at Rees' feet, but the flashes of really thrilling offense just aren't there right now, with a strangled run game, too many early passes, and go-nowhere screens damaging the effort.

It's a bad sign that this team is continually getting worse as the season rolls on. You'd expect Michael Penix Jr. to be playing better football than he was fresh off a long injured stint early in the year, but he's not. You'd think this defense would be starting to figure things out with so many young players in the lineup, but they're getting destroyed by quality offenses. This coaching staff is not going anywhere, as I've said repeatedly, but it would be extremely unideal for them to go into a pivotal 2027 with any shadows of doubt hanging over them. Right now, it's hard not to feel like this staff is failing to get more out of a team that looks incredibly sloppy and penalty-prone, at the very least.

This is a team that's not even in the same stratosphere as real contenders in the NFL. They're not even in the same breath as the teams they're nominally just behind in the NFC, frankly.

A bye week. We'll take stock of what has passed and what's to come, and then get ready for the Vikings.

#2772. Christian McCaffrey, 49ers run past Cowboys 46-40

49ers fans took over AT&T Stadium on Sunday, out-drawing and out-yelling Cowboys fans. They booed the Cowboys running onto their own field, and they loudly celebrated a 46-40 San Francisco win.

In an entertaining game, the 49ers moved to 8-1, and the Cowboys fell to 4-6.

Christian McCaffrey had a career-high 161 receiving yards on four catches, two of them touchdowns, and ran for 62 yards and a touchdown on 13 carries. He is the first player in the Super Bowl era with at least 150 receiving yards, two receiving touchdowns, 50-plus rushing yards and at least one rushing touchdown.

The 49ers led 38-19 with 11:26 remaining in the fourth quarter. But George Pickens caught a 5-yard touchdown pass, which was followed by a missed 2-point conversion. Ryan Flournoy’s 11-yard score with 3:42 left cut the Cowboys’ deficit to 38-32. The 49ers burned only 2:26 on their possession in between, punting after four plays.

The 49ers showed the Cowboys who they are, though, when Brock Purdy hit McCaffrey across the middle of the field. Von Miller, who was covering McCaffrey, and his teammates had no chance of catching the running back, who went 66 yards to the end zone.

The Cowboys didn’t go away quietly, scoring once more on CeeDee Lamb’s 1-yard reception. Dak Prescott ran in the 2-point conversion.

Dallas tried an onside kick despite having three timeouts and did not convert.

Kaelon Black, who had 11 carries for 53 yards and a touchdown, fumbled on the second-down play. Quinnen Williams forced it, but Black was able to get back on the ball. The 49ers punted, and the Cowboys were left with only 9 seconds and in need of 91 yards and a miracle.

McCaffrey’s other touchdowns were a 74-yard reception and a 16-yard run.

The 49ers had 584 yards, the third-most the Cowboys have allowed in their history. It was not far from the 49ers’ team record of 621.

Purdy set a career-high with 389 passing yards and threw three touchdowns, completing 22 of 28 passes.

George Kittle had six catches for 74 yards, and new addition Keenan Allen five for 61. Deebo Samuel had three catches for 31 yards and a touchdown and three carries for 78 yards and a touchdown.

The Cowboys couldn’t keep up, even with 439 yards.

Prescott was 30-of-51 for 343 yards with five touchdowns and an interception. Pickens had 11 catches for 145 yards and three touchdowns, and Lamb seven for 72 yards and a touchdown. Flournoy added six catches for 71 yards and a touchdown.

#2771. Knicks refind clutch gene to hold on for tight overtime win over Raptors

TORONTO — At least for one night in Canada, the clutch Knicks were back.

Jalen Brunson saved his best shot for last, Karl-Anthony Towns stuffed the boxscore on his 31st birthday, Landry Shamet shined off the bench and OG Anunoby sealed a win at the foul line as the Knicks reaffirmed their long-standing dominance over the Raptors with a 112-108 overtime victory Sunday.

Brunson's 3-pointer from the corner gave the Knicks the lead for good with 33 seconds left in overtime, a shot that allowed the point guard redemption after he botched the final possession of regulation with a slip into a turnover.

Jalen Brunson of the New York Knicks celebrates during a game against the Toronto Raptors in Toronto on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

Karl-Anthony Towns of the New York Knicks drives to the basket against Scottie Barnes of the Toronto Raptors. NBAE via Getty Images

In OT, Brunson received an inbounds pass from Mikal Bridges — who was stellar defensively down the stretch — and knocked down the pullup jumper over Scottie Barnes. It was Brunson's biggest shot of the young season.

"I work on that shot," Brunson said, "and I'm happy it went in."

Anunoby hit a pair of clutch free throws, then thwarted a potential tying trey from Barnes, completing a comeback from 13 points down in the fourth quarter. Before Sunday, the Knicks were among the NBA's worst clutch teams, going 1-6 in games that were within one possession at any point in the final five minutes.

"That feels good. That was our time of the season where it's like, 'Let's buckle down. Let's go and work our way back for this one,' " said Shamet, who finished with 23 points in 30 minutes. "We had a few early in the year last year and obviously in the playoffs, but to get one under the belt and win one that way — that's an encouraging win for the group where maybe things didn't go the way you wanted to at times."

The Knicks (7-6) have won a remarkable 14 straight against the Raptors, a streak dating to 2023. Brunson has never lost to the division foe since joining the Knicks, but none of his victories last season were as dicey as this one.

"We know what we are capable of in those situations," Brunson said. "I'm just happy the way we fought. We could've easily given up, chalked it up to the next game. But we kept fighting."

The Knicks play the Raptors again Tuesday, giving the Knicks four days here. They left Sunday feeling good about themselves — even if they weren't satisfied with their play for much of the game.

Landry Shamet (44) of the New York Knicks shoots as Allen Graves (22) of the Toronto Raptors defends in Toronto, Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

"It's always good to win close ballgames like this. Especially when you feel like you played particularly well. You give Toronto a lot of credit because they were physical and tried to push the pace and got their hands on the ball a couple times. So for us to be able to find a way to get a win in a very ugly game was huge. … It helps with that belief. And that's a huge component of what our standard and what our culture is about."

The Raptors (5-8) were playing without oft-injured star Kawhi Leonard, who is out indefinitely with knee soreness.

Towns, who turned 31 on Sunday, extended his double-double streak with 28 points and 17 boards. Brunson dropped 28 points on 9-for-22 shooting in a season-high 41 minutes.

Anunoby (44 minutes) and Towns (43) also played longer than anticipated. But sometimes it's worth it to win a close game.
