#2768. Raptors fall to defending champs in overtime

The Toronto Raptors hosted the New York Knicks in the first of a home-and-home series tonight, a hard-fought, at times frustrating, and eventual narrow loss to the tune of 108-112. While this is their fourth straight loss, the seventh to a team over with.a better record, and another game where they gave up a double-digit lead, this wasn't a complete loss. Instead, it was an opportunity to see just how well the Raptors can play, making the defending champions sweat a little.

Scottie Barnes had a great first game back, barely missing a step as he found his shot from all over the floor, leading the team with 30 points, 9 boards, and 4 assists. Jamal Shead was undoubtedly Toronto's biggest difference maker though, with his intensity, speed, and facilitation shifting the tone of the game entirely in Toronto's favour every time he touched the floor. He contributed 19 points, 2 rebounds, and 4 assists. RJ, IQ, and Poeltl all chipped in double digit points as well.

Jalen Brunson played phenomenally for the Knicks, finishing with 28 points and 9 assists. OG Anunoby and Karl Anthony Towns contributed to the game as well to the tune of 21 points and 9 rebounds and 28 points and 17 rebounds, respectively. Landrey Shamet proved to be a solid bench option for New York, connecting well from long range and scoring 23 points including four 3s.

New York is still trying to find their way this year despite carrying over much of their championship roster from last year. Coach Mike Brown doesn't seem fazed in the slightest though, saying he's "happy where we are right now", recognizing the recent growing pains will better prepare them for the future. If they identify and deal with these problems now, they won't crop up as the playoffs. Especially important when you're defending a title.

Of course, for Knicks fans, some of the issues feel worth worrying about. The trifecta of their biggest concerns were things Toronto, at times, tried to capitalize on. Going into this game, New York is the slowest team in the League based on pace, with a far worse transition game than last year. Being able to get back and set up defensively is a huge asset to limit easy possessions, which actually leads to the Knicks' second problem. They are one of the worst shooting teams in the league right now, forcing contested shots in the paint rather than regrouping and making smart plays. This leads them to being the third-most blocked team in the NBA currently. Protecting the paint is crucial, Scottie and CMB the most capable of doing so. Finally, despite having some great individual defenders, collectively as a team they've underperformed, ranking 22nd and 27th in steals and blocks respectively. Taking advantage of their lacklustre defence through ball movement and finding the best shot should make the offence easy.

Scottie "our best player" Barnes was back in the lineup, a welcome sight for everyone. He took absolutely no time announcing his present, rolling off a screen and soaring in to dunk over defenders in the first possession of the game. He had 10 of their first 13 points, making a pair of long range shots in the process. An excellent indicator to his readiness to be back.

Collin Murray-Boyles got the start ahead of Poeltl, in an effort to match up better against Karl Anthony Towns who plays more as a stretch than a traditional centre. He did well, as KAT's early scoring was the result of switches that freed him from CMB.

Toronto certainly capitalized on those weaknesses early, allowing them to stay in the game despite their own turnovers, defensive lapses, and shooting struggles throughout the first quarter. They ended the frame 7-22 from the floor, but remained only two possessions behind the Knicks, 17-23.

Despite a low-scoring first quarter, there was no shortage of bodies flying to secure extra possessions when the ball was loose. Unsurprisingly, this started to translate into chippiness. Scottie Barnes almost dropped Tyler Kolek by ripping the ball from his hands. Alijah Martin thrived in this atmosphere, and was able to draw a flagrant foul from Jordan Clarkson likely from his peskiness.

The Knicks started to take their game outside the three-point line, finding a lot more success than inside the paint. New York gradually started to build a lead, but Toronto countered well, working to run them off the line and forced them to make unfavourable shots. At the same time, their own shots were starting to fall, allowing them to work their way back and eventually tie the game. Jamal Shead made his presence known with a pair of fast-break full-speed layups.

The Raptors continued to probe the paint and found more success than from beyond the arc but New York fought harder in the final minutes of the half, heading to the locker room with a narrow 47-43 lead.

The third quarter wasn't smooth sailing by any means. Unforced turnovers and miscommunications on the offensive cost the Raptors possessions. Toronto's defense kept them in the game through these slumps, forcing the Knicks to take tough shots that weren't falling for them. CMB was in foul trouble before the halfway point of the third quarter, forcing him to head to the bench, but in his absence, Poeltl managed to play solid defence in the middle.

The biggest shift came with the presence of Shead on the floor. He continued to push the pace in his minutes, forcing New York on their heels. Without a set defence, Shead was able to dictate the game, distributing to the open man but also making his own shots. In a departure to his last few games, where he was left open on the 3-point line, struggling to make shots, he feasted from long range, cashing in back-to-back buckets and forcing the Knicks to respect him. This energy gave Toronto their first significant advantage since the first frame, closing the third with a 74-67 lead.

Toronto showed flashes of disorganization again in the final frame, still working on their ability to finish games. New York weren't willing to yield and the Raptors weren't trying hard enough on every possession. Give-away rebounds that allowed the Knicks to get second and third chances were their undoing to an extent, leaving the door open for New York to get back into a game that they previously trailed by double-digits. A series of empty trips seemingly sucked all of the air out of the building until Scottie Barnes took over. The Raptors lead was back, going shot for shot with the Knicks in the final seconds, cashing in a game-tying three-pointer. Then he put his body on the line, tossing himself on the floor to trap the ball and prevent the Knicks from getting a final shot up, forcing OT.

Extra time matched the tone of the first 48 minutes of the game, with fans on their feet from start to finish. Scottie led offensively, CMB had a phenomenal block that sent the ball deep into the stands, and they were all tied up.

Inhuman shot-making by Brunson meant that the Raptors were once again behind. Clutch free-throws from Walter allowed Toronto to try and foul to regain possession, but they weren't able to make the final shot, submitting to the Knicks in overtime.

After the game, Darko attributed the loss to poor decision-making at points throughout the game, and especially in the final minutes. Shead echoed this, pointing to missed rebounds and lapses in judgement, saying "we played 44 minutes of good basketball", remarking that this is a growing experience for them, and all it will do is make them better.

They'll have their chance to make up for tonight's loss and finally break their losing streak versus the Knicks on Tuesday when they host them for a second time. Tune in at 7:30pm ET on Sportsnet.

#2767. Grades: Lions offer hope despite Hutchinson injury

There was plenty to love about the Detroit Lions' dominant win over the New England Patriots. And while Aidan Hutchinson's injury may be the biggest headline from the Munich game, there was plenty from Allianz Arena that should keep Lions fans optimistic about the team moving forward.

Here is my Lions Week 10 report card and positional grades for Detroit's 35-10 victory.

Jared Goff threw two interceptions; both were his fault, and the second was an inexcusable decision that took points directly off the board. Because of those two plays alone, it feels like I can't give him a grade above C+ in good faith.

But the truth is the rest of his day was pretty dang good. I thought he navigated the pocket well, especially on his 50-yard pass to Jahmyr Gibbs. He didn't make a ton of downfield throws or display any jaw-dropping plays, but he was very efficient, finishing with an electric 9.8 yards per attempt and a 101.9 passer rating.

Jahmyr Gibbs was incredible all freakin' day. He finished with 252 scrimmage yards and two touchdowns. The Patriots couldn't handle his speed, his change-of-direction, or his strength. What was even better about his performance than normal is that the negative plays were almost completely non-existent. He had just one touch that went for negative yards, and only a couple more were stopped for zero yards.

Sione Vaki was very efficient, too, earning 28 yards on just six carries (4.7 YPC).

Overall, the Lions produced an impressive 55% success rate and +0.21 EPA/play on running plays vs. the Patriots. For comparison's sake, the Patriots were allowing just a 36.9 success rate going into this game and had produced a negative EPA/run.

I was a little disappointed with Sam LaPorta's play as a receiver. He didn't create much separation against the Patriots' defenders, and he had a touchdown grab knocked out of his hands. He finished with just a single catch for 16 yards on four targets.

However, the Lions used a ton of tight ends against the Patriots in the running game, and that played a significant role in Detroit controlling the line of scrimmage. LaPorta (26), Brock Wright (29), and Tyler Conklin (17) all logged over 15 run-blocking snaps on the day.

Amon-Ra St. Brown was seemingly unstoppable on Sunday. It was going to take the entire country of Germany to stop him on both of his long catch-and-run touchdowns, and they certainly weren't going to do that against their most beloved NFL player.

Jameson Williams' day shouldn't be overlooked, either. He caught four passes for 50 yards, including an impressive toe-tapping catch on the sidelines. Even Isaac TeSlaa got in on the fun with a highlight-reel touchdown grab.

This unit lived up to its full potential for the first time in several weeks.

Outside of some early pass protection issues, the Lions' offensive line was nails in Munich. They were getting significant push in the run game, and after settling down, they helped Jared Goff breathe comfortably in the pocket.

When the offensive line plays this well, the Lions' entire offense is as close to unstoppable as we've seen.

While the Lions' pressure was inconsistent at times without Aidan Hutchinson in the lineup, they still gave the Patriots hell for most of the game. In the run game, the Patriots were unable to do anything. Their running backs combined for 17 carries, 31 yards, and just 1.8 yards per carry.

The pass rush generated five total sacks, six quarterback hits, and over a 50 percent pressure rate:

It will be tough to maintain that without Hutchinson and against a better offensive line, but Derrick Moore, Alim McNeill, DJ Wonnum, and Skyler Gill-Howard have all played some pretty sound football, and all were disruptive on Sunday.

The linebackers deserve a lot of praise for Detroit's stout run defense, but they were a bit of a liability in the pass game again. It didn't end up costing the Lions too much in this game, because once Drake Maye went down, it looked like Tommy DeVito just didn't see the field very well. But coverage against tight ends and running backs continues to be a bit of an issue.

Still, this defense continues to play good football without its field general at MIKE linebacker, and that means something.

I thought the safety play was fantastic on Sunday. Brian Branch was all over the place in the run game and the pass game. Chuck Clark flipped a couple Patriots and made the receiving corps pay for every DeVito murderball.

I can't give them an A, though, because of a couple of stupid and costly pass interference flags. It wasn't a great game for Ennis Rakestraw—who also missed a key tackle—nor Nick Whiteside. But the good news is the top corners in this game—Rock Ya-Sin and Roger McCreary were very, very good. Or, as Dan Campbell said:

"I thought the back end played outstanding," Campbell said. "We played some sticky coverage today, bought us a little bit of time."

Nothing too notable from this group on Sunday. The return team didn't look particularly good, but coverage was good on both punt and kickoff. Jake Bates is still perfect when Jack Fox isn't blocking his kicks. He did put a kickoff out of bounds and a touchback in the end zone.

This was a tough week for both coaches. Flying across the globe, adjusting to a time zone six hours away, and dealing with all of the crazy logistics of getting ready for Sunday is not easy. It's clear one team was way more prepared than the other.

On top of that, Lions offensive coordinator Drew Petzing is really starting to come into his own, building plays off of previous plays, and seemingly having the right call in the right moment more often than not. As he hits his stride, the Lions offense can carry them a long way.

But don't sleep on the defensive coaching, either. Kelvin Sheppard has had to deal with two emotionally draining injuries to two of their best players. Yet through a heavy rotation at every level of the defense, things have never looked more steady and controlled. Say what you will, facing a beat-up Patriots offense with a backup quarterback leading most of Sunday afternoon, but Detroit used to get beat up by backups all the time. The defense finally feels like it's coming together.

#2763. Knicks 112, Raptors 108 (OT): Scenes from our first bonus basketball of the season

There's trouble when Mike Breen calls the Knicks out. Right before tip-off, the lifelong fan and broadcasting GOAT called them a "mediocre" basketball team, then acknowledged that they know it's a problem and they're trying to fix it. We noticed it, too; New York had lost two straight and been outhustled by the outclassed Indiana Pacers on Friday.

For 40 minutes tonight, the Knicks proved Mike's case. They led after one because Toronto couldn't shoot, and much the same was true at halftime. Then the Dinos began to pull away, nearly doubling up the Knicks in the paint and beating them to the boards. The Americans trailed by seven to start the fourth and by as many as 14 before finally showing some fire and desire. They went ahead with less than a minute left, but Scottie Barnes (30 PTS, 9 RBS, -9) scored Toronto's last nine points to force overtime. The Knicks never trailed in the fifth frame, and a Brunson dagger with 33 seconds left put them ahead for good, 112-108.

Back from a groin injury, Barnes scored 10 of Toronto's first 13 points, hitting back-to-back threes to put the Raptors up 13-4. Scottie was merriment and light while the Knicks were a smear of discouragement. Birthday boy Karl-Anthony Towns (28 PTS, 17 RBS) pitched two passes into the front row in the first four minutes, and Jalen Brunson (28 PTS, 9 AST, 41 MIN) had three dimes and one basket in the quarter. The bench improved matters. A Mikal Bridges (5 PTS, 7 RBS, 32 MIN . . . +15!) steal and a Towns bunny sparked a 9-0 run that included five points from Landry Shamet (23 PTS, 30 MIN, +12) and a tying dunk from Andre Drummond, courtesy of Josh Hart (0 PTS, 5 RBS, 26 MIN, -15).

Allen Graves stripped Brunson and Jakob Poeltl laid it in at the other end to put Toronto up 17-14. Then the Dinos, hardly renowned for their shooting, came up blank for the final 3:45. Tyler Kolek fed Towns for the tying three and Miles McBride for the one that made it 23-17 at the break.

Shamet scored six quick points to put the Knicks up 32-22. He hit a three after Kolek picked off an RJ Barrett pass, then made all three free throws after Barrett fouled him on another attempt. Toronto answered with a 14-2 run. Poeltl picked Jordan Clarkson's pocket and finished at the other end, starting center Collin Murray-Boyles dunked back a shot Shamet had blocked, and Jamal Shead (19 PTS) scored eight points in 76 seconds to put the Raptors ahead 38-36. During Toronto's 10-0 stretch, the Knicks burned a full shot clock and missed four straight shots.

OG Anunoby stopped the run with two free throws, and Towns put New York back in front with a three. Barrett tied it at 42, but Brunson answered with a step-back three, his only field goal of the quarter. Bridges, who'd barely figured into the offense, set up that shot with 45 seconds left and hit his first basket, a 21-footer, with seven seconds to go. Barnes managed just two points in the second, and Barrett had as many turnovers as baskets (two).

The Knicks were lucky to lead 47-43 at the half. The shooting gap was small (44% to 41%), but Toronto owned the paint, 26-14, won the boards by four, and turned 12 Knicks giveaways into 16 points. The three-ball kept our heroes afloat (42% to Toronto's 26%). For those keeping track, Bridges was 1-for-2 for two points, with two rebounds, an assist, and a steal . . . but stay tuned for this:

On to Q3: the Knicks led 57-54 midway through the third before Toronto scored seven straight. Brunson's three cut it to 63-62, but the Raptors answered with an 11-0 run, including two Shead threes (the kid was cooking). Barrett had eight points and three assists, and Shead scored nine as Toronto won the quarter 31-20 and took a 74-67 lead into the fourth. Cap scored 13 of New York's 20 points, KAT had four, Bridges made one free throw, and Hart continued to deal with a devastating allergy to buckets.

On to Q4: Immanuel Quickley hit two threes from at least 29 feet to put Toronto up 84-71 with 8:55 left. The Knicks answered with a 12-2 run. Kolek found Anunoby for two quick buckets, and Towns picked Barrett's pocket to send Bridges the other way for a layup. Towns had 15 points and seven rebounds in the quarter, while Brunson went scoreless but handed out five assists.

Down five with under two minutes left, New York scored seven straight. Bridges grabbed the offensive board that set up Shamet's tying three, and Towns put the Knicks ahead with a hook. Towns then hit from 28 feet to make it 95-92 with 20 seconds left, but Barnes answered with a step-back three six seconds later. He had 11 in the quarter and put the clamps on Brunson as time expired.

On to OT: Shamet and Brunson scored seven apiece in the bonus frame. Quickley kept Toronto close with two early buckets, one off a Bridges turnover. Barnes whiffed on free throws with 1:47 left, banked in a three to tie it at 104, and lobbed to Murray-Boyles to tie it again at 106. Out of a timeout, Bridges found Brunson for the go-ahead fadeaway three with 33 seconds left. Anunoby hit both free throws to restore the three-point cushion, Barnes missed a chance to tie it, Towns grabbed his 17th rebound, and then he split a pair at the line to seal the win.

Mo is gassing up his recap. The Knicks stay over the border for game with the Raps on Tuesday. Rest up, Knickerbockers.

Maye does not have a set timetable for a return, but multiple reports on Monday, Nov. 16, indicate that the Patriots' quarterback will miss significant time with a leg injury.

ESPN and NFL Media insider Ian Rapoport reported that Maye's injury may be severe enough to cause him to miss the rest of the season. The insider went on to write that the quarterback "will seek more medical information" following his team's return to the United States from Germany.Insider Adam Schefter later reported that Maye may have "fractured his ankle" and will undergo further testing to decide if surgery is necessary.

Tommy DeVito came in to relieve Maye and finished the game for New England.

DeVito's claim to fame came as a member of the New York Giants, but he's often better known for his Italian heritage than his play on the field.

He should be next in line to start if Maye is forced to miss time.

#2759. Raiders TE Brock Bowers leaves loss to Seahawks early with ankle injury

Brock Bowers didn't last long on Sunday afternoon.

The Las Vegas Raiders tight end was ruled out of their 21-13 loss to the Seattle Seahawks due to an ankle injury he suffered early in the first quarter. That knocked him out for the majority of Fernando Mendoza's starting debut at Allegiant Stadium.

Bowers, in the first quarter of the contest, went up to block Seahawks safety Nick Emmanwori for running back Ashton Jeanty. But as Jeanty cut the other way, Bowers had his legs rolled up on in a pile and he went down awkwardly.

Bowers remained down for a few moments while the team's training staff helped him, and he then limped to the sideline.

Bowers did return to the game briefly after that, which helped lead the way for Mendoza's rushing touchdown to get them on the board. But he left the game again late in the second quarter, and the team ruled him out for good just before the start of the second half with the ankle injury. Clearly, it was just too much for him to overcome.

Bowers may have escaped the contest without a major injury, per NFL Network. Early reports suggest the tight end is more day-to-day with his ankle issue. He'll undergo tests Monday to determine the severity of the injury.

Bowers finished with two catches for 18 yards. He entered Sunday with 658 yards and six touchdowns this season, his third in the league after the Raiders took him with the No. 13 overall pick out of Georgia in 2024.

Though the Raiders entered the locker room up by a field goal, the Seahawks scored a pair of touchdowns in the third quarter to break the game open. Jadarian Price ran it in from 12 yards out first, and then Jaxon Smith-Njigba hauled in a 71-yard pass from Drew Lock to give Seattle an 11-point lead at the time.

That was enough to secure the eight-point win.

Lock ended up going 14-of-17 for 240 yards with two touchdowns in the win for Seattle, which improved to 6-4 on the season. Zach Charbonnet had 94 rushing yards on two carries, and Smith-Njigba had 171 yards and a score on eight catches.

The Raiders dealt away quarterback Kirk Cousins at the deadline, which paved the way for Mendoza, the former Indiana star and reigning Heisman Trophy winner, to get the first start of his career. Mendoza went 17-of-29 for 143 yards in the loss. Mike Washington led them on the ground with 23 yards, and Jeanty had 46 receiving yards on four catches. The Raiders now sit at 5-5 on the year.

Though Mendoza appears to be holding his own so far, losing a target like Bowers for any substantial amount of time will make things much more difficult for him as his NFL career gets going.

#2752. As LeBron soars up all-time assist list, his teammates need to have their hands ready

Fourteen games into the season, the Sixers are noticing the LeBron James effect in just about every facet of life. After a win over the Indiana Pacers, Tyrese Maxey zoomed to the podium to knock out his media availability with the majority of the Sixers beat in the locker room interviewing James.

"I love LeBron James," Maxey said as he sat down in front of a room with only a couple reporters.

Of course, they're noticing it in plenty of ways on the court as well. That win saw LeBron record 11 assists, good enough to move him up ahead of Jason Kidd for third in all-time career assists. He now only trails Chris Paul and John Stockton.

It may not sound like it would be, but playing next to such a prolific passer is something they have to get used to. The fact that your teammate could hit you with the ball at any given moment is an adjustment.

On the first play of the game, Maxey was cutting down the baseline just for the sake of cutting through. He thought all he was doing was helping create space on the side of the floor he was vacating, not realizing that LeBron had found him wide open under the basket.

"I was not planning to get the ball and the ball hit me in my chest and I looked up I was at the rim so I had to lay it in and I missed it," Maxey said, "but it's just like plays like that where you got to be ready at all times."

The idea of being ready for the ball at any time when James is on the floor is something that the Sixers are trying to make a point of emphasis. As was the case with Maxey's smoked bunny, the process of learning that can look ugly at times.

James joked that the key to guys figuring it out is to "hit 'em in the head a couple of times." According to James, VJ Edgecombe was a particularly frequent victim of that during training camp.

"Even when you don't think you're open, you're gonna be open," is what James told Edgecombe and, frankly, all of his teammates. "I just tell my guys, always be paying attention to me when I got the ball because I definitely see plays develop before they happen."

Off-ball movement is often looked at as "dirty work" in the NBA, something the Sixers haven't excelled at in recent years. Because of James' ability to reward cutters, it's made the Sixers not just buy into it, but happy to do so.

"He makes you want to cut. He makes you want to play without the ball," Maxey said. "He makes you want to always have your hands ready and be ready to score the ball because he's that unselfish and he's going to find you."

They say raw assist numbers are not the truest mark of a passer or a facilitator. One of James' best assists of the game against Indiana was not given to him in the stat sheet, but it was entirely created by what he saw from outside the perimeter.

Dean Wade cut out of the strong side corner to open that up from the ball handlers, before hearing James tell him to run back. James saw that Wade's defender would help on Edgecombe once Edgecombe drove to the basket, leaving Wade wide open for a corner three. Steve Jones, a brilliant Xs and Os guy for The Dunker Spot, clipped the play.

After being around James for training camp and a handful of regular season games, Wade said he's not really surprised by LeBron's ability to make that kind of read in the moment.

"He sees everything that's going on," Wade said. "He knows what their defense is doing."

James has had a reputation for being able to diagnose opposing team's plays as they're being called. Pacers head coach Rick Carlisle, who called James an "NBA basketball AI machine," said that LeBron is the reason he doesn't have play calls anymore. James said that ability is something he's just always had with him.

"I've always, since I was a kid, had the ability to see plays before they actually happened," he said, "seeing the movement, being able to see like cracks in the defense before they was even open. It's something that's been with me since I was a kid."

The Sixers have struggled so far to put together all of this absurd offensive talent in a way that really clicks. Even after beating the Pacers, they are still 19th in the league in points per 100 possessions, per Cleaning the Glass.

Getting used to the tendencies of one of the best passers of all time should help things look smoother as the season goes on.

The Bengals wanted to create a special “white out” environment for Sunday’s game, with the home team wearing its “White Bengal” uniform and helmet.

After the performance against the Steelers, they may want to make that alternate kit permanent.

Quarterback Joe Burrow and receiver Ja’Marr Chase were stellar on Sunday night, with Cincinnati defeating division-rival Pittsburgh 38-18.

In just the first half, Burrow had 302 yards and three touchdowns before finishing the contest 35-of-44 for 409 yards with four TDs. Joe Flacco came in for mop-up duty midway through the final period.

Burrow also tied Peyton Manning’s record streak of five consecutive games of at least four touchdowns.

It was the third-highest output of Chase’s career and the fourth time he’s gone over 200 yards in a regular-season game.

The Bengals scored on four of their five first-half possessions, and would have made it all five if Evan McPherson had hit his 43-yard field goal attempt that sailed wide right. That was McPherson’s first missed kick of the season.

But McPherson had opened the scoring with a 24-yard field goal to cap the opening drive. Drew Sample had a 3-yard TD catch, Chase Brown had a 2-yard score, and Dohnte Meyers had a 15-yard touchdown reception to give the Bengals a 24-3 halftime lead.

Brown caught his second touchdown in the third quarter to make it 31-3. And Samaje Perine closed the Bengals’ scoring with his 1-yard touchdown run with 10:08 left in the fourth quarter.

Pittsburgh had just four first downs and 40 total yards at halftime.

With the win, the Bengals are now 7-2 on the season and have sole possession of first place in the AFC North. They will have an extra day to prepare, as they’ll face the Commanders next Monday night.

The Steelers fall to 6-3 and will be on the road to face the Eagles next Sunday afternoon.

#2748. 5 takeaways from Bills win over Jets

The Buffalo Bills beat the Jets 31-12 in Week 10 on inside MetLife Stadium, in a game that went from defensive slugfest in the first two quarters to blowout in the second half.

At 8-1, the Bills are out to their best start since 1991.

These are my takeaways from Buffalo's victory.

During the Bills' four-game win streak entering this game, which included dominance after the bye week, it felt natural to narrow focus on Buffalo's entire operation, checking for any component of the team that could improve.

And in wins over the Rams, Raiders, Ravens, and Vikings, Buffalo seemingly lacked efficiency from the pass game in a classic sense. You know, Josh Allen standing in the pocket and completing the football to pass catchers within the intended design of the play. It hadn't happened at the frequency one would expect in games in which the Bills scored 37, 33, 36, and 23 points (against the No. 1 defense in football on the road).

But in the second half against the Jets, the Bills demonstrated their ability to move the ball through the air in a normal, rhythmic way… at all levels of the field. And there was an explosive element that's been mostly missing over the past four outings.

For as good as Allen has been creating this season, and for as reliable as Buffalo has been on the ground, this team needs to be able to win with classic dropback passing too, and in the third and fourth quarters against the Jets, the Bills did just that.

The turf at MetLife Stadium has one of the most notorious reputations in the NFL. And a handful of Bills were dinged with injuries in this game, unsurprisingly.

Here's to hoping the likes of Christian Benford, Dorian Williams, and Dee Alford are OK. In their absence, Buffalo's defensive depth was immediately tested. And it shined.

The Bills defense didn't skip a beat with Kaleb Elarms-Orr, Jordan Hancock, and Maxwell Hairston on the field. But it wasn't just that trio making relief appearances for those sidelined in-game with injury.

Rookie T.J. Parker played the second-most snaps of his NFL career to date (38) and had five pressures with two sacks on 26 pass-rush snaps. Javon Solomon chipped in 12 snaps and registered a pair of pressures in his two pass-rush opportunities.

As we've come to know during the Allen era, depth can be vital in the playoffs, and Buffalo's backups are not only getting a decent amount of run this regular season but they're playing respectable football.

Brown was listed as doubtful going into this game. Ankle injury. He didn't practice Thursday or Friday. Then he told reporters while warming up pre-game he was going to play.

And I don't think anyone would've blamed him if he struggled against surging rookie, No. 2 overall pick David Bailey, on the edge. But that didn't happen.

Per Next Gen Stats, Brown squared off with Bailey 13 times and didn't allow a single pressure of Allen.

He was also the blocker attached to star veteran linebacker DeMario Davis 10 yards downfield on James Cook's 74-yard touchdown run that put the game away in the fourth quarter.

It was such a gutsy performance from Brown, who is still getting better in Year 7 at right tackle. With his height, agility, explosiveness, balance, and power, he's one of the most unique players at his position in football.

And this game was the latest piece of evidence that Brown is incredibly tough too.

So maybe not a takeaway just from this game, but I was reminded of just how tremendous of a football player Cook has become in his 157-yard performance in Week 10 that was capped with the long touchdown sprint.

Cook isn't Bijan Robinson or Derrick Henry. He's not regularly jump-cutting the opponent's entire linebacker group or running it over.

He's incredibly flexible in his lower half with outstanding vision as he works through blocks from his offensive line and one of the most dynamic open-field running backs in the game.

Only Jahmyr Gibbs has more 10-plus yard runs (34) than Cook (27). And Gibbs is the only back in football with more 15-plus yard runs (16) than the Bills feature back (14). Cook is up to 971 yards on the ground this season at 5.2 yards per. He can wear down a defense three or four yards at at time — like vs. Vikings — on 31 carries, or hit explosive plays on the ground like he did against the Jets in this one.

Through the first month of the 2026 campaign, this specific subheading would've been insane. But it's a testament to how things can change for a team — and a position group — throughout a long season in the NFL.

Terrel Bernard is 27 years old. Prime of his career. Dorian Williams is playing for a second contract. Elarms-Orr looks as ready to go in Year 1 as a team can expect from a fourth-round pick at linebacker.

In this contest, that trio had 19 tackles, two tackles for loss, three total pressures, and a sack without any missed tackles. And it aligned with how the those three have played over the past month or so and certainly since the bye week.

And Bernard, Williams, and KEO aren't simply thriving downhill. In this game, they allowed five catches for 30 yards in their coverage area. And that aligns with how well the group has collectively covered this season.

#2746. Dylan Harper wills the Spurs to a twelfth straight victory

A win is not always pretty. A Sunday afternoon game against the Utah Jazz got weird quickly, but the San Antonio Spurs were able to pull out a 110-102 win – their 12th in a row.

It probably wouldn't have happened without the late-game heroics of Dylan Harper, who scored a career-high 31 points.

As usual, Harper was excellent in transition. All game long, he ran the break to score buckets through and around the Jazz. This play shows what makes Harper tough to cover in transition. He's so fast and has a big frame that blocks defenders from getting to the ball, and he finishes with soft touch at the rim, even under duress.

Oh, and Harper is incredibly strong. He's shooting an eye-popping 82.3% from 0-3 feet away from the hoop this season. Already he is one of the best rim finishers in the NBA.

San Antonio's offense was best when it could get out and run. The Spurs had 29 points in transition. The team kept pushing the ball up the floor to catch the Jazz backpedaling. Utah is a youthful, athletic team, but even they weren't able to keep up with San Antonio's uptempo offensive attack.

Harper was helped by Victor Wembanyama, who was unstoppable in the first half, but cooled down a bit in the second. Wembanyama had 26 points, 10 rebounds, 6 assists, and 5 blocks. The Jazz did a pretty good job cutting off lanes for lobs, but the Spurs were able to find Wembanyama in transition for looks at the rim. It helps when your 7-foot-5 center is willing to run the floor ahead of the opposing big.

Wembanyama battled with Mo Bamba all game. Utah is extremely banged up at center, missing three potentially starting big men. Bamba filled in admirably with 26 points on 10-for-13 shooting and hit all 6 of his three-pointers.

Sometimes an assist is generated by the passer, and others are made by the scorer. This one was driven by the scorer, as Luke Kornet got all the way up to tip this lob in.

Perhaps the best play of the game came in the final minute, when Stephon Castle grabbed a long rebound and turned it into a windmill dunk. The Spurs were already in control of the game, but this play put the exclamation point on it.

#2744. Romelu Lukaku retires from international football after 16-year Belgium career

Belgium's all-time record goalscorer Romelu Lukaku has retired from international football at the age of 33.

The forward made the announcement on Monday, a day after being an unused substitute as Belgium beat Italy 4-1 in the Nations League.

Lukaku had been named in the Red Devils' squad for this month's Nations League fixtures, but missed last Thursday's 2-1 win over Turkey with a hip injury and then failed to make it off the bench against Italy.

He scored 94 goals in 135 appearances for Belgium over a run that began with his debut in 2010.

The former Chelsea and Manchester United striker revealed his decision in a statement on his official Instagram page.

"Over these 16 years, I gave everything for the national team," Lukaku said. "I experienced every emotion imaginable. I was lucky enough to play alongside extraordinary teammates, to whom I will always be grateful. I want to thank them all.

Lukaku now plays for Fenerbahce in Turkey after previously starring in the Premier League (Getty)

"I also want to thank all the coaches who pushed me to give my best and trusted me to help the team. It was a wonderful journey, and I cherished every moment.

"To the Belgian fans, thank you for all the support you have given our team. I am proud to have represented my country at four World Cups and three European Championships. I will never forget those moments.

"I am at peace with my decision to stop here. It was incredible. I enjoyed it immensely. I am grateful. Thank you."

His final Belgium appearance came in a 4-1 defeat by France last month.

He leaves the international stage six goals short of a century, having struggled with a number of injuries in recent years.

The Fenerbahce attacker was still a central figure at this summer's World Cup, finding the net against New Zealand, Senegal and the United States.

Those goals made him Belgium's outright leading scorer at World Cups with eight, moving him past the previous record-holder, Marc Wilmots.

Across a lengthy international career, Lukaku helped Belgium finish third at the 2018 World Cup. He also reached back-to-back European Championship quarter-finals with his country in 2016 and 2021.

#2743. Jahmyr Gibbs in Hall of Fame company with a long list of statistical achievements

Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs had another phenomenal game on Sunday, and in his fourth NFL season he has hit a long list of statistical milestones that only Hall of Famers have reached before him.

In Sunday’s 35-10 win over the Patriots, Gibbs carried 22 times for 153 yards and two touchdowns, and added seven catches for 99 yards. After the game, the NFL distributed a list of Gibbs’ stats that show him either equaling or exceeding the accomplishments of some of the greatest running backs ever to play the game. Among Gibbs’ milestones:

Gibbs has the most touchdowns in NFL history in a player’s first four seasons. He has now scored 62 touchdowns (50 rushing and 12 receiving), breaking the previous record of Hall of Famer Terrell Davis, who had 61 touchdowns in his first four seasons.

Gibbs’ 50 career rushing touchdowns make him the third player in NFL history to run for 50 touchdowns before turning 25. The other two are Hall of Famers Barry Sanders with 52, and Emmitt Smith with 50. Gibbs doesn’t turn 25 until after this season, so he’s a near-lock to move ahead of Sanders and into first place on the all-time list.

Gibbs and Hall of Famer LaDainian Tomlinson are the only players in NFL history to have multiple games with at least 250 scrimmage yards and two rushing touchdowns before turning 25.

Gibbs, Tomlinson and Hall of Famer Eric Dickerson are the only players to have four games of at least 200 scrimmage yards and two rushing touchdowns in their first four seasons.

Gibbs has topped 1,200 scrimmage yards and 10 rushing touchdowns in each of his first four seasons. The only players who have done that before are Tomlinson, Dickerson, Hall of Famer Earl Campbell and future Hall of Famer Adrian Peterson.

Gibbs and Amon-Ra St. Brown have played 24 games together in which they’ve both scored touchdowns, surpassing Bills Hall of Famers Thurman Thomas and Andre Reed, who both scored in 23 games, for the fourth-most games in which running back-wide receiver teammates both score. All the players ahead of Gibbs and St. Brown are Hall of Famers: Emmitt Smith and Michael Irvin did it 32 times for the Cowboys, Lenny Moore and Raymond Berry did it 31 times for the Colts, and Edgerrin James and Marvin Harrison did it 25 times for the Colts.

Only three and a half seasons into his NFL career, it’s too early to put Gibbs in the Hall of Fame. But everything about the way he has played so far indicates that some day he’ll have a bust in Canton.

#2741. Travis Hunter now has two games with a catch and an interception. Deion Sanders had nine.

Jaguars cornerback Travis Hunter intercepted a pass on Sunday against the Titans, and doing his part-time job as a wide receiver, he also caught two passes. It was the second time Hunter has both caught and intercepted a pass in the same game.

That's a rare feat in the modern NFL, where few players play both ways. It's been four years since any player other than Hunter had both a catch and an interception in the same game. The last player to do it was New England's Marcus Jones, who did it twice in 2022.

Since the 1970 AFL-NFL merger, the player who has had both a catch and an interception in the same game the most times is Hunter's college coach, Deion Sanders, who did it nine times. Sanders did it three times while playing for the Falcons and six times while playing for the Cowboys.

Hunter is primarily a defensive player: He played 56 defensive snaps and only six offensive snaps on Sunday, and that's been typical for him this season. Overall in 2026, Hunter has played 84 percent of the Jaguars' defensive snaps and 9 percent of the Jaguars' offensive snaps. But the Jaguars say they view Hunter as a two-way player for the long term, so there's a good chance that he'll have more games with both a catch and an interception, and perhaps eclipse Sanders' modern-era record of nine such games.

But Hunter is unlikely to break the all-time record of Packers Hall of Famer Don Hutson, who had 21 games with both a catch and an interception between 1940 and 1945. Hutson had some statistics that don't look possible, such as the game when he outscored the Chicago Cardinals all by himself with six catches for 86 yards and two touchdowns, plus two interceptions for 84 return yards and a pick-six, in a 35-14 Packers victory. Hutson was by far the best receiver of his era and one of the best defensive players of his era, and he was also a pretty good kicker by the standards of the 1940s. There will never be another Don Hutson.

What Hunter is doing in 2026, however, is a special accomplishment that also deserves celebration. There's no one else playing the game in quite the same way Hunter is playing it.

The Minnesota Timberwolves suffered their worst defeat of the 2026-27 season on Saturday, as the lowly Chicago Bulls beat them 117-106 at the Target Center. There was plenty of blame to go around for this loss, but Rudy Gobert, in particular, came under fire for another disastrous offensive performance.

Finch has almost always defended the oft-criticized Gobert, but even he chose to call him out here. Now, the 34-year-old has never been viewed as even a good offensive player, but he's been woeful this season.

"I mean, both, really," Finch said. "… I mean, we came out just trying to hoist up threes, hoping that they would go in. They were so, so shots. Some were okay, some of them weren't. "When we were able to, they snuck behind us for cheap rebounds or relocated when we were not paying attention to our guy off-ball," Finch added. "So yeah, really, really unacceptable performance."

The Bulls shot 44-90 (48.9%) from the field and 14-30 (46.7%) from beyond the arc on the night. It was one of their better offensive showings of the season.

As for the Timberwolves, they went 38-91 (41.8%) from the field and 9-38 (23.7%) from beyond the arc. It was the first quarter that really cost the hosts, as they scored just 17 points in the period after missing all 10 of the threes they attempted.

#2737. Mike Macdonald praises Tory Horton's "tremendous play" on late kickoff return

After the Raiders cut the Seahawks’ lead to 21-13 by kicking a field goal with 2:04 left in Sunday’s game, they wanted to force a touchback that would allow them to use the two-minute warning as a third timeout in hopes of getting the ball back.

“It was a tremendous play,” Macdonald said, via the team’s website. “Tory’s actually trying to catch that ball, albeit with one hand. Just an incredible play. With George Holani going down, we had to take [Jadarian Price] off of kickoff returns, so those are guys that haven’t necessarily practiced a bunch in a while, especially with this game plan. So to be able to step in and be able to execute some of those critical situations is some great stuff by them, great job by our coaches, and it really helped us close the game out. . . . We told them that was the situation going. Now, there’s a difference between catching it 8 yards deep in the end zone and making a play like that, which is just some really, really great stuff.”

The Seahawks were likely to win the game regardless of how the kickoff played out, but Horton made closing things out easier and his effort will be on the minds of many people around the league if they find themselves in a similar situation.

The Los Angeles Lakers have been one of the best teams in the NBA through the early stages of the season, entering Phoenix riding a seven-game winning streak and sporting an 11-2 record. As the game progressed and Los Angeles built a 31-point lead, I resigned myself to the fact that the chasm between their excellence and the Suns' mediocrity was painfully apparent. Considering where things stood earlier in the afternoon, that's a small victory in and of itself.

What Sunday afternoon ultimately reinforced, however, was how fundamentally broken the Phoenix Suns' starting lineup is. Because the brand of basketball we've come to associate with this team is alive and well in Phoenix. We saw it in the fourth quarter. The energy, the defensive aggression, the connectivity, and the collective determination to make life uncomfortable for the opposition. Unfortunately, those characteristics are often masked by questionable roster construction, duplicative player archetypes in the starting five, and a lack of clearly defined roles.

There's an identity within this basketball team waiting to emerge with greater consistency, and we continue to see flashes of it when Jordan Ott turns to his bench. Meanwhile, the starting unit remains heavily dependent on Devin Booker's ability to manufacture productive stretches of basketball through his individual brilliance. When he can't, the unit begins to crumble under the weight of its own deficiencies, particularly its inability to rebound the basketball.

How much longer can you continue rolling out a starting five that routinely puts your second unit in a position where it has to resuscitate the basketball team?

#2735. Florida ranks fourth most expensive for entry-level NASCAR tickets

Florida ranked fourth most expensive for entry-level NASCAR tickets in a new analysis of listings on SeatGeek.

Westgate Events calculated an average starting ticket price of $97 across eight Florida events. Only Connecticut, Ohio and California had higher averages.

The figure represents the average of the lowest-priced tickets listed for each event, rather than the average price of all tickets purchased.

Connecticut had the highest average starting price at $162, followed by Ohio at $114 and California at $112.

New Hampshire had the lowest at $37, followed by Georgia at $38 and Delaware at $42.

Florida's cheapest individual ticket in the dataset was $40.

Researchers examined 101 events, with active pricing available for 90 across 23 states. The dataset included several racing series and other event listings, including FANZONE access.

The comparison reflects available listings rather than completed ticket sales. It does not measure the full cost of attending a race, including transportation, lodging and food.

Daytona International Speedway's upcoming schedule includes the return of the Clash on Feb. 13 and the Daytona 500 on Feb. 21.

#2732. Rapid Recap: Hawks 113, Bucks 106

The Milwaukee Bucks led by as much as 22 at the start of the second quarter, blew the lead by halftime, and never retook the lead in Sunday's 113-106 loss to the Atlanta Hawks. The Bucks threatened to take the lead late in the fourth quarter, largely thanks to a career-high night from Kasparas Jakucionis, who scored 25 points (21 of which came in the second half). However, the Bucks struggled with turnovers and unnecessary fouling, which slowed their momentum and allowed the Hawks to hold on. Gary Trent Jr. scored 18 points, while Kyle Kuzma and Brayden Burries had 14 and 13, respectively. CJ McCollum and Nickeil Alexander-Walker each accounted for 20 points, while Onyeka Okongwu had 16 and Jalen Johnson added 14.

The Bucks started the game with the upper hand. Kyle Kuzma poured in the first three, splashing a bomb as the shot clock expired, and the Bucks kept the hot shooting going. Myles Turner added one, and Kuzma made two more triples within the first six minutes, prompting a quick timeout from Hawks head coach Quin Snyder. Milwaukee forced frequent Atlanta turnovers, kept them cold from the perimeter, and shot well on offense. Jaime Jaquez Jr. even scored a fading corner three to push the Bucks' lead to 13 points, and after Kel'el Ware swatted a Corey Kispert layup attempt off the glass, Gary Trent Jr. fired a transition bomb to give the Bucks a first-quarter lead of 16! Trent's fast-break layup with just over 36 seconds left gave Milwaukee a 37-18 lead by the end of the first quarter—their best quarter of the season by a country mile.

Milwaukee pressed its advantage to open the second quarter, with Trent and Jaquez connecting on early triples, but Atlanta slowly began to break out of its shooting slump. The Hawks embarked on an 11-3 run, led by an Alexander-Walker layup that trimmed Milwaukee's lead to just 13. RayJ Dennis found Onyeka Okongwu open in the paint with a slicing pass, and Okongwu dunked on Myles Turner to quiet the raucous Fiserv Forum. Jalen Johnson powered in a fast-break dunk, cutting the Bucks' lead to single digits, and the home team suddenly found itself on the back foot. Milwaukee's hot first-quarter shooting had failed them; they shot just 3/15 from three in the second quarter as the Hawks upped their defensive intensity. The Bucks' intensity, by contrast, seemed to wane as their lead shrank, giving up several offensive rebounds and turning the ball over on silly errors; Milwaukee totalled eight second-quarter turnovers. A pair of McCollum free throws tied the game with a little over a minute remaining, and a fadeaway from Alexander-Walker after lazy rebounding efforts gave them the lead; up 55-53 at half.

Atlanta extended its lead after the half. Dyson Daniels connected on a pull-up jumper, Alexander-Walker scored from the midrange, and NAW cashed a three, pushing Atlanta's edge to eight with nine minutes remaining in the third. The Bucks looked like they'd been punched in the mouth as Taylor Jenkins called the first timeout. However, the Hawks struggled to pull away; despite leading by ten points midway through the third, Milwaukee's defense tightened to cool Atlanta's hot shooting and continued to cut the lead. Milwaukee's shooting improved, especially from Jakucionis, who poured in 10 points in the third quarter. Daniels got a floater to go at the end of the third quarter, leaving Atlanta up 87-80 entering the final frame.

With Milwaukee's second win of the season on the line, they didn't let up. The Bucks stayed competitive, opening the final frame with a four-point play by Trent (yes, Gary Trent Jr.). The Bucks feasted on the Hawks' lack of ball security, cutting the deficit to as little as one, and they sought contact on both ends of the court, a welcome sign for a young, developing team. Jakucionis and Turner each had huge and-ones, the latter trimming Atlanta's lead to just two points with 6:32 left. However, Milwaukee got into foul trouble late, and Burries and Jakucionis missed crucial jumpers that kept the game close. Milwaukee, especially the frontcourt, was too handsy on defense and kept sending sharpshooters like McCollum and Johnson to the line. Jakucionis kept the Bucks in the game, though, spearheading fast-break opportunities and hitting some big jumpers down the line. His three-pointer with 1:57 remaining trimmed Atlanta's lead to three, up 109-106, and they remained in the game when Okongwu fumbled an easy fast-break layup. Jakucionis saw his heat-check three-pointer go in and out, and McCollum went down the other end and iced a step-back midrange jumper to give the Hawks a two-possession lead with just 17 seconds left, which they wouldn't relinquish.

The Hawks had 15 fourth-quarter free throws to the Bucks' nine. The Bucks, and especially Myles Turner, were undisciplined down the stretch when it came to foul discipline. Those needless fouls derailed Milwaukee's comeback bid and gave an otherwise struggling Hawks team a free source of points.

It's time to give Kasparas Jakucionis a starting spot. The second-year guard fired from all cylinders in the second half, and his career-high 25 points came with great efficiency (9/16 from the field and 4/10 from beyond the arc). The Bucks' starting guards also struggled on Sunday; Tyler Herro had just five points on 13 shots, and Burries was pretty mediocre. Jakucionis could be an enticing option for Jenkins to turn to in response to the backcourt's inconsistency.

#2731. 100 years ago: Rangers begin life in NHL by blanking Stanley Cup champs

The New York Rangers officially cap their Centennial celebration when they host the Montreal Canadiens on Monday night at Madison Square Garden. The "Capstone Game" commemorates the 100th anniversary of the Blueshirts' NHL debut, when they defeated the defending Stanley Cup champion Montreal Maroons 1-0 at the third Madison Square Garden (about a mile north of the current MSG, which opened in February 1968).

And what an evening, when an estimated 13,000 well-dressed spectators filled the Garden to greet their new team.

"The usual high-hat society crowd gathered early," Brooklyn Daily Times writer James J. Wood wrote in the next day's paper. "There was enough fur, silk and satin in the arena boxes alone to decorate all the shop windows on Fifth Avenue — and we don't mean Brooklyn."

The Rangers weren't New York's first hockey team. That honor belonged to the New York Americans, who began play in 1925 after the franchise moved from Hamilton, Ontario. The "Amerks" used the new Madison Square Garden as their home – and drew enough fans that the Garden's owner/president, "Tex" Rickard, persuaded the NHL to grant another New York franchise.

Hockey 100 years ago was vastly different that the current product. The rosters were smaller (the Rangers dressed 10 skaters and a goaltender on opening night), the slap shot, red line, curved stick and goalie mask were decades away from being invented, and there were limitations on forward passing that limited attackers.

But the competitiveness was just as intense.

There was plenty of pre-game hoopla, including movie star Lois Moran presenting a handmade hockey stick to Rangers captain Bill Cook, before referee Lou Marsh dropped the puck for the first face-off in Rangers history.

Marsh, who was using a dinner bell instead of a whistle, according to The New York Times, was the busiest man on the ice during the first period; neither team scored, but he handed out eight minor penalties. The goalies – Clint Benedict of the Maroons and Hal Winkler of the Rangers – were flawless, with Winkler stopping 19 shots and Benedict making 16 saves.

After the opening 20 minutes, Katie Schmidt from the Winter Garden in Berlin and her 12 internationally famous ice ballet dancers took over and rendered a specially composed theme for the occasion. Not exactly like today's between-periods "entertainment."

Then it was back to hockey. The game remained scoreless until late in the second period, when Cook put his new stick to good use.

Bill and younger brother Fred "Bun" Cook "staged a great brother act," The Times wrote, "and after a brilliant sally down the ice, Bill scored the first goal of the game at 18:37. Bunny passed from the left of the net out to Bill, who had practically an open net after Benedict had fallen when he blocked the preceding shot.

"The crowd roared as Bill put in the shot," but Benedict had to leave the ice briefly for repairs after hitting his head on the goal post.

The third period was scoreless — but not without a historic moment. Frank Boucher, who centered the Cook brothers on the "Bread Line," would go on to win the Lady Byng Trophy, given for "skillful and gentlemanly play," so often (seven times) that the NHL finally gave it to him and had a new one created. But on this night. Boucher got into a fight with Montreal's Merlyn Phillips – the only one of his Hall of Fame career. The two battled with fists and sticks, with each assessed a five-minute major penalty and $15 fine.

"Boucher – small as he was – fooled us all by drawing the first five-minute major penalty for fighting," wrote Kerr N. Petrie of the New York Herald-Tribune.

By night's end, Marsh had assessed 18 penalties – 11 to the visitors, seven to the home side. Four of the penalties, all minors, went to Maroons star center Nels Stewart.

In the end, Winkler's 48-save effort and Bill Cook's goal enabled the Rangers to hold off the defending Cup champs 1-0. The headline on writer Seabury Lawrence's story noted simply that "Rangers Capture Hockey Opener." One of the subheads added a dash of spice by noting: "Game is Fiercely Fought."

The win turned out to be the start of a successful beginning for the Blueshirts. Led by Bill Cook's NHL-best 33 goals, they finished first in the American Division in their inaugural season, then won the Stanley Cup in 1927-28 – ironically, by defeating the Maroons.

Both Cook brothers and Boucher are in the Hockey Hall of Fame, though none of the three had his number retired by the Rangers. They were among the honorees on the first of last season's Centennial games, when the Rangers honored members of the original Blueshirts on "Birth of the Franchise" night.

#2728. Travis Hunter now has two games with a catch and an interception. Deion Sanders had nine.

Jaguars cornerback Travis Hunter intercepted a pass on Sunday against the Titans, and doing his part-time job as a wide receiver, he also caught two passes. It was the second time Hunter has both caught and intercepted a pass in the same game.

That’s a rare feat in the modern NFL, where few players play both ways. It’s been four years since any player other than Hunter had both a catch and an interception in the same game. The last player to do it was New England’s Marcus Jones, who did it twice in 2022.

Since the 1970 AFL-NFL merger, the player who has had both a catch and an interception in the same game the most times is Hunter’s college coach, Deion Sanders, who did it nine times. Sanders did it three times while playing for the Falcons and six times while playing for the Cowboys.

Hunter is primarily a defensive player: He played 56 defensive snaps and only six offensive snaps on Sunday, and that’s been typical for him this season. Overall in 2026, Hunter has played 84 percent of the Jaguars’ defensive snaps and 9 percent of the Jaguars’ offensive snaps. But the Jaguars say they view Hunter as a two-way player for the long term, so there’s a good chance that he’ll have more games with both a catch and an interception, and perhaps eclipse Sanders’ modern-era record of nine such games.

But Hunter is unlikely to break the all-time record of Packers Hall of Famer Don Hutson, who had 21 games with both a catch and an interception between 1940 and 1945. Hutson had some statistics that don’t look possible, such as the game when he outscored the Chicago Cardinals all by himself with six catches for 86 yards and two touchdowns, plus two interceptions for 84 return yards and a pick-six, in a 35-14 Packers victory. Hutson was by far the best receiver of his era and one of the best defensive players of his era, and he was also a pretty good kicker by the standards of the 1940s. There will never be another Don Hutson.

What Hunter is doing in 2026, however, is a special accomplishment that also deserves celebration. There’s no one else playing the game in quite the same way Hunter is playing it.

#2722. JJ Redick gets real on Lakers ‘ceiling,’ frustrating blown leads

Before the season began, he raised eyebrows with a bold claim: he was "confident" the Lakers could become "a championship-level team this year."

They were miles behind the Thunder and Spurs in the Western Conference.

But 14 games into the season, Redick is the one chuckling at his detractors after the Lakers won eight games in a row and are tied for the best record in the league at 12-2.

Some of the wins haven't been pretty, including Sunday's 131-123 win over the Suns in which they watched a 31-point lead disintegrate to five points in the fourth quarter before Quentin Grimes banked in a 3-pointer and Luka Doncic made a pair of free throws to save the day.

Despite Lakers coach JJ Redick having his analytics department prepare a 21-page audit detailing where LA can improve offensively and defensively, it's clear the team has wildly surpassed expectations.

Los Angeles Lakers head coach JJ Redick looks on during the first quarter against the Milwaukee Bucks at Fiserv Forum in Milwaukee, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Getty Images

And Redick thinks this is just the beginning.

"I don't think we should put a ceiling on this group," Redick said. "This group is committed to getting better every single day, recognizing that this is a process to become a high-level team. And that's what I want from this group, is hold each other to that standard every single time. And that's the frustrating part at times because you see how good we can be. There's no reason to ever play less than that standard, you know?"

Redick is like the never-satisfied father who sees the potential in his son. He rides him. He pushes him.

That style is working with this Lakers team.

Luka Doncic is playing MVP-level basketball, including finishing with his seventh 40-point performance in 12 games on Sunday, with 43 points, three rebounds and five assists.

Luka Doncic (77) of the Los Angeles Lakers shoots against the Phoenix Suns in Phoenix, Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

Walker Kessler had his fifth straight double-double against the Suns with 14 points and 12 rebounds. And Austin Reaves, who was sidelined Sunday because of a bruised heel, looks like the best No. 2 in the league.

They also have some things going wrong: When Doncic isn't on the floor, the Lakers blow leads. Their third unit can't be trusted. And defensively, they're ranked No. 18.

But they're the top-rated team in the league on offense and they entered Sunday's game leading the league in scoring (122.2 points per game), field goal percentage (50.3%), steals (11 per game) and points off turnovers (24.5 per game).

Walker Kessler of the Los Angeles Lakers looks on during a game against the Phoenix Suns in Phoenix on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

Redick is right not to put a ceiling on the Lakers.

He got them to buy into their championship potential.

And now he's pushing them to believe they haven't even tapped into who they could become despite being atop the league.

"Honestly, I think we have a lot of space for improvement," Doncic said. "Obviously one thing for now is blowing some leads. I think we got to work on that, for sure. But I think every aspect of the game, I feel like we have a lot of improvement left."

The Lakers blew a 25-point lead to the Warriors in a 112-95 loss on Oct. 30. At least Sunday, they pumped the brakes and recovered. The Lakers are still figuring things out.

Burrow and the offense came out firing, confident in their ability to have their way with any defense, even one as intimidating as Pittsburgh's.

#2719. Emotional Kirk Cousins: "It's been a tough three years. There's more to the story being written."

Three years ago, quarterback Kirk Cousins played the last game of his first stint with the Vikings at Lambeau Field, tearing an Achilles tendon during a Week 8 game. The first game of his second stint happened on Sunday.

The Vikings won, 30-10, completing the season sweep of the Packers and moving to 7-2 on the season. And Cousins was visibility emotional during his an-field interview after the win with Lindsey Thiry of ESPN.

“It was emotional, you know, coming to the stadium, three years ago, tearing my Achilles here,” Cousins said, voice breaking multiple times. “It’s been a tough three years,”

He also made good decisions in key moments, helping the Vikings’ offense convert eight of 15 third-down situations.

It all happened after Cousins showed up only four days before the game. He now has a full week to prepare for a game against the 49ers — the last team he played during his nine-game run in Las Vegas.

#2718. Nets’ jumbo lineup proving to be intriguing wrinkle — even with mixed results

It was deadly in New Orleans. It misfired the next game in Memphis — albeit with lesser ammo. But the Nets have it all the same.

Coach Jordi Fernández will likely use his historically big lineup less as Brooklyn's young guards eventually command more playing time. But he has the supersized wrinkle in his arsenal, ready to go to whenever he needs.

"Yeah, I think it helps," Fernández told The Post. "I mean, you think about Danny [Wolf] at the quote-unquote two, but obviously his versatility of shooting, being able to playmake, also a big body defensively that can rebound: All those things are important. Let's see how we keep evolving."

In each of the past two games, the Nets started five players all 6-foot-9 or taller.

No NBA team had started such a lineup in 37 seasons, when the Lakers fielded A.C. Green (6-foot-9), Magic Johnson (6-9), Mychal Thompson (6-10), Orlando Woolridge (6-9) and James Worthy (6-9) back on April 21, 1990.

Danny Wolf #2 of the Brooklyn Nets dribbles during a game against the Memphis Grizzlies at FedExForum in Memphis, Tenn., Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

For Brooklyn, it provided intriguing — albeit mixed — results.

"It just speaks to the type of players we have," center Day'Ron Sharpe told The Post. "For us to have five 6-9 or higher on the court, speaks to the ability to switch one through five or switch one through four. And it gives a size for rebounding, which has been a big key for us.

"So even if I'm out there on the perimeter, you've got Danny, you've got Michael [Porter Jr.], you've got Julius [Randle], you've got Egor [Dëmin], who all could come back here and rebound. We've just got to keep buying into it."

In the past two games the Nets started Sharpe, Randle, Dëmin and Wolf, the latter's rare combo of size and ballhandling making him a 6-11 off-guard. They split the games, winning in New Orleans and falling Saturday in Memphis. The difference was leading scorer Porter missing the Grizzlies tilt, replaced in the starting lineup by Noah Clowney.

"Yeah, last year, we started off very small. Then, we transitioned over time to a bigger lineup and more length," Porter, who'll be back Monday vs. the 76ers, told The Post.

Julius Randle (30) of the Brooklyn Nets looks on during a game against the Memphis Grizzlies at FedExForum in Memphis, Tenn., Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

"It just helps out for sure in different aspects of the game. Danny's a great piece to connect players; he can rebound, he can push the ball, he can dribble the ball and just facilitate, he has a high IQ. So he's helped on the boards as well. And obviously having Egor back was big for us."

With the 6-foot-9 Dëmin returning from a bone bruise — and 6-foot-4 pure point guards Nolan Traore (sore calf) and Mikel Brown Jr. (illness) sidelined against New Orleans — the supersize starting lineup powered a 145-111 victory.

The starters logged a dozen minutes together and were a plus-18. All scored in double figures and were at least a plus-17, led by Randle's plus-38 — tied for the best in Nets history for a road game.

Michael Porter Jr., left, Terance Mann and Moritz Wagner react during a game against the New Orleans Pelicans on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026, in New Orleans. Getty Images

But with Porter out against the Grizzlies, Fernández subbed Clowney in his place. That version was nowhere near as effective in a 129-110 loss, the Jumbo Lineup a minus-2 in 13 minutes. Every starter was a minus-7 or worse, except Sharpe (plus-4).

Granted, the competition was a lot tougher, the Pelicans 4-10 and losers of six straight while the Grizzlies are 9-4. Just as important was Porter, whose absence is expected to just be for one game.

Fernández himself has admitted Dëmin is best deployed off the ball, which means he'd eventually go back to two-guard and relegate Wolf back to the bench. The point guard spot would then be manned by either Traore or eventually Brown, the sixth overall pick and heir apparent once he's off his current minutes restriction.

But with Porter back, the Jumbo Lineup remains dangerous.

"Yeah, for sure. Obviously, it's a unique lineup," Wolf said. "And there's definitely some things that I've done well and a lot of things I can continue to work on.

"It also gives us a unique look defensively and on the glass. We've just got to continue to rebound at a high level with so much size out there."

#2716. NFL analyst gives apt description of Panthers' frustrating Week 10 win

To be totally fair, some of the flags that the officials threw against the Carolina Panthers on Sunday were questionable. The offensive pass interference against tight end Darren Waller comes to mind, as does the late face-mask call against linebacker Tyrel Dodson that could have changed the game.

But even if half of the penalties they drew were incorrect, the Panthers still committed far too many of them in their 20-17 win against the New Orleans Saints.

All together, Carolina was flagged a franchise-record 17 times, losing 152 yards in the process. They also got just 200 passing yards and zero touchdowns from quarterback Bryce Young, while wideout Jalen Coker was completely shut out.

Fortunately, running back Chuba Hubbard was able to shoulder the load on offense, with two touchdowns and 172 yards from scrimmage on 32 touches. Plus, their defense came to play—holding the Saints to 222 yards and taking the ball away three times.

Here, in NFL.com's Week 10 takeaways, is how Bobby Kownack describes the triumph:

Carolina won in the most frustrating way possible. The Panthers were responsible for laundry littering the field from the very start, beginning the game with a kickoff out of bounds and failing to clean things up thereafter . . . The Panthers' lack of discipline was made even more glaring by New Orleans only committing three penalties, plus the litany of late-game lapses that almost cost Carolina. The Saints offense only accounted for 28 yards on its nine-play drive to take a 14-10 lead late in the final frame. The Panthers gave up the other 42 yards on penalties.

Sloppy games happen to every NFL team, but this isn't the first or the second or the third time this season that the Panthers have shot themselves in both feet with procedural penalties. Head coach Dave Canales told reporters after the game that those flags are the ones he's concerned with.

"I mean, some of the penalties that are judgment calls—they're gonna call them how they see them," Canales stated. "The things that I'm gonna focus on are the ones we have to take control of—which is offsides penalties, pre-snap deals, delay of games, those types of procedural penalties. We gotta eliminate those.

"The competitive calls are gonna happen. There's ways to talk about the technique. But it's really just the things that we can control that we really have to focus on."

Somebody should tell Canales that it's his job to make sure that happens. The peak Seattle Seahawks teams that Canales was a part of early in his coaching career were good enough to overcome a parade of flags in practically every game, but this team is definitely not.

#2715. Lakers guard mimics Paul Pierce’s iconic line after burying Suns

PHOENIX — Quentin Grimes broke out of his early-season shooting slump in a major way during the Lakers' 131-123 win over the Suns on Sunday at Mortgage Matchup Center.

And he arguably had the biggest sequence of the game to seal the victory.

Quentin Grimes of the Los Angeles Lakers handles the ball against the Phoenix Suns in Phoenix, Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

After the Suns cut what was once a 31-point Lakers lead late in the third quarter to five points with just over a minute left in the game, Jake LaRavia missed a corner 3-pointer that could've given the Lakers a larger cushion or given the Suns an opportunity to make it a single-possession game.

Grimes made sure the latter didn't happen, crashing the offensive glass and grabbing the rebound off LaRavia's miss to give the Lakers another shot at scoring.

Quentin Grimes (5) of the Los Angeles Lakers dribbles the ball against the Phoenix Suns on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026, at Mortgage Matchup Center in Phoenix. NBAE via Getty Images

The veteran wing took matters into his own hands when he banked in a pull-up 3 to put the Lakers up 129-121 with 32.2 seconds left to ice the game.

Did Grimes call bank before making the game-sealing 3?

"I called game," Grimes said before repeating the line twice. "I mean, the bank ain't open on Sunday. I called game. Trying to get out of here and get back to L.A."

Paul Pierce, who was playing for the Wizards at the time, famously responded "I called game!" after banking in the game-winning shot of Game 3 of the Wizards' Eastern Conference Semifinals playoff series against the Hawks.

Los Angeles Lakers guard Quentin Grimes speaks to reporters following a game against the Phoenix Suns in Phoenix on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

While Grimes had fun with his response to whether he intentionally banked in the 3, Sunday was an important step for him to break out of his shooting slump.

The sixth-year guard made a season-high five 3s against the Suns, with his performance on Sunday increasing his 3-point percentage from 24.2% to 33.3%.

The Lakers are confident Grimes, who's shot just over 36% on 3s for his career, will continue to find his groove with his perimeter shot.

"Watching him every day, when he is in the gym, he's very consistent with his routine," coach JJ Redick said. "And we tell players this all the time: Whether you're shooting well or you're shooting poorly, you should just keep the same routine. Because otherwise, then it becomes, 'is shooting a superstitious thing?' I don't think it is, right? Shooting is based on form and reps and confidence, and the only way to build that confidence is through the reps.

"He's just handled it really well. He's been in the gym, he's got the shots up, he's done his routine. He's historically had some really good shooting seasons both from catch-and-shoot and off-the-dribble. We don't think he's a 26% [3-point shooter] or whatever he is, I don't know what he's been before [Sunday] but somewhere in the 20s. He's a high 30s guy."

Ai microfoni del podcast Sky Calcio Unplugged condotto da Gianluca Di Marzio è stato intervistato l’ex diesse della Lazio, Igli Tare

Ai microfoni del podcast Sky Calcio Unplugged condotto da Gianluca Di Marzio è stato intervistato l’ex diesse della Lazio, Igli Tare.

CLICCA QUI E SEGUI LAZIOPRESS.IT ANCHE SU INSTAGRAM

Sono felice per la Lazio di oggi. La società ha creato una squadra competitiva e ha scelto Gattuso, che ha creato un clima positivo: tutti gli vogliono bene. Questa è una società con grande storia, rimarrò sempre legato alla Lazio. Ho un legame forte con questo club.

Abbiamo avuto degli approcci ma era più un'idea di Lotito. Conosco Rino, ho un rapporto molto bello con lui. Sono molto contento per lui.

Penso di sì. Era una storia molto bella. Prima della pandemia eravamo devastanti, dopo 20' eravamo già 2-0 o 3-0 per noi". Una chiacchiera significativa con Inzaghi, al tempo allenatore della Lazio: "All'inizio della stagione parlai con Simone e mi disse: ‘Igli, sei preoccupato?’. E io: ‘Io per niente, sono straconvinto che lotteremo per vincere lo Scudetto’. E lui: ‘Ma tu sei matto’. E io: ‘Fidati che sarà un'annata particolare ma molto bella per noi.

Penso che Ciro sia un ragazzo unico. Molto sensibile, aveva bisogno dell'ambiente che gli dava fiducia. E poi è stato straordinario, ha scritto la storia della Lazio. Un giocatore irripetibile.

Parliamo di un centroavanti fenomenale per il modo di interpretare il gioco e nella Lazio, per vari motivi, non ha dato quello che poteva dare. Aveva un aereo privato con destinazione Parigi al PSG. Ma lui ha rifiutato per venire alla Lazio. Ha rifiutato anche più del doppio di stipendio che gli è stato proposto da altre parti per venire in Italia.

Lui aveva l'ambizione di giocare il Mondiale 2014 e all’epoca nessun club gli dava un contratto con più di un anno. C'erano Galatasaray, Valencia, ma sempre per un anno. Io gli ho dato un contratto di tre anni, ho convinto anche Lotito. Quando abbiamo firmato tutti mi hanno massacrato perché stavamo pagando uno di 32 anni che aveva vissuto un anno negativo con qualche infortunio. Ma dopo il primo/secondo allenamento tutti hanno capito che era un fuoriclasse.

Con lui ho un legame molto speciale, abbiamo giocato insieme. Ha intrapreso una carriera che per tanti era una sorpresa ma per me mai. La reputo una persona molto curiosa, intelligente nella gestione. Poi è cresciuto tanto con l’esperienza alla Lazio e all'Inter. Quando tornerà, non so se in Italia o all’estero, penso che sarà un allenatore completo. L'esperienza più bella che ho vissuto? Con Delio Rossi. Ero giocatore con lui per tre annie quando Lotito gli comunicò che io sarei stato il nuovo DS lui rimase sorpreso e disse 'allora mi vuoi mandare via?’. Cambiare da giocatore a diventare "il capo di un allenatore" era una sorpresa anche per me, non mi aspettavo questa scelta di Lotito.
