#2648. Celtics fans from Maine have room in their hearts for Cooper Flagg

About 95 minutes before tipoff Sunday night, a group of kids sitting behind the Dallas Mavericks bench were doing everything in their power to get Cooper Flagg's attention.

"WE'RE FROM MAINE!," they yelled toward the court, where Flagg was working through his pregame routine.

I had wandered over after spotting a large Maine state flag draped across the first row of seats. As someone who grew up in Maine, I was naturally curious. And as someone still getting comfortable with the whole credentialed-media experience, I figured hanging around some fellow Mainers might help settle my nerves.

Flagg was not far away, working through jump shots and post moves while the kids continued their campaign to get him to acknowledge them. A woman standing nearby, who appeared to be one of the children's mothers, turned to me.

"It'd be a lot easier if you guys just got him over here so they'd stop yelling," she joked.

I laughed. Sure, it would. But kids yelling at NBA players during warmups is about as common as overpriced beer at TD Garden. Usually, the player keeps working and maybe signs a few things near the entrance tunnel before disappearing into the locker room.

But a few minutes later, Cooper Flagg started walking toward us.

He stepped off the court, made his way over to the first row behind the Mavericks bench, and began signing everything the kids put in front of him. Basketballs, cards, jerseys. And, of course, that giant Maine flag that had caught my attention in the first place.

The kids looked absolutely stunned. I think I did, too.

A TD Garden usher standing beside me watched the interaction with what appeared to be equal astonishment.

He was referring to how unusual it was to see a visiting player walk away from his usual exit route to spend time with fans in the stands.

I'd of course seen players sign autographs before, but this was different. There was something surreal about watching Flagg cross that little boundary separating the court from the rest of us, the place where a kid's basketball dreams come true from the place where most of us spend our lives watching other people live them.

And here he was, standing right in front of a group of kids who'd been shouting that they were from the same state he grew up in.

Kids who just met their idol are then asked to pose for a picture taken by an obscure writer who they've 100% never heard of or care for.

The mother who'd joked about getting Flagg to come over was now thanking him repeatedly, her voice noticeably shaky as he signed her custom jersey.

Her jersey was half Celtics green, half Mavericks blue, with Flagg's name crossing the green and blue divide on the back. I don't know if she had the jersey specially made as some sort of elaborate voodoo ritual to bring Flagg to Boston someday, but I fully support her play at dark magic if that's what was happening.

The jersey perfectly captured the unusual position basketball fans from Maine find ourselves in these days, myself included. We've spent our lives rooting for the Celtics. And now, somehow, one of the brightest stars in the entire NBA is a kid from our humble little state. Someone we can proudly call our own, even when he's wearing the wrong colors.

Turns out, there's enough room in our hearts for both.

I've been a Celtics fan for as long as I can remember. I grew up playing basketball in Maine, eventually winning a high school state championship, and spent much of my childhood imagining what it would be like to play on the same court as the guys I watched on television.

For most kids from Maine, the NBA might as well have been located on another planet. We could drive down to Boston, buy tickets to a Celtics game and watch our favorite players from the stands. But the idea of somebody from Maine actually becoming one of those players, let alone a superstar? Good luck.

A kid from Newport, Maine, went to Montverde, became a superstar at Duke, was selected first overall in the NBA Draft, and suddenly one of the best young basketball players in the world was someone who'd grown up in the same state as us.

I wrote about Flagg's first appearance at TD Garden back in March, which happened to coincide with Jayson Tatum's return from his Achilles injury. It was my first credentialed Celtics game, and I spent much of the night watching Flagg try to navigate a building that was simultaneously celebrating him and hoping he'd lose by 40.

Sunday was his second NBA appearance in Boston, and the novelty clearly hadn't worn off. When the Mavericks were introduced before tipoff, the usual boos greeted the first four Dallas starters. Then the PA announcer called Flagg's name.

The reaction changed immediately. Cheers poured out of the stands. You could practically hear the collective decision being made across TD Garden.

The massive Maine flag wasn't the only sign of Flagg's popularity. Mavericks blue dotted sections of the crowd, mixed in with plenty of Celtics green. Some wore Duke gear, a convenient loophole for fans hoping to support both Flagg and fellow Blue Devil Jayson Tatum.

And then there was that remarkable half-and-half jersey. Celtics green stitched together with Mavericks blue, a combination that felt mildly sacrilegious at first glance. Somewhere, a lifelong Celtics fan sitting behind that woman was probably experiencing mild chest pains.

But the more I thought about it, the more the jersey made perfect sense. You could spend your entire life rooting for Boston and still feel an enormous sense of pride watching someone from your home state succeed elsewhere.

Of course, all that goodwill was about to be tested when Flagg started trying to score against the Celtics.

Sunday's game was supposed to be an opportunity for Flagg to show New England just how much he'd grown since his first appearance in Boston. Instead, the Celtics spent the opening quarter making Dallas look like a group of guys who'd accidentally wandered into the wrong gym.

The 33-point advantage was the largest first-quarter lead in Celtics franchise history. Dallas made two field goals in the entire period.

Derrick White had 11 points by himself. Jordan Walsh was flying around the floor, attacking the basket and helping set the defensive tone. The Celtics looked fresh after several days off, while the Mavericks, playing the second night of a back-to-back, looked like they'd have gladly accepted an earlier flight home.

Flagg missed his first few attempts and went scoreless in the opening quarter. Meanwhile, I was having a wonderful time watching the Celtics.

Because once Boston built a lead of approximately one billion points, I found myself feeling comfortable secretly rooting for one particular Mavericks player.

Cooper, buddy. Come on. Take the shot. Show these people what you can do.

I was surrounded by Celtics reporters, doing my best to look like a normal, impartial member of the media while silently begging a Mavericks player to score. I know we're a humble state. Mainers generally aren't the type to kick down the door and announce their arrival. But really, Cooper. You're supposed to be OUR GUY!

He finally got on the board in the second quarter, backing down Payton Pritchard for a basket and a foul. I swear I could feel the collective exhale of hundreds of Mainers pass through the arena. A few minutes later, he threw down a dunk in transition, drawing another audible reaction from the crowd.

Boston still led by more than 30 points. Everything was fine. I could enjoy watching Flagg do Flagg things without worrying that he'd ruin the Celtics' night. If anything, this was starting to feel like the ideal arrangement for a Celtics fan from Maine.

Boston wins comfortably. Flagg provides a few highlights. Everybody goes home happy. Well, maybe not everybody wearing a Mavericks uniform.

What impressed me was that Flagg kept trying to make the right basketball play, even as the deficit grew increasingly ridiculous. He continued finding open teammates and celebrating their baskets, including a third-quarter alley-oop to Daniel Gafford that earned a little fist pump from Flagg despite Dallas still trailing by around 30.

Mavericks coach Dusty May noticed it, too.

"I do think Coop made a lot of really good decisions with the ball in his hands tonight," May said afterward.

Flagg was playing through an illness, which became noticeably apparent when he addressed reporters after the game. But he didn't seem particularly interested in talking about excuses.

"I need to step up and be a lot better," he said.

That's the kind of answer you want to hear from a player carrying the expectations of an entire NBA franchise. And, apparently, a good portion of Maine's 1.4 million residents.

By the end of the third quarter, Boston led 104–71. Tatum had piled up 32 points, including 21 in the third, and the Celtics were preparing to rest their starters with another game scheduled for Monday.

Flagg was on the bench to begin the fourth quarter, too. I figured that was probably it for his night. And I was a little disappointed.

I'd watched those kids spend their pregame screaming for his attention. I knew people had traveled from Maine to be here. Depending on where you're coming from, getting to TD Garden can be a pretty significant undertaking.

I live in Vermont now, and the drive takes me about three hours. Plenty of the Mainers in attendance had traveled just as far, if not farther, to watch him play. All those miles, all that excitement, and the guy everyone came to see might be finished after three quarters of a game that had never really been competitive.

Then, with roughly eight minutes left in the fourth quarter, something unexpected happened.

I mentioned how surprising the decision seemed to fellow CelticsBlogger Trevor Hass, who was sitting next to me in press row.

"Must be for the fans who made the trek to see him," Trevor suggested.

I have no idea whether Dusty May was thinking about the fans when he sent Flagg back onto the floor. But I liked the theory, and Flagg gave those who stuck around a few more highlights.

He knocked down a beautiful stepback three that drew oohs and ahhs from the crowd, then delivered a lob to a teammate and emphatically celebrated the finish. Keep in mind, the Celtics were still winning by approximately 40 points.

For a few minutes, those of us who'd been quietly hoping to see more from Flagg got our wish. I wondered whether the same kids who'd spent pregame yelling "WE'RE FROM MAINE!" had started another campaign directed toward the Mavericks bench.

Given how well their strategy worked the first time, I wouldn't have put it past them. Maybe that mother had finally figured out the secret to influencing an NBA team's decisions.

Either way, Flagg got a brief fourth-quarter curtain call before checking out for good. He finished with 17 points, three rebounds and four assists in Boston's 131–94 victory. The Celtics had won their sixth straight game. Their starters got plenty of rest, the crowd got Gino Time, and everyone in green had reason to celebrate.

But I couldn't stop thinking about the people who came to see Coop.

After the game, Flagg was asked about the support he receives from the fans who travel to see him play in New England.

"It's special," he said. "Just being able to come here and play and feel that love and support every time is going to be really special. It's something that I'm not going to take for granted. It's such a blessing."

He also acknowledged that playing close to home means something extra, even when he isn't feeling his best.

"Obviously, being back home with a lot of people showing up to watch, it means a little bit more," Flagg said.

I thought about those comments and the people I'd watched throughout the night. By the time the fourth quarter reached its final few minutes, fans were already streaming toward the exits. Fair enough. The Celtics had been winning comfortably since approximately six minutes after tip-off, and getting out of TD Garden after a game can be its own competitive event.

But the fans gathered near the visitors' bench? A lot of them were still there.

Some had come wearing Celtics green, others Mavericks blue. Regardless of which team they wanted to win, they'd come hoping to watch Cooper Flagg do something special.

Even before the final buzzer sounded, fans began gathering around the Mavericks tunnel, holding out jerseys and phones, hoping for one last glimpse of Flagg. The basketball game had been decided ages ago, but plenty of people weren't ready for the Cooper Flagg experience to end.

Cooper Flagg makes his way to the visitors' locker room, but not before a few hundred fans say goodbye.

That felt familiar. After Flagg finished signing autographs before the game, I'd asked the kids with the Maine flag if I could take their picture. They happily obliged, still riding the high of just meeting their idol, though they seemed a little less certain about what exactly I intended to do with it.

I explained that I wrote for CelticsBlog. Blank stares.

I told them they could follow CelticsBlog on Twitter. More blank stares.

Right. Of course. Forgive me for speaking the ancient language of a civilization that apparently no longer exists.

Whatever they thought of the strange CelticsBlog writer asking for their picture, I doubt I did much to diminish the excitement of what they'd just experienced.

And somewhere along the way, a Celtics writer from Maine had wandered over hoping to feel a little more comfortable in an unfamiliar environment, only to find himself witnessing something he wouldn't soon forget.

Maybe that's part of what makes Flagg so special to people from Maine. We've spent our lives traveling to Boston to watch basketball players we admire. Now we get to make that same trip to watch somebody who grew up where we did.

He's wearing the wrong uniform, sure. We'll work on that.

But for now, I'll happily settle for watching the Celtics win by 37, Cooper Flagg get his moments, and a group of kids take home a Maine flag bearing the autograph of a player they'll probably spend the rest of their lives talking about.

For Mainers, Cooper Flagg is worth the traffic.

#2647. Duval Dispatch: Jags earn ‘A-’ in win over Titans

The Jaguars went on the road and beat the Titans 40-23 in a divisional matchup, pushing Jacksonville to 7-2 on the year and keeping them right in the race at the top of the AFC.

For their efforts, CBS Sports' John Breech gave Jacksonville a very strong "A-" this week. Here's what he had to say about their recent performance:

"The Jaguars offense is suddenly starting to look unstoppable. This marked the fourth straight game where they scored at least 30 points, and one reason everything is working for them is that Trevor Lawrence has so many weapons. The Jags' QB, who threw for 352 yards and three touchdowns, completed at least one pass to NINE different receivers. Parker Washington, who finished with seven catches for 152 yards, is slowly evolving into a true No. 1 receiver. The Jags defense struggled some, but that was to be expected due to Liam Coen's decision to keep Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates III on the bench. Those two trade reinforcements will be playing their first game with the Jags next week, and at that point, the defense will need to be better."

#2645. Hassell appointed interim Barnsley CEO

Barnsley have appointed former captain Bobby Hassell as their new interim chief executive officer (CEO) after Jon Flatman's departure to Cardiff Rugby was confirmed.

Hassell spent a decade at Oakwell between 2004 and 2014 and made 299 appearances in total for the Tykes.

He was a part of the squad which achieved promotion to the Championship via the play-offs in 2006, as well as the one with reached the FA Cup semi-finals two years later.

After retiring from playing, Hassell rejoined the club in 2015 as the academy's head of recruitment.

In a club statement, Barnsley wrote Hassell will be in interim charge of the footballing side of the club while the process to appoint a new CEO is "well underway."

The news of Flatman's departure was announced last month after he spent three years at the club.

Flatman joined the Tykes as chief revenue officer before being appointed permanent CEO, after a spell as interim, in 2024.

"On behalf of the board, I'd like to thank Jon for his hard work and commitment to Barnsley Football Club, and wish him every success for the future," chairman Neerav Parekh said.

"I want to reassure our supporters that the club is in good hands in the interim.

"Bobby has lived and breathed this club as a player and a member of staff, and he will lead our football operation alongside Daniel [Stendel, Barnsley manager] and his staff through the January window."

#2642. 4 things the NY Giants have to do better to win the NFC East

The New York Giants' loss to the Washington Commanders on Thursday tightened the NFC East race and made their weekend off less enjoyable than it could have been. Thanks to the San Francisco 49ers outscoring the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday, though, the Giants' division lead entering Week 11 is not as tenuous as it could have been.

The 5-3-1 Giants have a 2½-game lead over the 4-6 Cowboys and a two-game lead over the 3-5-1 Commanders. The Athletic's playoff simulator gives the Giants a 56% chance of winning the NFC East and making the playoffs. The Cowboys are at 28%, and the Commanders 16%.

Much has been made of the fact that the Giants' schedule, beginning this weekend with the 7-2 Jacksonville Jaguars, is about to get tougher. Over the Giants' first nine games, their opponents were a combined 25-49-1, a .340 winning percentage. Their upcoming opponents are a combined 43-33, a .566 winning percentage.

Head coach John Harbaugh said recently that the Giants "don't live in that scared world" of worrying about schedule difficulty.

The Giants are a resilient team. Harbaugh has made them that way. They have, to this point, overcome the losses of quarterback Jaxson Dart and star edge defender Brian Burns. In each of their five wins, they have made plays late in the game to secure the victory.

Fight and resilience alone, though, won't win the NFC East title for the Giants. The Giants are an imperfect team that has things to fix in order to win the division. Below are some of the things the Giants are going to have to do better over the final eight games.

The Giants, holding a 21-17 lead, intercepted Washington quarterback Jayden Daniels twice in the last 5:31 of Thursday's game. That should be enough for the Giants to have won that game. But it wasn't.

The Giants went three-and-out after both interceptions, failing to run significant time off the clock or force the Commanders to use up their timeouts on either occasion.

The first possession included three runs, with the last being a Jameis Winston third-and-1 sneak on which running back Cam Skattebo never really got out of his stance to participate in the play. Harbaugh explained that this was a straight sneak, not a tush push.

The second possession, which started at the Washington 46-yard line with 2:15 to play, also featured three runs. The last was a designed quarterback run for J.J. McCarthy on which the Giants didn't even have a running back on the field.

You can see from the jump he got that Washington linebacker Sonny Styles knew this play before the ball was snapped. Center Bryan Hudson had no chance to block him.

"We had thought we had good runs. We thought we could get it with the runs. Also keep the clock running and make them burn the timeouts. We thought we could do both," Harbaugh said. "But looking back on it, I think a good pass there might've been good too. I think if you throw the ball and you throw three incompletions or whatever, the question is flipped, you know, "why didn't you run the ball, make them burn the timeouts?" Being successful really is the bottom line. It's not like we're trying to play it safe or anything like that. We're not afraid to throw the ball there. The run that we had, the last run that got the two-yard loss, that's got a chance to crack them. It's a quarterback-driven run with an extra blocker. They had everybody up on the line. Honestly, on that one play, we can block that play better. And so that's the way the game went in that situation."

The problem is, four-minute offense failure has been a theme for the Giants.

In Week 3 against the Tennessee Titans, the Giants got the ball with 5:31 to play, protecting a 12-7 lead. They got a quick first down on a 12-yard Jameis Winston to Malik Nabers pass, but then punted with 3:12 to go after two runs and an incomplete pass. Jevon Holland bailed the Giants out, intercepting Cam Ward in the end zone with :24 to play.

In Week 4 against the Arizona Cardinals, the Giants got the ball at midfield with a 3-point lead and 4:47 to play. They could muster only 16 yards in five plays, with a Dominic Zvada 52-yard field goal giving them a 20-24 lead with 2:16 to play. It took a Deonte Banks 98-yard interception return on the final play to seal that victory.

In Week 5 against Washington, Skattebo's fumble at the two-minute mark in overtime cost the Giants a chance to win.

In Week 8 against the Philadelphia Eagles, the Giants got the ball with 1:56 to play after a Jake Elliott field goal pulled the Eagles within one score. After three handoffs to Devin Singletary netted just 2 yards, the Giants punted and once again relied on their defense to bail them out.

"That's something that I've always prided myself [on], playing on an offense that's able to ice the game," fullback Patrick Ricard said after Thursday's loss. "I feel like this year we haven't been able to do that as an offense. Only probably Week 1 that we actually ran the ball or got first downs, and were able to kneel the game out.

"We've always had to rely on our defense, and our defense is very clutch, and they've been winning a lot of games for us. It's something that we as an offense have to really harp on to finish games out like that because we can't keep relying on our defense to keep going out there and just keep getting stops after stops. We need to be able to convert first downs in those moments."

I don't have the answer. A head coach in his 19th season and a veteran offensive staff, though, need to do everything they can to figure it out. The Giants can't ask their defense to close every game in the final seconds. We saw that on Thursday night.

We went in-depth on Zvada's issues from the right hashmark on Saturday. It simply isn't possible to design an offense to get every field goal attempt from the left hashmark. This is something that Zvada and veteran special teams coordinator Chris Horton are going to have to figure out.

Harbaugh's refusal to move on from Zvada, an undrafted rookie who won the job with a fantastic summer, after his struggles since Week 9 has driven the fan base to distraction.

I understand Harbaugh's desire to ride things out with Zvada and hope he becomes the kicker the Giants believe he can be sooner rather than later. Look around the league. For every team that has a Brandon Aubrey, Cam Little, or a solid veteran like Chris Boswell, there are teams riding what former special teams coordinator Thomas McGaughey called the "kicker train", and finding it an unpleasant experience.

Just like there aren't 32 top-10 caliber quarterbacks in the NFL, there aren't 32 kickers teams feel good about every time they need three points. Or even one point.

Zvada, 23, has the leg strength and talent to be one of those long-range placekicking weapons every team is seeking. Hall of Fame kicker Adam Vinatieri kicked for 24 years, but made 80% of his field goal attempts just once in his first four seasons.

Former Giants kicker Lawrence Tynes certainly believes in Zvada:

Over the years, the Giants have seen many good young placekickers like Chris Boswell, Brandon McManus, and Joey Slye get away from them and go on to have excellent careers. They don't want Zvada to be the next one.

Still, with a playoff berth at stake, how patient can they be?

Everything good about the Giants' season comes from Harbaugh. The credibility he brought when the Giants hired him and the way he has led this team and made it believe it deserved to, and could, win have meant everything. Hiring Harbaugh is the best decision the Giants could have made. He is the biggest reason the Giants have a chance to win their first division title since 2011.

Harbaugh, though, was never going to be perfect. He wasn't in Baltimore, which is a big part of why he is now in New York.

In a game Harbaugh said was "for all the marbles," against Washington, the Giants were far too cautious.

The Giants punted three times in Commanders' territory. Two of those came in the fourth quarter. Two were also within field goal range for Zvada. When I asked him about those, Harbaugh said they were "risk-reward" decisions and that with the weather conditions "sometimes it's better to play a field position game."

I used to criticize former Giants coach Joe Judge because he seemed to have a "play for later rather than try to win the game now" philosophy. This, to me, was that kind of game for Harbaugh.

In our post-game podcast, Tony Del Genio raised the idea that Harbaugh showed a lack of faith in the Giants' offense. My take is a little different. I see it as an old-school coach employing old-school "take as few risks as possible" thinking.

I always say that good play calls or decisions are those that work. Bad decisions or play calls are those that don't.

Still, I thought Harbaugh and the Giants were too conservative a couple of times in the fourth quarter. Early in the fourth quarter, the Giants had third-and-three at the Washington 46-yard line. Analytics were clear that this was a for-for-it if you got to fourth down situation.

Instead, J.J. McCarthy threw a pass that Theo Johnson dropped, and the Giants punted. Johnson, of course, could have made the Giants right. He did not.

The other situation was the McCarthy third-and-3 run after the Ar'Darius Washington interception with 2:15 left in the game. It's easy to say a short pass to Isaiah Likely or Malik Nabers was the right call, because it probably was. The biggest problem with the run play, to me, is that the personnel (no running backs in the game) and formation made it crystal clear what the play call was.

By re-litigating this, we are crying over spilt milk. Nothing can be done about the Washington game now. A lesson, though, needs to be learned.

You don't win games by trying not to lose them. Especially with the Giants stepping up in class for many of their final eight games, they are going to have to be willing to take some risks.

By some measures, Abdul Carter has been excellent. Through Week 9, Carter was second in the NFL in pass rush win rate at 35%. He is tied for seventh in the NFL in quick pressures with 17, per NextGen Stats. His time to pressure of 2.42 seconds is 19th among edge defenders and linebackers. And, yes, it seems like Carter is forever being held — though many of them go uncalled.

Still, it is a production game. Carter has just two sacks despite, per NextGen Stats, his 285 pass rush opportunities being the most of any linebacker or edge defender in the league. Carter's pressure percentage of 9.8 is 104th. His sacks percentage of 0.7 is 94th.

Whatever the stats are, and whatever the reasons are for the low sack numbers, the reality is the Giants need more from the 2025 No. 3 overall pick.

Former Giants linebacker Carl Banks has some ideas:

Whatever it takes, the Giants are going to need Carter to make more plays.

#2641. 10 takeaways as Celtics steamroll Mavericks for 6th straight win

The Celtics have learned this season that no lead is safe in the NBA.

They blew a 22-point advantage against the Pistons in their opener and overcame a 22-point deficit versus the Raptors on Wednesday.

When they built a 33-point cushion through 1 in Sunday's 131-94 victory over the Mavericks, it would have been easy to accept that the game was definitively theirs. Instead, they continued to play with urgency and didn't let Dallas come anywhere close to a comeback.

Here are 10 takeaways as Boston played one of its most complete games to date and earned its sixth consecutive win.

To say the Celtics dominated the first quarter would be putting it lightly. They built a 42-9 advantage through one, shooting 59 percent from the floor and 54 percent from 3. It was the largest lead after the first quarter in franchise history.

The Mavericks were at 11 percent from 3 and 0 percent from distance, and they turned it over six times. Not much went wrong for Boston, and not much went right for Dallas. It was complete and total domination.

Jayson Tatum had the second-highest plus-minus (plus-33) in a single quarter in NBA history.

Joe Mazzulla wasn't ready to assume the Celtics were on their way to a stress-free victory.

"It tests your ability to remain focused on the process," Mazzulla said.

There was a brief moment in the second quarter where it felt like maybe, just maybe, the Mavericks were onto something. They cut it to 24, then Boston finished the quarter strong to take a 67-37 lead into halftime.

Runs are going to happen, but the Celtics are learning how to counteract what the opposing team does with their own move to maintain a comfortable cushion.

"It goes back to the formula that we're trying to create," Mazzulla said. "It's not about hanging onto leads. That's a passive mindset. It's not about building on them. It's just understanding the ebbs and flows of the game."

Tatum was solid in the first half, then exploded for 21 in the third quarter to finish with 32 for the game on 11-of-18 shooting.

It was one of his best performances of the season and the kind of showing where you look up from your screen and suddenly he has 25.

"Obviously it's easy to really bring it when it's a close game, or things like that," Tatum said. "Just trying to challenge our mindset of we're up 25 to 30, can you try to put the game away? I think we did a really good job of that today."

Tatum continues to make the game look rather easy. Efficiency is always key with him, and he was extremely efficient Sunday night.

Jordan Walsh was aggressive from the opening tip, scoring 8 points in the opening five minutes to help the Celtics build an early 22-4 advantage.

"Jordan is continuing to develop the mindset that we need him to have versus great players," Mazzulla said. "A great team has to have a group of guys that they can rely on make it difficult for the other team's best player every single night. It has to be by committee. Jordan is on that list. He's on that committee. He's taking ownership of that."

Walsh hit a corner 3 and finished in traffic twice, looking confident and in command against a disorganized Mavericks defense. It was his most shot attempts (nine) on the season and his most points (11) since Oct. 27 against the Nets.

On the other end, he locked up Cooper Flagg at times, got in various Mavericks' faces and rotated well defensively. When asked where he stacks up in that respect, Walsh didn't hesitate.

"I think I'm the best defender," he said.

He continues to provide energy, versatility and burst for the Celtics, and the additional offense is a nice bonus.

Walsh said he is not graded by the box score, but rather how much he affects the other team's primary ball handler and other pest-like metrics. At the same time, when he gets the ball, he is as confident as ever and it shows.

"I'm just trying to find pockets to be aggressive," Walsh said. "I don't get a lot of shots, so when I do catch the ball, I'm looking for an opportunity to score instead of trying to passing it. I'm trying to create a real threat."

Neemias Queta swished a corner 3 with ease early in the third quarter. Queta, who also hit one Wednesday against the Raptors, is now 4 for 5 on the season.

He's not going to magically morph into Steph Curry (though his percentage is higher), but his ability to keep defenses honest goes a long way for this team. When he's open, he should let it fly.

Queta finished with 8 points (3 of 3), 6 rebounds, 2 assists, 1 block and 0 turnovers (plus-31) in 15 minutes and took the rest of the night off.

"His growth and his role has gone kind of under the radar," Mazzulla said. "He's more important than just with defense. He's important in the locker room, he's important on the offensive end. He continues to get better and better. It's easy to overlook it because of how easy he makes it."

Derrick White helped set the tone Sunday with a sizzling first quarter and ended the night with 16 points on 6-of-11 shooting.

White, who added 19 against the Raptors (7 of 15) is averaging 13.4 points in November. While his efficiency isn't quite where he wants it to be, it is trending positively. Whether the shots go in or not, White needs to keep taking them as long as they are high-percentage looks.

Baylor Scheierman contributed 12 points, Ron Harper Jr. 10, Hugo González 9 and Chris Cenac Jr. 6. Devin Carter and Luka Garza also fared admirably.

Harper Jr. has the talent of a rotational player. Whether that opportunity comes with the Celtics or a different team remains to be seen.

Cenac showed some bounce and looked like he belonged. Carter hustled on both ends and was a steady presence.

Flagg, playing in front of a sea of supporters, was scoreless in the first quarter but grew progressively stronger as the game progressed.

He finished with 17 on 5-of-15 shooting and was a game-low minus-30. Flagg had his moments, with a silky step-back 3 and a thunderous dunk, but overall it was a lukewarm New England homecoming for the Maine native. Even so, despite the outcome, he enjoyed the environment.

"It's special," Flagg told reporters. "Just being able to come here and play and feel that love and support every time is going to be really special. It's something that I'm not going to take for granted. It's such a blessing."

It was too bad Kyrie Irving didn't play. I'm sure he would have been showered with love from the Boston faithful. But seriously, it was a shame he wasn't out there.

The game may have unfolded differently. Irving's tenure in town was complicated, but the man can hoop like few others in NBA history.

A Tatum versus Irving showdown, with both back from injury and in a groove, would have been fun to watch.

The Celtics are one of the hottest teams in the NBA and are showing no signs of slowing down.

It's still early, but this team may have a higher ceiling than last year's team. The top of the East is anyone's game, and the Celtics are very much in that mix with the 76ers, Pistons and Knicks.

After a home game against the Magic on Monday, a grueling stretch of six of seven games on the road will test them. If they can go 4-3 or 5-2, that should be viewed as a success.

#2639. Eagles offensive line depth: Who steps in after Fred Johnson's exit

The Eagles' decision to waive Fred Johnson leaves their offensive line with a clear question coming out of the bye: Who enters if Jordan Mailata or Markel Bell cannot finish a game?

Philadelphia's supplied depth chart lists no backup at either tackle position. The interior has more defined alternatives, with Jake Majors behind center Drew Kendall and Micah Morris behind right guard Tyler Steen. Practice-squad linemen provide additional possibilities, but their availability requires a roster move before kickoff.

Practice-squad options John Ojukwu and Kiran Amegadjie; Bell could shift sides

Morris; center/guard alternatives Kendall and Majors

Majors or Kendall; practice-squad guards Evan Neal and Evan Beerntsen

Practice-squad options Ojukwu and Amegadjie; Steen has tackle experience

The additional alternatives reflect positional backgrounds and possible combinations, rather than an announced replacement order.

Ojukwu is listed as a tackle on the practice squad, making him a player to watch for an elevation or promotion. Amegadjie offers another possibility after entering the NFL as Chicago's third-round pick in 2024. His background includes left tackle and right guard at Yale, along with an NFL start at left tackle.

Bell could move to the left side if necessary, but that would create an opening at right tackle. Steen's tackle background offers another potential contingency, although moving the starting right guard outside would require an interior replacement. Philadelphia has not established either arrangement as its preferred response.

Morris is the only reserve explicitly listed behind a guard in the supplied chart. The rookie from Georgia is positioned behind Steen, but Philadelphia still must establish who would replace Lampkin at left guard.

Kendall and Majors both carry center/guard designations, while Lampkin is also listed as a center/guard. That overlap gives the Eagles several possible interior combinations. Majors also has recent starting experience, having stepped in at center against Jacksonville and Carolina when Kendall was injured.

The complication is that using Kendall or Lampkin elsewhere creates another vacancy. Their versatility helps, but it does not eliminate the need for a clear substitution plan.

Alongside Ojukwu and Amegadjie, Philadelphia has Beerntsen and Neal available on the practice squad. Neal is listed as a guard despite his previous NFL work at tackle, giving the Eagles another player with experience across positions. His current designation should guide expectations until Philadelphia indicates otherwise.

The next meaningful development is which linemen Philadelphia makes available against Pittsburgh. That decision should help clarify the first tackle off the bench and how much positional reshuffling the Eagles are prepared to use.

#2638. NFL news, live updates: Aidan Hutchinson suffers 'significant' knee injury while celebrating sack; Brock Bowers exits early with ankle injury in Fernando Mendoza's first start

Another NFL Sunday is in the books, with just one game left in Week 10 as the Baltimore Ravens host the LA Chargers on "Monday Night Football."

Sunday kicked off with a bang as the Detroit Lions and New England Patriots faced off in Munich, Germany, with injuries to two stars that will have all eyes drawn as the new week plays out. Lions star defensive end Aidan Hutchinson suffered what is feared to be a season-ending knee injury while celebrating a sack against Patriots quarterback Drake Maye … who suffered an ankle injury on that very sack, which knocked him out of the game and could cost him the season.

Week 10 also offered us our first look at Las Vegas Raiders No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza as a starter. He led scoring drives on each of the Raiders' first two possessions and entered halftime with a 10-7 lead over the Seattle Seahawks, but Drew Lock rallied with two passing touchdowns in the third quarter to take the lead, improving to 3-0 as a starter for Seattle this season. Raiders star tight end Brock Bowers exited the loss with an ankle injury.

Follow along with Yahoo Sports for the latest NFL news, injury updates and more coming out of Week 10.

Detroit Lions pass rusher Aidan Hutchinson reportedly tore his ACL while celebrating a sack of Drake Maye, per NFL Network.

Early reports Sunday suggested Hutchinson was dealing with a "significant" knee injury. Initial tests reportedly confirmed as much Monday.

Hutchinson will miss the rest of the 2026 NFL season as he recovers from the injury. It's unclear whether his availability will be impacted next season.

Brock Bowers didn't last long on Sunday afternoon.

The Las Vegas Raiders tight end was ruled out of their 21-13 loss to the Seattle Seahawks due to an ankle injury he suffered early in the first quarter. That knocked him out for the majority of Fernando Mendoza's starting debut at Allegiant Stadium.

Bowers, in the first quarter of the contest, went up to block Seahawks safety Nick Emmanwori for running back Ashton Jeanty. But as Jeanty cut the other way, Bowers had his legs rolled up on in a pile, and he went down awkwardly.

Bowers remained down for a few moments while the team's training staff helped him, and he then limped to the sideline.

Bowers did return to the game briefly after that, which helped lead the way for Mendoza's rushing touchdown to get them on the board. But he left the game again late in the second quarter, and the team ruled him out for good just before the start of the second half with the ankle injury. Clearly, it was just too much for him to overcome.

Further specifics of his injury are not yet known.

The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are currently on bye, but unfortunately, they are still in the news.

Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield is dealing with a lower-leg injury that he suffered during last week's loss to the Chicago Bears, NFL Network's Mike Garafolo reported on Sunday morning.

Mayfield's status is uncertain for Tampa Bay's Week 11 matchup with the Detroit Lions. It is unclear where Mayfield picked up the injury against the Bears. The quarterback was sacked four times, but he never left the game. This week, he was reportedly spotted in a walking boot, rehabbing and resting.

This would not be the first time this season the Buccaneers have played without their starting quarterback. Mayfield dislocated his thumb in Week 3, which kept him out for three games. Tampa Bay turned to undrafted rookie quarterback Jalon Daniels, who went 1-2 as the starter.

Mayfield has played in six games so far this season and is 2-4. He has not looked like himself all year, throwing for just 922 yards, 3 touchdowns and 4 interceptions. In a bad-weather Week 8 game against the Atlanta Falcons, he finished 0-for-3 for zero yards in the team's 16-0 win, making infamous history.

A frustrating season for Los Angeles Chargers wideout Ladd McConkey will continue in Week 10. While the receiver was initially listed as questionable on the team's final injury report, he will not play against the Baltimore Ravens on "Monday Night Football."

McConkey was ruled out for the game due to back spasms. He did not travel with the team to Baltimore, the Chargers announced.

McConkey has been limited by multiple injuries throughout the regular season. He was held to just 35 yards in Week 2 thanks to a rib injury and missed Week 5 due to a foot issue.

He caught just one ball in Week 6 before resting during the bye week. While the wideout looked to be close to 100 percent with an 86-yard performance in Week 8, McConkey missed Week 9 with back spasms. The injury reportedly occurred just before game time. He was expected to play in the contest.

Those back spasms have apparently continued to plague McConkey throughout the week. He was held out of practice each day leading up to Week 10, though the team still held some hope he would play, initially giving him the questionable tag.

But the issue was bad enough that the team opted against throwing McConkey on the field Monday night.

Raiders tight end Brock Bowers reportedly avoided a major ankle injury in Week 10. Bowers will have more tests done Monday, but the early indication is that he's more day-to-day.

Bowers left Sunday's game against the Seahawks due to the issue. He finished with just 18 yards.

The injury put a damper on the debut of No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza, who lost his best receiver in the contest.

The New England Patriots could be without quarterback Drake Maye for the rest of the season. Maye may have sustained a serious leg injury during Sunday's loss to the Detroit Lions, with the Patriots fearing a possible ankle fracture.

Maye did not travel to the United States with the team after Sunday's game, staying in Germany to undergo additional tests. Those tests could reveal whether Maye needs surgery.

No matter what those tests reveal, Maye is looking at an extended absence, if not a season-ending one.

Detroit Lions star Aidan Hutchinson made his presence known early against the New England Patriots. On the Patriots' first offensive drive, Hutchinson broke through the line on third down and sacked Drake Maye.

Following the play, Hutchinson got up to celebrate the sack. He jumped into the air and immediately fell to the ground after landing. Hutchinson appeared to be holding his right knee.

Hutchinson walked off the field, but headed straight to the medical tent on the sideline. He was later spotted on the broadcast heading to the locker room.

He was deemed questionable to return with a knee injury, but late in the third quarter, he was ruled out for the remainder of the game.

Detroit eventually cruised to a 35-10 victory.

Early reports suggested Hutchinson may have sustained a "significant" knee injury, per NFL Network. Detroit is reportedly not expecting good news. While a second opinion is coming, it's possible Hutchinson will not return this season.

#2635. Women's Hoops Week 2 in Review

The second week of the season is in the books and the Basketball Gods saved the best for last. Let's get right to it!

With many of the biggest/best games of the week not happening until Sunday in women's hoops, I have been writing this post out of order while waiting for certain games to finish. Watching the Louisville Cardinals methodically choke the life out of the UConn Huskies on Sunday evening confirmed that this is the proper tact to take because before that game, Louisville was not in this spot. After demolishing 12-time national champions UConn, however, they are in this spot with a bullet!

The Cardinals started the week off with a dominant 36-point win over Lindenwood and then traveled to Ball State to complete their home-and-home from last year, on Thursday, and smoked their fellow red birds by 21. Finally, the mighty UConn Huskies trekked south to the KFC Yum! Center for a heavyweight clash on Sunday.

Playing in the birthplace of Muhammad Ali, only one team seemed to know when the bell rung. The Cardinals never trailed in their buzzer-to-buzzer victory and ended up beating UConn by 18 points. Junior guard Imari Berry scored a game-high 21, including the first 11 points of the fourth quarter to slam the door shut on any crazy talk of a "Huskies comeback," and added six boards and a steal. She averaged 16.0 ppg, 4.7 rpg, 3.3 apg, and 1.3 spg during Louisville's 3-0 week and shot a scorching 45.5% (10-of-22) from beyond the arc.

Zamareya Jones couldn't keep her name out of the play-by-play data, scoring 10 points, grabbing nine boards, dishing out five assists, and recording three steals AND three blocks versus UConn. Mackenly Randolph also had 10 points and nine rebounds, while Tajianna Roberts ruined the symmetry by scoring 11 points and adding eight rebounds.

This was a banner week for Louisville, which announced itself to the nation as the ACC favorite and a serious Final Four contender. If they go to Austin and beat the Longhorns on Dec. 2...the Hype Train for Jeff Walz's squad will be in danger of running on the tracks.

Honorable Mention: I also enjoyed what the Iowa Hawkeyes (crushed Northern Iowa; beat Vandy by 10) and Illinois State (beat Green Bay and went on the road to clobber Saint Louis to continue their undefeated start to the season).

Consistent excellence is not something to be taken for granted or overlooked when discussing prestigious weekly awards given out by a guy at his laptop. We should not become numb to Hannah Hidalgo's stat lines just because she can't stop recording 23+ points per game, double-digit steals, or nonchalant triple-doubles.

In Notre Dame's two games last week, the All-American guard averaged 27.0 ppg, 8.5 rpg, 6.0 apg, 3.0 spg, 1.0 bpg, and only 2.0 turnovers per game. The Fighting Irish scored 108 points in both wins and have only failed to break the century mark once this year, which was in their first game of the season when they scored a pathetic 99 against Villanova.

Hidalgo shot 13-of-14 at the rim last week, drained all 13 of her free throws, and made 33.3% of her threes (right at her career average FWIW) last week. She's a threat to score from anywhere on the court the moment she steps off the bus, and she'll probably do it after stealing the ball from you. Keep your head on a swivel!

To round out the weekly starting five, here are four other players who hooped at a high level this week.

Britt Prince (Nebraska) had Kansas in hell on Saturday, scoring a career-high 35 points (12-of-18 FG, 2-of-6 3P, 9-of-9 FT) and also adding two rebounds, two assists, and two steals. Her other game last week only resulted in a 24 point, three rebound, two assist, three steal, and one block performance. The Huskers are 4-0 and Prince is the engine powering Big Red forward.

You wanna see a crazy stat line? I'm going to show you a crazy stat line. Freshman Jessica Dimaro (Virginia Tech) was having a nice start to her collegiate career and then the Hokies traveled to VCU for a game and she lost her damn mind. In an 11-point victory, she went for 23 points, 24 rebounds (17 offensive!!!), and two blocks. The total rebounds and offensive rebounds were both program records, while just the total rebound mark was the second-best in ACC history. She followed it up with a 14-and-16 outing (another two blocks as well) on Sunday.

Despite suffering an upset loss to Tulsa (see below) Liv McGill (Oklahoma State) had an excellent week of hoops. She averaged 23.3 ppg, 4.7 rpg, 7.7 apg, and 2.7 spg to move the Cowgirls to 4-1 on the campaign.

All-Big East guard Jasmine Bascoe (Villanova) averaged 23.0 ppg, 4.0 rpg, 4.7 apg, and 3.7 spg in three games last week, helping the Wildcats to a 2-1 record with wins over Merrimack and at Fairfield.

One quick bonus shoutout to Neso Anisiobi (Little Rock), the rarely seen 5-foot-11 forward who hasn't shot a three all season and almost beat North Florida by herself on Thursday with the stat line of 26 points, 14 rebounds, two assists, and five steals.

Weekly Triple-Double Watch: Oklahoma's Sahara Williams went for 21 points, 10 rebounds, and 10 assists with a side of five steals in OU's win over Oral Roberts.

It doesn't always happen, but when The Game of the Century (of the Week) lives up to the hype, it is a treat. No. 1 South Carolina and No. 3 Southern California battled in Greenville, S.C. for the title of "The Real SC" and after four quarters of basically professional basketball, Dawn Staley's Gamecocks claimed the crown by four points, 89-85.

Tessa Johnson (28) and Joyce Edwards (20) each scored over 20 points for South Carolina and JuJu Watkins (25 points, two rebounds, two steals, two blocks) and Kennedy Smith (15 points, five rebounds, five assists) led the way for the Trojans. However, the biggest play of the game came from Jordan Lee with a little assist from Hudson Jacobs.

After Lee made an incredible chase-down block on Watkins with 15 seconds left and the Gamecocks up two points, the refs blew the whistle after Lee's block went out of bounds. Trojans ball. But Jacobs, South Carolina's long-time video coordinator, told Staley to challenge the call because he thought Watkins was actually the last one to touch the ball.

He was right. The Gamecocks got the ball, safely inbounded it, and Johnson made two free throws to seal the deal. You should read the AP's story on how Jacobs almost didn't even make it to the game, because it's a good one.

We as basketball fans can only hope that this is the first matchup between these two teams this year and that Watkins, Smith, Jazzy Davidson, Saniyah Hall, and co. get another crack at "The Real SC" in March.

Honorable Mention: Memphis' 20-point comeback win over Alabama and Fairfield's win at Seton Hall

The state of Oklahoma has a wealth of talent in women's basketball and not just at the power conference level, where OU and Oklahoma State both entered this week ranked in the top-20. After three straight blowouts at home, though, Jacie Hoyt's squad's first road trip of the season proved to be far more challenging. A mere 63 miles away, the Tulsa Golden Hurricane awaited.

After a pair of made free throws by Audi Crooks gave OSU a two-point lead with 8:50 left in the first quarter, the Cowgirls didn't have another lead until there was 5:10 left in the third quarter. Tulsa held a four-point advantage at halftime on the No. 19 team in the nation but entered the final frame down three. There were nine lead changes and a dozen ties in this game and neither team held a lead greater than six points during regulation.

Oklahoma State leading scorer Mady Cartwright made two free throws with 58 seconds left to tie things up and then both teams traded empty possessions before a bonus five minutes of hoops. The Golden Hurricane made a trio of three-pointers in a row to open OT, but Oklahoma State wasn't going down without a fight and eventually Crooks made a layup with 1:06 to go to tie things up again. After a tie-up with 38 seconds gave the ball to OSU underneath the basket, Alexa Kinas attempted a jumper from the baseline and OSU's Callin Hake just clipped her on the way up. Kinas made both free throws which proved to be the winning shots.

OSU had multiple chances (missed Liv McGill open three, missed Stailee Heard jumper in the paint, bad pass from McGill to Crooks on an inbounds with three seconds left) but Tulsa's defense stood tall. Alisha Peavy ended the game with a double-double (12 points/11 boards) and three blocks and Dora Toman added 10 points, seven rebounds, six assists, three steals, and two blocks.

Oh yeah, this was the first win over a ranked opponent in Tulsa women's basketball history! That definitely qualifies as "upset of the week" material.

Honorable Mention: Grand Canyon took down Oregon and USF beat in-state rivals Florida

#2634. Brewers bash champion Dodgers to brink of NLCS sweep; CBS Sports Preseason All-America team revealed

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2633. The Solar Report, Week 4: Phoenix shows progress while familiar roster concerns persist

Week four is in the books for the Phoenix Suns, and as I sit here contemplating what I learned this past week, it was more of a reminder that we all need to consume a healthy dose of settle-down juice early in the season, despite some of the concerns that have presented themselves. Those concerns might be entirely valid, but there's a reason they play 82 games. Over a large enough sample size, regression to the mean can occur, individual performances can stabilize, and the true identity of a basketball team can begin to reveal itself.

It was an interesting week given all the chatter surrounding Dejounte Murray and his potential arrival in Phoenix, which feels an awful lot like Klutch Sports agent Rich Paul attempting to orchestrate a landing spot for one of his clients. The connection makes sense. Paul has a relationship with Suns owner Mat Ishbia, and Phoenix already employs plenty of Klutch clients. While national reporters with connections to Paul, such as Chris Haynes, have indicated that the Suns have interest in Murray, local reporting has suggested otherwise.

It's a dangerous game in and of itself, and one of the lessons we were reminded of this week is that being disappointed in a player's performance, as many of us have been with Jalen Green thus far, doesn't mean you ship him out of town the moment another player bats his eyes at you or his agent starts campaigning for a change of scenery. We've been through the eye-batting bullshit before with Bradley Beal. There's no reason to make another rash decision, particularly when it involves bringing in somebody whose attitude raises legitimate questions.

For all the challenges Green has encountered thus far this season, his attitude appears to remain intact. I'd much rather have that disposition in the building and exhaust the possibilities of making things work than bring in a player whose handling of his current situation raises concerns about how he might conduct himself in Phoenix when things inevitably become difficult.

Disappointment can, and perhaps should, lead to change. But change comes in many forms. It doesn't necessarily require a different jersey, a different locker room, or another transaction that fundamentally alters the composition of your basketball team. Sometimes it means a trip to the second unit, where a player can rediscover his confidence, find his rhythm, and settle into a role more conducive to his success. There are plenty of avenues worth exploring with Jalen Green before entertaining the idea of sending him elsewhere. We're four weeks into an 82-game season. Pass the settle-down juice.

Week four was supposed to be a get-right week for the Phoenix Suns, and ultimately, it was. They beat the teams they were supposed to beat and lost to the teams they were expected to lose to. But frustration persisted along the way, rooted in issues we've identified throughout the early stages of the season that are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. We'll get into those in greater depth below.

As far as overall production pertaining to restocks is concerned, week four was Khaman Maluach's worst of the season in that category. From my perspective, if you're generating somewhere around 16 restocks per 36 minutes, you're having a fairly impressive defensive impact relative to your time on the court. That isn't what we saw from Maluach this past week. He never eclipsed 14 restocks per 36 minutes, with his best performance coming during the limited action he saw against the Los Angeles Lakers on Sunday.

Truth be told, I think Maluach's situation is intertwined with why the Suns continue to suffer so mightily on the glass. The coaching staff simply doesn't appear to trust him enough to leave him on the court for extended stretches. During a week in which Phoenix encountered some sizable opponents, Maluach averaged only 17.8 minutes per game.

I can understand why certain aspects of his game haven't earned him more playing time, most notably his tentative hands and occasionally poor positioning. But he also possesses the highest rebounding percentage on the team at 15.3%. Considering rebounding has been the Suns' most glaring statistical deficiency this season, you'd think that would warrant a little more run.

I understand that he's 20 years old. I understand that development requires patience, and I understand that this past week was his least productive in our restocks category. Now that we have a month's worth of data at our disposal, we're beginning to develop a clearer picture of how Maluach has performed this season. Inconsistent is probably the most appropriate adjective, and a weekly average of 10.6 restocks per 36 minutes doesn't necessarily inspire a great deal of confidence.

Perhaps fatigue is a factor. Perhaps it's a lack of connectivity with his teammates or the constantly evolving nature of his role within the rotation. Given the inconsistencies we've witnessed throughout the lineup, my hope is that Maluach's opportunities begin to stabilize, providing him with a greater sense of what is expected of him on a nightly basis.

Growth requires repetition, and for a team desperately searching for answers on the glass, there's certainly an incentive to invest in that growth.

Yeah, the starting five doesn't work. Of the 16 five-man lineups across the NBA that have played at least 80 minutes together this season, the Suns' starting unit ranks dead last in plus/minus, dead last in net rating, and fourth worst in rebounding percentage.

We can spend plenty of time dissecting the why, but that's the what. And the what is downright pitiful.

No rest for the weary, as the Phoenix Suns are right back at it tonight in Denver to take on a Nuggets team that defeated them 127–120 in their final game of October. Denver enters the matchup with a 7–4 record, good for the seventh seed in the Western Conference, and a victory could go a long way in helping the Suns establish some positive momentum.

Why? Because the road doesn't get any shorter from there. Phoenix travels to Sacramento on Wednesday before heading to Utah on Friday to complete its week five slate of games, a three-game road trip that will provide another opportunity for this team to find its footing.

That's it for this week, Bright Siders. Stay frosty.

#2631. Alcaraz dominates Tiafoe in ATP Finals opener and extends winning streak to 10 matches

TURIN, Italy (AP) — Facing a player who had pushed him to five sets in their previous two meetings, Carlos Alcaraz made sure not to get into an extended battle with Frances Tiafoe this time.

The third-ranked Alcaraz kept up his strong end-of-the season form with a dominant 6-2, 6-2 victory over Tiafoe in his opening match at the ATP Finals on Monday.

Alcaraz had tape around right knee but showed no signs of discomfort as he raced all over the court in a commanding display to extend his winning streak to 10 matches.

Alcaraz finished off the first set in a mere 28 minutes after racing out to a 4-0 lead and also broke early in the second.

Alcaraz is aiming for his third straight title indoors after lifting trophies in Vienna and Paris. He's also aiming to claim the title at Finals for the first time after losing last year's championship match in Turin to Jannik Sinner.

Sinner, the two-time defending champion at the ATP Finals, ended his season early due to a right knee injury.

Alcaraz required five sets to beat Tiafoe in the 2022 U.S. Open semifinals and the third round of Wimbledon in 2024. He went on to claim the title after both of those victories.

After shaking up his diet and training regimen, Tiafoe had the most consistent year of his career, reaching the U.S. Open semifinals for a third time, and is now making his Finals debut at age 28.

Later in the same group, home player Flavio Cobolli — also in his Finals debut — faces Daniil Medvedev, the 2020 champion.

Alexander Zverev and Ben Shelton won their opening matches in the other group on Sunday.

The top two finishers in each round-robin group advance to the semifinals of the season-ending event for the year's top eight players.

#2629. Turns out, four paid subscriptions aren’t enough to watch live NBA games

I would love to be able to share things I saw from last night's game between the Wizards and Rockets. Unfortunately, the NBA's local blackout rules prevented me from watching despite me having active subscriptions for NBA League Pass, Amazon Prime, Peacock, and ESPN.

Four streaming services, and I would have needed to shell out another $21.64 to watch this game. This is dumb. I've been a die-hard fan for multiple decades. I live 1,200 miles from the team I follow, and I pay for four streaming services that carry NBA games (including League Pass!). And I still couldn't watch last night's game.

NBA Commissioner Adam Silver thinks we're all wasting time watching the actual games. Apparently, we should just wait for highlights. | NBAE via Getty Images

My experience fits neatly into Adam Silver's aggressively dumb comments last year, part of which included the gem that the league he leads is a "highlight" sport. Hey fans, says the NBA Commissioner, you don't need to watch the games. Just catch what other people thought was good on ESPN or YouTube.

At last for me, that doesn't work. Nor does waiting 72 hours to watch a game. I watch large chunks of more than 200 games a year during the regular season, and then dozens more in the postseason. Even when I'm not watching to write about the Wizards, I enjoy the actual games. That's because basketball is way more interesting than the highlights. I mean, I love the highlights too, but I appreciate the tactical battle that develops over the course of the full game.

I'm talking the individual matchups, as well as the game plans, sets and systems, counters, adjustments, counter-adjustments. Sure, the finishing dunk at a key moment is awesome. What's really cool is seeing how it builds from a superbly designed play the team's been setting up for weeks by doing the same thing in the same situation for two weeks — to put the action on film, to get the opponent to think one thing is coming, and then to hit them with something different.

It's great to see the offensive system work…and then not work and see a couple smart teammates improvise something that gets a decent look with the shot clock running down. It's even fun to see clever play work perfectly and have the shooter miss.

Heck, I love the weird and quirky stuff that comes from League Pass Premium — when the national anthem just lands, when that halftime entertainment that sounds impossibly stupid turns out to be impossibly entertaining, when the hype crew looks like they dressed in the dark from a grab bag of team fan gear, and leftover costumes from Wicked.

But, not last night. Because with revenues north of $14 billion, and profits literally guaranteed because of how the collective bargaining agreement and TV deal is constructed, the NBA's gotta wring just a little more money out of fans.

Sure, they want to protect local broadcasting and streaming. Thing is, that can be done easily — it would just take a little thought and some programming. With AI, the programming would probably take a few minutes. And fans would never feel it. Because the NBA and their broadcast partners know when someone like me watches a Rockets game on League Pass. It's all streamed, and they can track on an incredibly granular level. It would be trivial to develop an algorithm to shift the dollar or two or three generated by me watching a game on League Pass to the local broadcaster. Especially since I'd be WATCHING THE LOCAL BROADCAST.

This may be a strange concept for the billionaires running the NBA, but it's good to think of your fans and their experience now and then. Especially a fan die hard enough to watch virtually every game played over the past 40 years by the Washington F. Wizards — a practice that continued even when I moved 1,200 miles away.

I wrote the preceding during the first quarter. Naturally, this being the Wizards, they went full #SoWizards and thoroughly undermined my point. I'm expecting a call from Adam Silver any minute saying the league actually did me a favor. Because, ugh.

What a debacle this season is becoming. The Wizards lost their seventh straight game and dropped to 4-10. The final score was 147-119 — a 28-point drubbing. The game was out of reach by halftime. Sure, the Rockets are among the league's better teams, but the Wizards were supposed to be competing this season. And the indicators 14 games into the season say they're still among the NBA's worst teams.

The Wizards had some achievements. Like, Trae Young went scoreless in a game for the first time in his NBA career. He did have three turnovers, though. Washington let the Rockets post a 66.1% effective field goal percentage, and rebound 42.5% of their misses. They also gave Houston 34 free throws. All that tallied to a staggering 147 offensive rating for the Rockets. League average so far this season is about 114.

Below are the four factors that decide wins and losses in basketball — shooting (efg), rebounding (offensive rebounds), ball handling (turnovers), fouling (free throws made).

eFG% (effective field goal percentage, which accounts for the three-point shot)

TOV% (turnover percentage — turnovers divided by possessions)

FTM/FGA (free throws made divided by field goal attempts)

PPA is my overall production metric, which credits players for things they do that help a team win (scoring, rebounding, playmaking, defending) and dings them for things that hurt (missed shots, turnovers, bad defense, fouls).

PPA is a per possession metric designed for larger data sets. In small sample sizes, the numbers can get weird. In PPA, 100 is average, higher is better and replacement level is 45. For a single game, replacement level isn't much use, and I reiterate the caution about small samples sometimes producing weird results.

POSS is the number of possessions each player was on the floor in this game.

ORTG = offensive rating, which is points produced per individual possessions x 100. League average so far this season is listed in the Four Factors table above. Points produced is not the same as points scored. It includes the value of assists and offensive rebounds, as well as sharing credit when receiving an assist.

USG = offensive usage rate. Average is 20%. Median last season was 17.7%.

ORTG and USG are versions of stats created by former Wizards assistant coach Dean Oliver and modified by me. ORTG is an efficiency measure that accounts for the value of shooting, offensive rebounds, assists and turnovers. USG includes shooting from the floor and free throw line, offensive rebounds, assists and turnovers.

+PTS = "Plus Points" is a measure of the points gained or lost by each player based on their efficiency in this game compared to league average efficiency on the same number of possessions. A player with an offensive rating (points produced per possession x 100) of 100 who uses 20 possessions would produce 20 points. If the league average efficiency is 115, the league — on average — would produced 23.0 points in the same 20 possessions. So, the player in this hypothetical would have a +PTS score of -3.0.

Players are sorted by total production in the game.

#2622. AC Milan prepare sensational €60m bid for Real Madrid's Endrick but Jose Mourinho builds a wall

AC Milan have emerged as serious contenders for Real Madrid prodigy Endrick, readying a substantial financial package to lure the Brazilian to the San Siro. However, the Rossoneri face a significant obstacle in the form of Jose Mourinho, who has no intention of sanctioning the departure of his young attacker.

Milan are preparing to test Madrid's resolve with a lucrative proposal for Brazilian wonderkid Endrick. The Italian giants are reportedly willing to offer a base fee of €60 million, which could eventually rise to €70 million through various performance-related bonuses. According to reports from Corriere dello Sport, to make the deal more palatable for the Spanish champions, Milan are also prepared to include an €80 million buy-back clause, allowing the La Liga side to reclaim the forward in the future.

Despite the significant financial commitment, the deal hinges on the approval of the coaching staff at the Santiago Bernabeu. While Florentino Perez may be tempted by such a structured offer for a player with limited minutes, the final decision likely rests with the man in the dugout. The Rossoneri hope that the inclusion of the buy-back option proves their willingness to act as a stepping stone for the player's development while providing Madrid with long-term security.

The primary hurdle for the Milanese leadership remains the steadfast stance of Mourinho. The former Chelsea and Inter boss has reportedly "built a wall" around the Brazilian, viewing him as a technical investment that will yield massive returns for Madrid in the coming seasons. Mourinho believes that the depth of the squad and the density of the fixture list will eventually provide the youngster with the opportunities he needs to shine in Spain.

This firm rejection has also affected other potential suitors in Serie A. Roma have also been monitoring the situation, primarily exploring the possibility of a loan deal to bolster their attacking options under the guidance of sporting director Mauro D'Amico. However, the message from the Spanish capital has been consistent: the player is not for sale, and he will not be leaving on loan, as the manager expects him to play a part in the club's trophy pursuit.

If Milan are to break through this resistance, they may rely on high-level corporate synergy rather than traditional negotiations. The club recently appointed Brett Yormark as the CEO of Milan Sports & Entertainment. Intriguingly, Brett is the twin brother of Michael Yormark, who serves as the president of Roc Nation Sports International, the agency that manages Endrick's professional interests. This family connection could provide Milan with a unique advantage in reaching the player's inner circle.

Furthermore, RedBird owner Gerry Cardinale maintains a long-standing professional relationship with Roc Nation, the entertainment company founded by Jay-Z. These ties between the Milan hierarchy and the player's representatives could be the "hidden card" that allows the Rossoneri to keep the dialogue open, even when the Madrid coaching staff remains publicly opposed to a move. The hope is that these off-field relationships can eventually sway the player's camp toward a move to Italy.

Milan's interest in the Brazilian comes at a time when the club is looking to add elite quality to its frontline. While other targets like Tommaso Tresoldi have been linked with a move to the San Siro, the pressing of Milan for the Madrid star remains the most ambitious play of the current regime. The club is clearly looking for a marquee signing to ignite their title charge and secure a long-term successor for their aging strikers.

The saga is expected to intensify as the January transfer window approaches. While Mourinho's current position is one of total closure, the pressure of a €70 million total package and the influence of Roc Nation could yet alter the landscape. For now, the Brazilian remains in Madrid, but Milan have made it clear they are willing to do whatever it takes to bring one of football's brightest young talents to the San Siro this winter.

#2619. Lions star Aidan Hutchinson out for season with knee injury: Report

The Detroit Lions are now down their best defensive player.

Edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson is reportedly out for the season after "what initial tests showed to be a torn ACL in his right knee," according to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport. Rapoport also reports there is concern about Hutchinson's meniscus.

Hutchinson hurt his knee celebrating a sack of New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye in the first quarter of their 35-10 win over the Patriots on Nov. 15, 2026.

He was eventually ruled as out and didn't return to the game.

At the time of his injury, Hutchinson led the Lions with six sacks on the season and has played like one of the NFL's best edge rushers. He signed a four year, $180 million contract extension in 2025 that will keep him in Detroit through 2030.

This isn't the first time Hutchinson will miss significant time with a leg injury, however.

Hutchinson broke his left leg in October 2024 in a game against the Dallas Cowboys, with the Pro Bowl defender missing the final 12 games of the 2024 regular season. The Lions went 11-1 in those 12 games, finishing the regular season with a 15-2 record but losing to the Washington Commanders in the divisional round without Hutchinson (and several other key defenders) on the field.

The Lions pass rush still did well without Hutchinson in the game against the Patriots, recording four sacks (two from rookie Derrick Moore, one from Alim McNeill and another from D.J. Wonnum) as the defense held New England to just one touchdown. Moore will likely get more playing time in Hutchinson's absence.
