#2618. Parker Washington has been dynamic for Jaguars

If the NFL playoffs began right now, the Jacksonville Jaguars would host the Pittsburgh Steelers on Wild Card weekend.

As we noted during Week 9, the Jaguars should be considered among the league's elite teams. Jacksonville leads the NFL with a point differential of +125 (the San Francisco 49ers are second in the NFL with a differential of +85) and the Jaguars are in the top five in both Offensive and Defensive Expected Points Added per Play. Jacksonville has an Offensive EPA/Play of 0.125 (ranking them fourth behind San Francisco, Cincinnati, and Buffalo) and a Defensive EPA/Play of -0.103 (ranking them fourth behind Minnesota, Tampa Bay, and the Los Angeles Rams).

They are the only team in the top five in both categories.

General manager James Gladstone made some aggressive moves ahead of the trade deadline including adding safety Jessie Bates III and defensive tackle Jordan Davis, but another key player for the Jaguars right now is wide receiver Parker Washington. Washington has grown into a reliable target for quarterback Trevor Lawrence in the passing game, and enjoyed a career outing against the Tennessee Titans, catching seven passes for 152 yards and a touchdown, as Jacksonville improved to 7-2 with a 40-23 win.

And Washington delivered some highlight-reel moments in the process.

His first catch of the game was actually his touchdown, which came on a slant route with the Jaguars knocking on the door of the end zone:

Washington's next reception came on a seam route, working against man coverage. Watch as he releases to the outside out of the left slot, avoids any jam from the defensive back, and makes a tough adjustment on a throw that is slightly behind him as well as high:

The receiver also showed his skills working along the sideline. ON this completion from late in the first quarter, Washington runs a deep out pattern. Lawrence makes this throw with pristine timing and anticipation, but the adjustment and body control Washington displays as he pulls the throw in and gets both feet down, are elite:

Then came this corner route late in the first half. Working against a two-deep coverage, Lawrence targets Washington on the corner route, squeezing in a throw between the half-field safety and the cornerback sinking under the deep route. While the Titans do what they can to try and take this route away, Washington simply wins at the catch point:

And yes, I have Gus Johnson saying "he goes up and … gets it" in my head every time I watch this clip.

But the play from Washington that had all of social media buzzing — and likely sent shivers down the spine of every defensive back in the league — was this catch early in the second quarter. Watch how Washington, working out of the left slot, puts Alontae Taylor in the spin cycle:

Now, I try and avoid "screenshot scouting" as much as possible but I have to ask: Is this good?

Washington initially starts by working across the field, and then takes a step vertically to flash a move to the outside. Taylor bites on that outside move and breaks toward the sideline, just as Washington continues across the field on his crossing route. This short throw, covering just six yards from the line of scrimmage to the catch point, ends up as a 50-yard gain.

Washington finished the game having caught seven passes for 152 yards — again, a career-high mark — and the touchdown.

Jacksonville's emergence as one of the AFC's elite teams is a huge storyline this season.

And Washington's emergence as a trusted target for Lawrence is a big part of that story.

#2617. Connor Hellebuyck trade: Jets send star goalie to the Devils in exchange for four players, two draft picks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Connor Hellebuyck is a now a Devil. The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B

#2616. Jahmyr or JSN: Who's the Offensive Player of the Year in the NFL this season?

Imagine you're an offensive coordinator in the NFL. And, as long as we're in the world of make-believe, imagine you have both Jahmyr Gibbs and Jaxon Smith-Njigba on your roster. And imagine you have exactly one play to get into the end zone.

Do you go with the running back who can stomp upstream through rush-hour traffic? Or do you go with the receiver who can create space in a mosh pit? Ground game or air game? Who's your favorite for NFL Offensive Player of the Year?

Sunday served as center stage for both Gibbs and Smith-Njigba, half a world apart. Before half the United States had even woken up, Gibbs began a methodical demolition of New England in Munich, rushing for 153 yards and two touchdowns and receiving another 99 through the air as Detroit won 35-10. A few hours later, Smith-Njigba caught eight passes for 171 yards, including a 71-yard beast of a touchdown, as Seattle outlasted Las Vegas 21-13.

Through Week 10, both teams remain in the hunt for playoff berths, in large part because of the outsized, generational performances of their stars.

After three seasons in the backfield alongside David Montgomery as a Sonic-and-Knuckles duo, Gibbs is now a solo act; Detroit thought enough of his potential that the Lions dealt Montgomery to the Texans. Gibbs validated the Lions' trust in him; this season, he leads the NFL in (deep breath) attempts, yards, touchdowns, first downs, rushing yards per game, touches from scrimmage, yards from scrimmage and combined receiving and rushing touchdowns.

Just three-plus seasons into his career, Gibbs is already starting to carve his way into the NFL record books. He just passed Terrell Davis for the most touchdowns through the first four years of a career, with 62. And he joined a couple guys named Emmitt Smith and Barry Sanders as the only players to rush for 50 touchdowns before turning 25.

"I think we have to pinch ourselves sometimes and not take for granted how special he is," Lions quarterback Jared Goff said after Sunday's victory. "He's just so explosive with the ball in his hands. I throw a check-down to him, and he goes for 50 yards. That's so rare for a guy to be able to do all the things he does."

Here, from Sunday, is a perfect encapsulation of everything Gibbs brings to the field: speed, power and a relentless drive into the end zone.

Also in his fourth year, Smith-Njigba is both a defending Super Bowl champion and the defending Offensive Player of the Year. While Seattle is struggling to defend its title, Smith-Njigba is authoring a brilliant sequel to his 2025. He currently leads the league in (another deep breath) receptions, receiving yards, receiving touchdowns, receiving first downs, longest reception, receiving yards per game and yards per touch from scrimmage.

His performance Sunday against the Raiders was nothing short of exceptional. He totaled 144 yards in a decisive third quarter, including that magnificent 71-yard touchdown … that came after he lost his footing starting his route.

"The thing that stuck out today was he's making [plays] in all phases of the game," Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald said after Sunday's game. "On the extended plays, he's able to uncover and go become a target for our quarterback as well. So it's really in every stage of how we're playing offense. So it's pretty remarkable. He's a beast."

The most impressive fact about Smith-Njigba's dominance is that everyone on the other side of the ball knows it's coming … and they still can't stop it. Seattle doesn't have any other true receiving threats on the roster; Cooper Kupp, the Seahawks' second-leading receiver, is nearly a thousand yards behind JSN's current total of 1,207.

The Offensive Player of the Year award now tends to reward non-quarterback skill players; the last QB to win was Patrick Mahomes in 2018. It's also an award with a wide pool of candidates; the last repeat winner was Marshall Faulk, who won the award three straight times from 1999 to 2001.

Back to the question at the top: You're that offensive coordinator blessed with more talent than any team should have. So who would you choose to score that one-play touchdown, Jahmyr Gibbs or Jaxon Smith-Njigba?

#2614. Ex-scout: Kevin O'Connell 'hated' J.J. McCarthy and pushed Giants trade

New York Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy produced the best statistical game of his young NFL career on Thursday night, completing 23 of 36 passes for 293 yards with a touchdown and an interception during a Week 10 loss to the Washington Commanders.

The outing led former NFL scout John Middlekauff to revisit the circumstances of McCarthy's September trade from Minnesota.

On his 3 and Out podcast, Middlekauff contended that Vikings head coach Kevin O'Connell disliked the quarterback and played a central role in moving him.

"If you're a Vikings fan watching that game, you have to be asking yourself -- and I'm not trying to play Monday morning quarterback -- it's just a reality. The move was made because he didn't play well and the coach hated him," Middlekauff said. "And if I wanted to speak for you in regard to J.J. McCarthy, you hated his guts as a player. You couldn't [expletive] stand him."

Middlekauff described the coach as the driving force behind demoting McCarthy to third string and supporting the trade, paraphrasing the internal view as "We gotta get this guy out of here. Fifth-round pick, I'll drive him to the airport."

He noted that coach-quarterback friction of this kind has occurred before and will again.

Middlekauff then contrasted McCarthy's recent work for the Giants under Matt Nagy and Greg Roman with the Vikings' quarterback situation afterward, observing that New York's version has looked better than what Minnesota fielded.

Selected 10th overall in 2024, McCarthy missed his entire rookie season with a torn meniscus. As a starter in 2025, he threw for 1,632 yards with 11 touchdowns and 12 interceptions while going 6-4 before losing his starting job and sliding down the depth chart. With the Giants, he has 915 passing yards on 63.5 percent completion with two touchdowns and two interceptions.

The comments raise fresh questions about O'Connell's handling of the former first-round pick as McCarthy continues to show signs of progress elsewhere.

#2613. MLB rumors: Tarik Skubal's market already hot, contenders eyeing Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is a bit more than a week old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. We've ranked the top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and built you a calendar of the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Friday's hot stove happenings.

The market for two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, far and away the offseason's best free agent, is already hot, according to the New York Post. Skubal is expected to sign in November, before the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, though a deal is not imminent. Talks are underway, however, and his market is moving.

Skubal is expected to sign a record contract at least in total value, and possibly in average annual value. Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million deal with the Dodgers is the largest pitching contract ever given out. Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander's matching $43.3 million salaries with the Mets years ago set the record for the average annual value for a pitcher.

The Dodgers, Mets, Padres, Phillies, and Yankees are among the teams linked to Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato, reports the New York Post. Unless MLB and the MLBPA unexpectedly avoid a lockout, Sato must sign before the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. Otherwise, he will return to the Hanshin Tigers for 2027.

We ranked Sato as the fourth-best free agent available this offseason, and the best available position player. He has significant power but also swing-and-miss and defensive concerns at third base, similar to Munetaka Murakami a year ago. Murakami slugged 35 home runs in only 127 games as a rookie this season, providing proof of concept for Sato.

The Nationals have signed center fielder Jacob Young to a four-year extension, reports FanSided. The deal is worth $23 million and includes an $8 million club option for a fifth year. The extension buys out Young's three arbitration years and one free agent year, with a club option for a second free agent year. He's now under Washington's control through 2031.

Young, 27, has always been a superlative defender. He unlocked a new level on offense this season, particularly in the second half, when he hit .301 with a .385 on-base percentage. Young had been speculated as a trade candidate since last offseason, but the new extension locks him in as part of Washington's long-term core.

#2611. Five under-the-radar MLB free agents who could make a big impact next season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is a little more than a week old now and we're still waiting for the first big trade or free agent signing. That isn't unusual, though. The hot stove, like the regular season, is a marathon, not a sprint. A lockout is expected when the collective bargaining agreement ends at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, and there should be a flurry of activity before then.

We ranked the offseason's top 50 free agents, and although it is not a great class, there are dozens of quality players available. You just have to know where to look. Here now are five players who did not rank among our top 50 free agents, but would nonetheless be good options and solid pickups for teams that want to raise their floor and improve their supporting cast.

It was a tale of two seasons for the 29-year-old Bryan Abreu, who had a 5.81 ERA before the All-Star break and a 1.71 ERA after. The under-the-hood estimators, like FIP and xERA, were better in the second half as well, though Abreu lost close to 2 mph off his fastball this year and, not coincidentally, a whole bunch of swings and misses. Abreu is third in appearances and second in innings among relievers since 2022 and it's possible the workload is catching up to him. There's still enough bat-missing ability and late-inning experience here for Abreu to contribute to a contender's bullpen. It just might happen as a seventh-inning guy moving forward, not as the Moment of Truth™ reliever who pitches in the game's biggest moments.

If you're looking for a bottom of the order guy who will take walks and give you 10-15 home runs, that's J.P. Crawford. His defense, specifically his range and arm, has slipped so much in his early 30s that he's no longer a viable shortstop, though he played 33 games at third base this past season. I like him better at second base, but third base works too. Crawford gets on-base at a decent clip and won't strike out excessively, plus he's long been regarded as an excellent teammate and grade-A clubhouse guy. It seems like his time with the Mariners is over and it's for the best. Crawford can go elsewhere, play a new position, and just be part of the lineup rather than one of the faces of the franchise.

Due to injury and ineffectiveness, it looked like Sean Newcomb was on his way out of baseball two years ago. He then reinvented himself as a sinker/curveball guy and carved out a nice second phase to his career as a workhorse utility reliever who won't beat himself with walks (an early career bugaboo) and will limit hard contact in the air. Newcomb, 33, worked at least 90 innings the last two seasons while pitching in every possible role. He closed out games, worked high leverage as a setup guy, soaked up innings in long relief, and opened a few times as well. Newcomb is likely miscast as a go-to bullpen option, though he can be a valuable third or fourth option for a contender. The utility reliever is all the rage these days and Newcomb fits the profile to a T.

Now 35, Emilio Pagán was sensational after returning from a hamstring injury in July, pitching to a 1.88 ERA with 34 strikeouts and only five walks in his final 28 ⅔ innings. The downside is the same as it's always been: Pagán is exceptionally home run prone (career 1.51 HR/9), which is a bad trait for a late-inning reliever who pitches almost exclusively in close games. His fastball remains firm, though, and his splitter is an elite swing-and-miss pitch that allows him to neutralize righties and lefties. As long as you're willing to live with the home run risk, Pagán remains a capable high-leverage reliever, one who is not out of place pitching important innings for a contending team.

Platoon DHs are not the hottest commodity, but Joc Pederson fills the role about as well as anyone in the game. He's a left-handed hitter, so he's on the heavy side of the platoon, and he authored a .245/.338/.496 line with terrific ball-tracking data (exit velocity, etc.) against righties. If you must play him in the field, Pederson can stand in right field or at first base for about six innings before being subbed out for a defensive replacement. He's essentially a bat-only player, though. Pederson will turn 35 in April and he's still a powerful and productive hitter against righties and an elite clubhouse vibes dude.

#2607. Giannis Antetokounmpo stunned by Doc Rivers' 'bitterness and pettiness' after former coach's criticism

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Miami Heat have gotten off to a slow start to Giannis Antetokounmpo's first season in south Florida, which has led to plenty of discussion about Antetokounmpo's fit with Bam Adebayo and the challenges of building around Giannis.

Among those to chime in on the topic is Antetokounmpo's former coach, Doc Rivers, who struggled to get the most out of the star in Milwaukee and never got Antetokounmpo and Damian Lillard on the same page. Rivers recently offered some critiques of Antetokounmpo, noting he's a difficult star to coach because of his play style and a defiance about changing how he plays.

On Sunday, after the Heat beat the Kings, Antetokounmpo was taken aback when asked about the comments by his former coach.

"You have his number, right? You do. I know you do. You gotta go ask him why he thought that; that's on him," Antetokounmpo told The Athletic. "That's not on me. I gotta focus on my team and what I gotta do and how can I be better and how can I help the team. But like, goddamn. That's crazy. Never let bitterness and pettiness get in front of your goals and dreams, man. For every athlete out there, never let that [happen]. That's insane, but you gotta go ask him why he said what he said. Not me."

Rivers' tenure in Milwaukee was a disaster: he took over for Adrian Griffin in the middle of the 2023-24 season with the Bucks 30-13 and proceeded to go 97-103 in his three years with the Bucks. Given Rivers' history of shifting blame, Antetokounmpo can more easily brush aside his critique as Doc once again finding someone else to blame for his team's shortcomings.

However, while Rivers might not be an infallible messenger, he did have some interesting comments about the challenge of coaching Antetokounmpo this week on The Bill Simmons Podcast.

"He has this great passing ability, but he doesn't necessarily have super IQ at the same time," Rivers said. "It's really a strange thing. And he really has one way. Downhill, forceful. Every play, he wants to force it.

"There's times where I wish he'd do one thing. I wish he'd learn how to execute better," Rivers added. "He's one of those guys, you get a lot of them from the U.S., AAU guys, who have never needed to execute, because they can do it on their own. That doesn't help the team."

It's not surprising that Antetokounmpo would balk at those comments, but viewing from the outside, there certainly seems to be validity to at least some of what Rivers says. Questioning a player's IQ will always understandably irk them, but watching Antetokounmpo play with Lillard and now Adebayo, the criticism of him wanting to attack downhill and not adjusting his play style has been apparent for some time.

What might help the Heat the most here is that, for as stubborn as Antetokounmpo can be, he is also fueled by a desire to prove people wrong. While Rivers may have been unable to get Antetokounmpo to buy into changing his style while playing for him, criticizing the former MVP might lead Giannis to show he can adapt his style purely out of spite.

#2605. MLB free agency: Six international players to know for the 2026-27 offseason

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Major League Baseball's free agency period opened earlier this week and teams are now clear to pursue any roster upgrades they deem necessary. That includes players coming over from Japan's Nippon Professional Baseball league, South Korea's Korea Baseball Organization, and Taiwan's Chinese Professional Baseball League. Those are high-level leagues that have sent many impact players MLB's way over the years.

Look no farther than the Dodgers to see how important international talent can be to a club. The Dodgers employed four different former NPB and KBO players this past season, including two-way star Shohei Ohtani, ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and starter Roki Sasaki. Ohtani was signed as an MLB free agent, but the others went to the Dodgers through the posting system.

Per the posting agreement with MLB, posted NPB and CPBL players get a 45-day window to negotiate and sign with an MLB team. KBO players get a 30-day window. Players who do not sign during that posting window return to their previous team in NPB, CPBL, or KBO. The MLB team that signs a posted player pays a fee to the player's former NPB, CPBL, or KBO team.

$5M plus 17.5% of contract value over $25M

$9.375M plus 15% of contract value over $50M

For example, the White Sox paid Munetaka Murakami's former team, the Yakult Swallows, a $6.575 million posting fee on his $34 million contract last offseason. That's $5 million on the first $25 million plus 17.5% of the remaining $9 million, which is $1.575 million. The $5 million plus $1.575 million equals the $6.575 million posting fee paid to the Swallows.

Unlike last lockout, MLB will not be pausing the signing window during the expected lockout, according to The Athletic. In other words, if owners lock players out on Dec. 1 as expected, that date will essentially serve as the same deadline for already posted NPB players unless the lockout ends before their 45-day window expires.

There are no superstar-caliber players like Ohtani or Yamamoto available in this winter's international free agent crop. There are, however, several interesting players who can improve an MLB roster in 2027. Here are the six best NPB, CPBL, and KBO players to know this offseason.

Japan's Triple Crown winner hit .306/.383/.609 with 39 home runs in 2026. He has a similar skill set to Murakami but is not exactly Murakami 2.0. He doesn't have quite as much power (but has plenty of it) and won't walk nearly as often, but he does swing and miss a bunch and is unlikely to remain at the hot corner long-term. Sato is a very aggressive hitter who ran a 66% contact rate this past season. That is below the 77% MLB average. The consensus seems to be that he will land at first base or in a corner outfield spot if not next year, then soon. Murakami successfully overcame his contact issues to slug 35 homers in only 127 games in 2026 around a hamstring injury. At minimum, that will have MLB teams reconsidering how they evaluate the Japan-to-MLB transition. Like Murakami, Sato carries risk, and like Murakami, his power makes that risk worth the dice roll. The Hanshin Tigers officially posted Sato on Nov. 1.

Listed at 5-foot-8, Taira gets outlier extension down the mound (close to seven feet despite his height), which creates a low release window. Hitters rarely see the ball come from where Taira releases it. He's not a gimmick pitcher either. Taira sits mid-90s with his four-seam fastball and backs it up with a cutter, sinker, sweeper, slider, changeup, and splitter. The sweeper and slider are distinct pitches, as are the changeup and splitter. The Seibu Lions used Taira as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, then started him in 2026, and he handled the assignment well. The breaking balls are just OK, and the fact of the matter is that pitchers this height don't often hold up under a starter's workload. I would assume the team that signs Taira will give him a chance to start. In the long run, though, he might be a reliever, perhaps even a multi-inning setup man. Taira was officially posted on Nov. 1.

A down 2026 season took some of the shine off Itoh, who won the 2025 Eiji Sawamura Award (Japan's Cy Young equivalent) after throwing 196 ⅔ innings with a 2.52 ERA. To be sure, Itoh pitched well in 2026 (3.18 ERA in 172 ⅔ innings), but he was not as consistently dominant as in the past. The 5-foot-9 right-hander is a seven-pitch pitcher with a low-90s fastball and the usual array of secondary pitches (sinker, cutter, curveball, slider, sweeper, splitter), none of which stands out as a plus offering. Itoh has thrown at least 150 innings in each of the last six seasons. He's seen as a crafty back-end starter in MLB, or perhaps even a reliever (Itoh sat 96 mph out of the bullpen in the World Baseball Classic). The Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters posted Itoh on Nov. 1.

Roh has an unusual agreement with the Hanwha Eagles. He signed the richest deal in KBO history in February (11 years and roughly $23 million), and as part of the deal, the Eagles agreed to post him for MLB teams this offseason, and Roh agreed to return to the Eagles to finish his career when his big-league stint is over. This past season, Roh, 26 in November, authored a .283/.360/.505 batting line with 29 home runs. He has real right-handed power and a good approach at the plate. There are concerns about his propensity to swing and miss as well as his arm at the hot corner. The Eagles formally posted Roh on Nov. 1.

The Seibu Lions posted Takahashi last offseason, but he was unable to find a contract to his liking, so he returned to Japan for another season and threw 148 innings with a 2.64 ERA. Takahashi, 30 in February, is an international free agent now, meaning he does not have to be posted and can instead negotiate at his own pace. More of a ground ball pitcher than a bat-misser, Takahashi sits in the 91-95 mph range with his fastball and has two good secondary pitches in his slider and splitter. He also throws a cutter and curveball. Takahashi is considered a potential innings guy for the back of an MLB rotation.

Tseng pitched for Chinese Taipei in the World Baseball Classic in 2023 and 2026 and he has been one of the CPBL's top relievers the last few years. In 2026, he saved 25 games with a 1.80 ERA and 65 strikeouts in 52 ⅓ innings. Tseng's fastball typically sits in the mid-90s and has run as high as 100 mph in the past, though it has been a few years. His go-to secondary pitch is a breaking ball that needs improvement for Tseng to carve out an MLB career as more than a middle reliever.

#2604. How Paul George is fittingly in perfectly (very) early in his Celtics tenure

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Paul George has been in the NBA since 2011. He's made nine All-Star appearances, six All-NBA Teams and four All-Defensive Teams, and scored nearly 20,000 points. But he knew that he would have to prove himself all over again in Boston after he arrived this summer in a blockbuster trade that sent Celtics icon and fan favorite Jaylen Brown to the Philadelphia 76ers.

"I understand my circumstances. I understand how huge JB was, not only for the organization, but here in the city. So, I didn't take it personal," George said at his introductory press conference, regarding the negative reaction to the trade. "To be honest, they should have a relationship, emotionally, to that trade. But my job is to kind of come into a great opportunity for me."

"It's a new group, a new opportunity," George continued. "I think they're getting someone that's ready to -- not fill the shoes or fill the void of JB -- but I think from a personal standpoint myself, I think I can come in and kind of still keep us in that contention. Give us a chance to win."

It's taken George just a few weeks to earn the trust of Celtics fans and show that he can still contribute to winning.

After pouring in 27 points in a 20-point win over the Milwaukee Bucks on Sunday, George is averaging 20.4 points, 5.2 rebounds, 4.1 assists and a career-high 2.3 steals, while shooting a career-high 42.5% from 3-point range for the 8-2 Celtics, who sit in second place in the Eastern Conference behind the 9-2 Sixers.

Those old rivals will meet Tuesday in a highly anticipated showdown that will be Brown and George's first games against their old teams.

"It'll be great to see those guys and compete against them finally," George said Sunday. "Obviously, Philly was a special place for me. It was a rough, you know, tenure, my two years there, but it'll be special to be in the building."

Ahead of George's return to Philadelphia, let's take a closer look at how he's shined so far in Boston:

"We have a superstar and that's [Jayson Tatum]," George said during his introductory press conference. "I'm not here to steal the shine or reinvent who I am. I'm here to help JT. He's the guy."

As great as Tatum and Brown were together, there was always some underlying tension over their place in the organization. Brown, who was named Eastern Conference Finals MVP and Finals MVP in 2024 when the Celtics won the title, saw himself as Tatum's equal. That was especially true after Brown led the Celtics to 56 wins last season while Tatum missed the majority of the campaign rehabbing from a torn Achilles.

Trading Brown for George established a clear hierarchy in the locker room. The Celtics are Tatum's team, and George is happy to play a supporting role. Celtics coach Joe Mazzulla praised George for being "very coachable, very open-minded" and setting a "very high" standard.

"The way we're asking him to play is maybe a little bit different than what he's been asked to do in the past. He enjoys that, he's open-minded to it and he just works at it. He's very hard on himself. Holds himself to a very high standard, constantly watching film, taking notes in his journal and just processing the game. He takes pride in learning and getting better and you're seeing the fruits of that," Mazzulla said Sunday.

George has always been a high-level 3-point shooter, but he's spent most of his career having to create looks for himself. In Boston, playing alongside Tatum in a system that prioritizes shooting and spacing, George has thrived as a high-volume catch-and-shoot threat.

He's shooting 46% on 5.6 catch-and-shoot 3-point attempts per game -- both marks are career-highs. George is tied for 10th in the league in catch-and-shoot 3-point attempts per game, and among the 16 players taking at least five such attempts, he's tied for second in percentage, behind only Steph Curry (54.9%).

Most efficient high-volume catch-and-shoot threats in 2026-27

By comparison, Brown has never shot 40% from 3-point range for a season in his career, and hasn't even shot above 40% on catch-and-shoot attempts since 2021. George's willingness to accept more of an off-ball role, and ability to knock down those shots at an extremely high rate, is a big reason why he's fit in so seamlessly in Boston.

George's five 3s against the Bucks on Sunday were all of the catch-and-shoot variety.

"Watching him shoot like that is unbelievable," Celtics big man Mitchell Robinson said Sunday. "Played against him quite a few times and to be on the same side of the ball with him and cheer him on instead of boo[ing him], it's great."

Overall, George is shooting 42.5% on a team-high 8.1 3-point attempts per game. His hot shooting is a big reason why the Celtics are sixth in the league in 3-point percentage (37.6%) even though Tatum (31.3%) and Derrick White (32.7%) have been ice cold to start the season.

George hasn't made an All-Defensive Team since 2019, when he finished third in Defensive Player of the Year voting with the Oklahoma City Thunder, in large part due to injuries. He remains an elite team defender, though, and will get back to the All-Defensive level this season if he stays healthy and keeps defending like he has through the first 10 games.

When asked about George on Sunday, Tatum singled out his new teammate's "super-high IQ" and "incredible defensive instincts."

George has been particularly impressive off the ball this season. He's wreaking havoc in the passing lanes with his length, timing and anticipation. George's 2.3 steals are a career-high and good for fourth in the league, and he's third in deflections per game with 5.1. Of the four players averaging at least five deflections per game, he is by far the oldest at 36.

George's effort is a big reason why the Celtics are forcing way more turnovers than they ever have under Mazzulla. Their opponent turnover rate is 17.4%, which ranks sixth in the league; in Mazzulla's first four seasons in charge, the Celtics never had an opponent turnover rate above 13.1% and never finished higher than 24th in the league in that category.

#2603. Nikita Kucherov trade request: Five potential landing spots for the reigning NHL MVP

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.
